<meta>This is the opening dedication page of the work, addressed to John Williams, Bishop of Lincoln and Lord Keeper of the Great Seal. It establishes the author's patronage relationship and sets a formal, laudatory tone common in 17th-century scholarly publications.</meta>

-> [Decorative headpiece with floral and cherub motifs] <-

# TO THE REVEREND FATHER AND LORD,

## LORD JOHN,
## MOST WORTHY BISHOP OF LINCOLN,
### MOST VIGILANT KEEPER OF THE <term>GREAT SEAL OF ENGLAND</term><note>The Great Seal was used to symbolize the Sovereign's approval of state documents; the Keeper was one of the highest-ranking officials in the kingdom.</note>, AND OF THE KING’S MAJESTY’S <note>original: "à Sanctioribus Consiliis"</note> PRIVY COUNCIL,

### MOST PRUDENT COUNSELOR.

**[Historiated initial 'N' depicting a figure seated at a desk]** **N**either the dignity of your eminent honor, nor the splendor of your title, place, or office—inasmuch as these things are momentary and are accustomed to last only by the pleasure of the Prince—nor your piety and humanity toward the poor who plead for justice, nor that unexpected public duty in affairs of state <note>This refers to his appointment as Lord Keeper, a role usually held by a lawyer, not a clergyman like Williams.</note> (fitting and agreeable for a man of this rank and dignity, as if he were the most certain pillar and support of the kingdom); nor, finally, that divine virtue of Justice, which is held in equilibrium by you, and is liberally dispensed with just scales to each according to their right (injury having been banished into exile) and distributed with a righteous measure: none, I say, of these gifts granted to you from heaven (**Most Reverend Father, most experienced Leader in the highest affairs**) is the occasion of this dedication of mine. For these qualities ought to be present (though it does not always happen so) in any excellent Chancellor, Keeper of the Great Seal, and protector, by virtue of his office in the sight of the Commonwealth.

But two virtues in particular, even closer to your heart and Nature, urge me and persuade me to now insist upon dedicating these my works and these my reflections—most dear to me and produced with much labor—to your Lordship and dignity above all others, and to freely and gladly bestow them upon you. The first of these, in order, is your nourishing charity toward the increase and exaltation of the sciences, and your voluntary and quite unforced love toward scholars. We can never sufficiently describe or explain this love, just as the sharp wit of the pen, resting on the wings of truth, records your happy deeds and actions for the memory of eternal posterity. This zeal of yours toward all men of letters [is shown by] its twin offspring, both of which already long ago...

<margin>):( 3</margin>

<summary>This page is a formal dedication to John Williams, the Bishop of Lincoln and Lord Keeper of the Great Seal, praising his judicial integrity and his role as a patron of scholars. The author argues that while Williams' political titles are impressive, his genuine love for the "exaltation of the sciences" is the true reason for this dedication.</summary>

*DEDICATORY EPISTLE*

...formerly bringing to light and celebrating characters <note>In this context, "characters" refers to the outward expressions or monuments of a person's inner virtues.</note> which, by nature and condition, are not at all different from one another. One of these has rendered that famous and renowned University of Cambridge richer in the tools of study and science, more adorned with magnificent buildings, and more pleasing and accessible to those eager for learning. Moreover, there is 그hat magnificent sanctuary of chosen books, a grand architectural work destined for the use of a Library—a gift pleasing to all literate men, providing ample utility to any seeker, and abundantly pouring forth (rather than withholding) a sort of sweet milk from the breasts of Minerva <note>original: "ex Mineruae vberibus"; Minerva was the Roman goddess of wisdom. Fludd uses the metaphor of a nursing mother to describe the life-giving nature of knowledge.</note> for the thirsty, liberally showering them with it. 

The other offspring or "character" of your fruitful charity is that outstanding Library in the monastery among the Londoners, most famous for the monuments and tombs of Kings, called Westminster. This was erected at no small expense to your Dignity and furnished and adorned with every necessary refinement, especially with rare books of the highest estimation. This library is celebrated and heralded throughout almost all of Britain, both for the beauty of its structure and arrangement and for the excellence of the books contained within it. It serves to depict and engrave the praises of its illustrious founder and patron upon the eternal monuments of fame more and more each day. Thus, it is clearly declared by this sweet and voluntary goodness of yours that your Honor and Dignity were born not for yourself alone, but for others, being inclined and devoted to doing good by a natural disposition of the soul.

Finally, there is a subsequent order and a reason closer to me, by which a cautious respect has led me and mature consideration has urged me to celebrate your name and honor through this dedication of my works. This is that close proximity of our spirits and the firm bond of blood relation <note>original: "consanguinitate nexus." Fludd is claiming a familial or ancestral connection to his patron.</note> by virtue of which bodies otherwise separate are nonetheless joined, bound, and united by the firmest chains and by a certain "magnetic glue of nature," as it were <note>original: "magnetico quodā quasi naturæ glutine." Fludd was a proponent of "Hermetic" philosophy and often used the idea of magnetism to explain spiritual attractions and the underlying unity of the world.</note>. 

Therefore, since these things are offered to your Lordship and Dignity with a sincere heart and a grateful mind, may you (Reverend Father, a President most worthy of such a place and office) deign for your part to receive them with a serene brow and a calm countenance. I earnestly entreat you to favor me with your goodwill, as I am most devoted to your Lordship in every duty of diligence and obedience. For my part, I humbly pray to God, the Best and Greatest, from the very center of my soul, that you may live long and happily, that you may be guided in your life by a favorable and propitious divine power, and finally, that you may remain forever in the service of holy goodness toward all people.

->Of your Greatness and<-
->Reverend Dignity<-

The most observant,

->*Robert Fludd. A Welsh-Briton by the origin of his lineage.*<-

[Decorative headpiece]

->PREFACE: IN WHICH IT IS DE-<-
->CLARED THAT THE LEADERS<-
->OF THE PAGAN PHILOSOPHERS<- in a
surreptitious manner, falsely claimed the foundations of their philosophy from the Priest **Moses** <note>Moses: The author is following the tradition of *Prisca Theologia*, which claimed that ancient Greek philosophers like Plato actually studied the writings of Moses and stole their best ideas from him.</note> for themselves, and poorly built the edifice of their philosophy upon them; and in this also the gross and palpable error of **Christian Philosophers** is pointed out as if with a finger, who, neglecting the **Holy Bible**, and rejecting the teachers of **hidden Theosophy** <note>Theosophy: "Divine wisdom." In this context, it refers to a mystical or esoteric understanding of God's presence in the natural world.</note>; flee to the vain doctrine of the **Pagans.**

[Decorative initial Q] **HOW** varied and differing among themselves are the opinions of both ancient and recent Philosophers concerning the essence, origin, and effects of **meteors** <note>Meteors: In the early modern period, "meteors" referred to any atmospheric phenomenon, including rain, wind, clouds, and lightning, not just falling stars.</note>; how unstable their assertions are, cannot be hidden from those who have given their labor a little more accurately to reading the books and volumes of Philosophy. Indeed, the reason for this is usually obvious to men endowed with a sharp wit; for where the foundations of the palace of Philosophy are found to be based on fables, there a weak structure—not unlike the shadows of a **Chimera** <note>Chimera: A mythical monster; used here to mean a groundless or impossible whim of the imagination.</note>—is to be expected, one that is stuffed and swollen with doubts and supported only by the wings of probability. What of certain truth is to be drawn from such "spurious" philosophy, produced by the foolish labors of the Pagans? For it was by no means granted to them by the **central light of nature**—that is, the Creator of nature and natural things—to truly penetrate the fountain of Christian Philosophy or the source of the sacred scriptures. What is the doctrine of **Aristotle**, of **Plato**, or of **Pythagoras**? What, finally, of the Greeks, **Hippocrates** and **Galen**, or of **Avicenna** and the rest of the **Arabs**, in both their Philosophical and medical teachings, if we look into the "marrow" of the holy Bible correctly, in a mystical manner, and with **Lyncean eyes** <note>Lyncean eyes: Referring to Lynceus, a figure from Greek mythology known for sight so sharp he could see through trees and stones.</note>? It is certainly nothing more than a deceptive vapor, vanishing smoke, and a plainly empty fiction. This is why **Saint Paul** tried so hard to pull us away from "vain Philosophy," since nothing can be drawn from it except trifles and barely probable ideas, rather than the reality of things. Do we not learn from the excellent teaching of the Prophet how impious and profane it is to abandon the way of truth and imitate the doctrine of the Pagans? For we are taught that the fountain of all wisdom must never be abandoned to seek art, science, and understanding in foreign lands, as the **Hagarenes** <note>Hagarenes: In this context, the author uses this biblical term (referring to descendants of Hagar) to describe the Arabic and Islamic scholars whose scientific works were widely studied in Europe.</note> did...

<summary>This preface introduces the author's critique of secular and ancient philosophy, arguing that thinkers like Aristotle and Galen provide only "vanishing smoke" compared to the "marrow" of biblical wisdom. The author claims that pagan philosophers secretly stole their best concepts from Moses but built a weak, deceptive system upon them.</summary>
<keywords>Theosophy, Moses, Aristotle, Plato, Meteors, Christian Philosophy, Ancient Philosophy, Natural Light</keywords>

->INTRODUCTION.<-

through their own imaginations. From this it came to pass that they attributed the efficacy and glory of so great a miracle not to God, the sole Creator, but to created Nature and the elements, which were brought forth and produced from the womb of that same Creator. From here arose the origin of Idolatry: namely, the worship of the Sun and Moon, the cult of Osiris and Isis, the adoration of Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, Venus, and Mercury, the sacrifices to Heaven, Ceres, Vesta, Proserpine, Vulcan, Pluto, and Neptune, and infinite other errors. By these, ignorant men are persuaded to stray and depart from the contemplation of the true GOD JEHOVAH, rather than approaching a perfect knowledge of their Creator. The cause of this error, however, was an ignorance of the operation and property of the divine Word and the Holy Spirit, and a neglect of the Holy Bible—the fountain and origin of all science and wisdom. But the Holy Scriptures contain the secrets of most sacred Philosophy revealed to us Christians, through which the miracles of the Word are made manifest to us by the mediation of worldly Nature. In these it is explained that *this Word was in the beginning (John 1) with God, and in God, and was God himself; and that it was the light of the world, in which was life; and that by this Word all things were made, and without it, nothing.* Therefore, by a true knowledge of the Word, we understand the nature of the Speaker, since the Son has a relationship to the Father. When these two are known, the spirit of holy discipline follows immediately, as a revelation proceeding from both. He who therefore does not know the Word of God knows nothing, *since by the Word God made all things (Wisdom 9:1),* and he who does not understand it cannot understand the truth; because Christ is the only truth, the true GOD, and eternal life—or, as the Apostle says in *1 Corinthians 1: the power and wisdom of GOD.* From this it follows that those who do not know Him cannot centrally <note>To know something "centrally" means to understand its internal essence or core reality, rather than just its outward appearance.</note> know the things created by Him and their essences. *From him, in him, and through him are all things (as the Apostle says); to whom be praise and honor.*

How great, then, is the madness in us Christians to venerate those pagan authors of philosophy and medicine as if they were deities; to read their writings with such diligence and confidence; to hold their inventions and arts in such immense estimation; and to defend their opinions in public Schools with such obstinacy? Indeed, we even cite their authorities so steadily and firmly in our writings and disputes, as if they had been poured out and distilled onto the earth divinely from heaven and immediately from GOD himself! Yet the sacred writings testify that Christ is the sole truth, and all truth of things comes from Him, the power and wisdom of GOD who teaches all things. Who, then, among all the philosophers can demonstrate nature or a natural thing by *a priori* reasoning <note>Reasoning from theoretical first principles or causes rather than from observed effects.</note> if they are ignorant of the true and primary cause of things? Are we not also taught that there is no truth of knowledge outside the true gift of the Holy Spirit, who is the only Teacher of doctrine and true science? This may be gathered from many places in the Holy Scriptures (*Exodus 28:3, Exodus 31:2, and 35:30*). Hence the Royal Psalmist says exultantly in *Psalm 119:99: I have become more intelligent than all my teachers, because the testimonies of GOD are my meditation.* What, then, of that Aristotelian "Nature"? It is certainly either a vain thing or a case of explaining the unknown by the even more unknown, since Aristotle himself was ignorant of Love <note>original: "Cupidinem." Here referring to Divine Love or the animating "Desire" of the universe.</note>, which is the true and shining spirit of all wisdom, the light of the world, the glory of the truly wise, the life of creatures, the mind of souls, and the prince of reason, governing in the very center of natural things. Aristotle, Plato, Pythagoras, and Hippocrates undoubtedly perceived a great light in nature from afar, having been instructed by the Ethiopians, Egyptians, Hebrews, and certain people of Armenia and the Arabs after long and tedious travels. Thus, by changing the names of the three principles of Moses, they falsely attributed these ideas to themselves. For what Moses called "darkness" or the "potential principle," Aristotle called "prime matter"; Plato called "formless hyle" <note>A Greek term for "matter" or "stuff."</note> or the "invisible and unformed species"; Pythagoras called "unity"; and Hippocrates called "deformed Chaos" or a "troubled universal mass." What Moses dictated as "the waters," Aristotle called "secondary matter"; Plato called "spirit"; and Pythagoras called the "Dyad" <note>original: "Diadem." Likely a typographical error for "Dyadem" (the Dyad), representing duality in Pythagorean thought.</note>; Hippocrates, along with Anaximenes, called it the "vast and universal air of the world." So also Light, the third principle of Moses...

The author claims that thinkers like Aristotle and Plato actually stole their core concepts from Moses and renamed them to hide their Hebrew origins.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the introductory "Prooemium" (Preface). The author, likely Robert Fludd given the style and subject matter, is contrasting "Pagan" philosophy with "Sacred" biblical philosophy, specifically regarding the nature of the atmosphere and its effects on health.</meta>

# PREFACE. 3

...Aristotle called it his "Form," Plato the "Soul of the World," Pythagoras the "Triad," and Hippocrates that immortal principle he called "the Heat" <note>original: *Calidum*. Hippocrates believed an innate heat was the source of life.</note>; when all these things were thrown into confusion, it receded to that highest region which the ancients called the **Ether**. Is there not here a monstrous theft among these Pagan <note>original: *Ethnicos*. In this context, "Ethnic" refers to non-Christian, classical Greek and Roman thinkers.</note> Teachers, by which they do not blush to claim for themselves—falsely and by subtle means—the principles and doctrine of the Divine High Priest? 

And yet we Christians—who are the possessors of the doctrine of Moses, and indeed of all the other prophets and writers, and have been truly instructed in them as if by a holy finger—are nevertheless moved by some unknown madness. Deserting the divine fountain and neglecting to look into the mirror of truth, as if intoxicated by a lethal cup, we do not cease to be submerged in the deceptive filth of the Pagans—into a **Philosophy** (I say) built on firm enough foundations, but poorly arranged insofar as it is fabricated and linked together by the various imaginations of its inventors: or rather, defiled and contaminated. For what does it profit to find stable and firm bases for a structure, when the parts of the house are joined together from reeds or straw, vulnerable to every wind? 

Therefore, the more learned of the sects of Pagan Philosophers perceived the "formal light" from afar with the shadowed eyes of their minds, but they were least able to penetrate to the deep fountain of all wisdom from which that form flowed. Wherefore it must be considered an extreme madness in us Christians to dwell instead in darkness, and to draw out a bastard Philosophy from the dung-heap and filth of the Pagans, rather than to drink in the subject of a sacred, naked, true, and clear Philosophy from the bright spring of life arising from the Holy Bible. 

Let us therefore reject those profane books of the Pagans and flee to the sacred lights and remains of the Patriarchs, Prophets, Apostles, true Philosophers, and mystical <term>theosophists</term> <note>A "theosophist" here refers to someone who gains knowledge of the divine through direct spiritual insight or sacred texts, rather than just rational logic.</note>, in whom we shall find—through the virtues of the spirit of holy discipline (whose role alone it is to teach all things)—the truth of all sciences. 

It shall be my task, (under God's guidance) in this volume of mine, to speak of the essences of <term>meteors</term> <note>In the 17th century, "meteors" referred to all atmospheric phenomena, including wind, rain, snow, and lightning, which were thought to be "mixed" substances in the air.</note>, inasmuch as they are the mothers of all composite things. Here I shall also strive to compare the positions and axioms of both the ancient Philosophers and their recent disciples regarding these "imperfectly mixed" things with the testimony of the Holy Bible, so that you may clearly perceive the difference between them and the sacred letters. Consequently, I wish for you to decide whether the most Holy Bible, or the vain, uncertain writings and truth-wandering sayings of the Pagan philosophers and their Christian followers, ought to be embraced. 

Indeed, the aim of this entire volume of ours is to show that **meteors** are daily produced by God in the world in a mystical manner; they are the immediate causes of health, restoration, and preservation, as well as of diseases and death, both in the <term>Macrocosm</term> <note>The universe or the world at large.</note> and the <term>Microcosm</term> <note>The human being, viewed as a miniature map of the universe.</note>. This I shall attempt to prove with testimonies derived from the most holy fountain, supporting it as if upon the shoulders of Atlas. 

From here, therefore, I shall endeavor to draw out and "fish" for the principles, differences, causes, and signs of both good and bad meteors, together with the cures for their worst effects, from the deep spring of the Bible and the theosophists or Hebrew and Egyptian Doctors. According to the smallness of my talent, I shall attempt to reveal and publish these things to the world—my loins girded with the belt of truth—with a favorable and propitious Deity helping me.

### *In which various opinions of philosophers, both ancient and modern,*
### *concerning the name and essence of the Meteor are examined.*

[Decorative initial Q] Although I have spoken at great length—both through the entire seventh book of our treatise on physics concerning the various natures of meteors (both physical and metaphysical), and also throughout the second portion of the first section of the third part, regarding the *History of the Preternatural in Both Worlds* <note>original: "De præternaturali vtriusque mundi historia"</note>—nevertheless, in this place, the profound contemplation of the subject at hand and the necessity of our undertaking compel me to penetrate toward their centers with a somewhat more accurate inquiry. For whoever desires to reach the very heart of meteors, and does not attempt to bring such a business to a happy conclusion, will surely admit that he has reached no small secret of God and nature. First, therefore, before I descend into the depths of a work of such great difficulty, I shall briefly and clearly explain what philosophers, both ancient and modern, have devised concerning the general name, essence, and origin of the meteor.

The Greeks assigned the name <term>meteor<note>The word comes from the Greek 'meteoros', meaning 'raised from the ground' or 'hanging in the air.' In this era, 'meteor' referred to any atmospheric phenomenon, including rain, wind, and lightning.</term> from the loftiness of its position in the region of the air. Among our own people, however, meteors are called <term>impressions<note>In Aristotelian science, these were seen as effects 'impressed' or stamped upon the air by the action of heat and vapors.</note></term> because they are seen to be imprinted and formed for the most part in the "sublime"—that is, in the high regions of the air. Yet, this name is attributed to them not from their essence or constitution, but rather from their location. With respect to their consistency, philosophers call them "imperfectly composed" and "imperfectly mixed" bodies—or (as some prefer) they are so called because of their sudden generation, inasmuch as they are observed to form in an instant, as if in a moment of time. Others maintain that they are called "imperfectly composed" bodies because their composition does not seem to occur according to a change of substance or a total alteration of qualities. Some call them "imperfectly mixed" insofar as they are compared to living (animate) and perfectly mixed bodies. Finally, there are others who assertively say that these "impressions" are called "imperfect mixtures" because a "perfect form" <note>In this context, 'form' refers to the defining soul or essence that makes a thing what it is; meteors were seen as too transient to have such a stable essence.</note> is not acquired in them, nor is a great alteration of parts found in such a composition; rather, the parts of slightly altered substances are merely confounded among themselves. And this is the reason why the parts of such an imperfect mixture are so easily dissipated from one another and dissolved back into their primary elements, from which they were previously coagulated without any perfect mixing or transmutation having taken place.

As for what pertains to the existence of these impressions, everyone agrees that two things are required: one, namely, that *in which* they are made, which is the air (serving as a medium or the lowest "spirit of the world," which is the <term>matrix<note>Literally 'womb'; the environment in which something is generated.</note></term> of all meteors); and another *from which* they are made. They conclude that this latter is vapor or—as others prefer—smoke, arising fundamentally from either the earth or the water. In this upward motion, they identify celestial heat as the principal and primary agent, and the air as the secondary agent. Then, they believe that this matter, having been raised upward, is gathered together and given form by the nature of a <term>coagulum<note>A 'rennet' or thickening agent; the process by which gas or vapor turns into a more solid or liquid state like rain or clouds.</note></term> that is partly celestial and partly elemental.

However, regarding the "material cause," some seem to disagree: while one chooses vapor alone as the universal matter of meteors, others assert that both vapor and <term>exhalation<note>Aristotelian science distinguished between 'vapor' (moist and cool, from water) and 'exhalation' (dry and hot, from earth).</note></term> are their material subjects. They say that vapor is hot and moist, and thus they believe that "watery meteors" (like rain) proceed from its substance; but they hold that "fiery impressions" (like lightning) come from exhalation, which is hot and dry according to the nature of fire. For this reason, they make "smoke" the common matter of meteors instead of vapor, since smoke participates in the nature of every element; it is sometimes hot and dry, and sometimes hot and moist, making its matter equally fit for the procreation of both aquatic and fiery impressions. But <term>Robert of Lincoln<note>Refers to Robert Grosseteste (c. 1175–1253), a famous English statesman, philosopher, and Bishop of Lincoln who wrote extensively on light and atmospheric science.</note></term>, supported by the authority of Aristotle, seems to include "exhalation" under the dimension of "vapor." Following the opinion of the said Aristotle, he established that vapor is threefold: namely, hot and dry; hot and moist; and cold and moist. He asserted that the first is materially extracted from the earth or earthy things, the last from water or watery things, and the middle from both (though with the watery nature dominating). It was from this, therefore, that he defined vapor as a subtle substance from any one or two of the lower elements—

-># On the Primary Principles of Meteors. 7<-

In my history of the Macrocosm <note>original: "Macrocosmi"; the "Great World" or the universe as a whole</note>, and later in Book 9, Tract 1, Chapter 9 of the Natural History of the Microcosm <note>original: "Microcosmi"; the "Little World," referring to the human being as a reflection of the universe</note>, as well as in the first and fifth chapters of the first book (section 1, portion 1, part 2) regarding the Kabbalistic and physiological discourse of both worlds—where the primary elements of Nature are treated—and finally in the third part (Section 1, Portion 1, Chapter 1) of that same discourse, where the threefold principles of the Macrocosm and Microcosm are discussed, these matters have been clearly explained. However, it is my intention in this place to briefly re-examine and recite them for the sake of fresh memory and a more certain method.

We say, therefore, according to the teaching of the High Priest Moses, that there are three principles of all things, and consequently the primary principles of meteors <note>In this period, "meteors" referred to all atmospheric phenomena including rain, wind, and lightning, not just falling stars.</note>: namely, **Darkness**, **Light**, and the **Intermediate Spirit** which participates in both. For its sublunary part <note>The region below the moon, i.e., the Earth's atmosphere</note> is more familiar with the earth and darkness, which is why it is subject to constant changes; but its empyrean and super-celestial part is seen to have a greater fellowship with the source of light, as it was the receptacle of the light created on the first day, and it is that over which the **Spirit of God** is said to have moved. Finally, its middle portion participates equally in both extremes; and for this reason, the sphere of equality—which is the solar orb, or rather the path through which the Sun passes daily—is, according to the Platonists, quite wisely described as being in its very center. From this, it is called the **Ether**.

Moses called this mundane spirit "the waters," the subject of which is the "secondary matter" arising from the depths of the shapeless darkness (which is the primary or "potential" matter itself). The procreator or beneficial midwife of this birth was that fiery power emanating from the Spirit of the Lord; this was that **fiery love**, by means of which the potential matter—hiding in the depths of the shapeless chaos or **Hyle** <note>original: "hylæ"; a Greek term for the raw, unformed substance of the universe</note>—was brought into the "act" of the waters.

Therefore, **Water** is the daughter of the darkness of the hidden God, while **Light** is the offspring of the divine power or splendor—that is, the revealed God. The midwife of both is the Word or the Divine Spirit. Hence the wise man said that God created the world out of "formless" or (as Jerome has it) "invisible matter" (*Wisdom 11:18*). And St. Peter says that "the heavens existed long ago, and the earth was formed out of water and through water by the word of God" (*2 Peter 3:5*). From this it is clear that the first matter of the world was "informal" <note>Matter without a defined shape or "form" in the philosophical sense.</note> matter, which was called by Moses "darkness" or the "dark abyss," and its secondary matter was "water," from which the heaven and earth were afterward made. The effector or worker of all these miracles was the Word with the Spirit of the Lord (*Psalm 33:6*). And this is why the royal Psalmist sings: "By the word of the Lord the heavens were made firm, and by the breath of his mouth all their power."

Thus we have confirmed from the sacred scriptures the **potential** or "privative" principle—namely, darkness or shapeless and invisible matter (which is why it is said that the earth was "void"). We also have the **positive** principle—namely, Light or the effect of divine power, by whose presence the invisible, shapeless, and potential matter was made visible and active. Finally, we have the intermediate subject or object of both—namely, **water**, out of which the heavens and the earth were fashioned by the mediation of "form."

For this reason, when natural philosophers describe the breadth of all beings, they place at the summit "pure act" without matter <note>referring to God</note>, and at the bottom "matter without form"—namely, darkness. They demonstrate that all intermediate things are a mixture of form and matter: specifically, water mixed with life-giving light. For this reason, we have also conceived the origin of our "formal" and "material" pyramids <note>A reference to Fludd’s famous diagrams of two intersecting pyramids representing the descent of light (form) and the ascent of matter.</note>. From these things it is clear that:
*   **Earth** is nothing other than "thick water" and the dregs of the spirit remaining after its extraction from the shapeless chaos.
*   **Universal Air** is "thin and subtle water," or the invisible spirit extracted from chaos.
*   **Visible Water** (from the sea, springs, or rivers) is the intermediate substance participating in both extremes. Because it is thicker and slower in its motion and heavier than air, it appears to have a connection with the earth; but insofar as it is clear, mobile, and not as heavy as the earth, it seems to taste of the nature of air and stand apart from the laws of the earth.

Therefore, when St. Peter said the heaven and earth consist of water and through water by the word of God, he understood "heaven" to mean the universal air (whose base is visible water), and by "earth" he seems to hint at all things dark, opaque, and dense. The order of these principles is also best denoted by those regular bodies of Geometry <note>The Platonic Solids</note>, where the **Cube** is defined as the extreme and most ample body, because it is the first-born and contains the ratio of the whole.

This body <note>The Cube</note> is held by the more occult philosophers to represent **Chaos** or **Hyle**, or the opaque, dark, and shapeless matter, from whose lap or womb both light and water emerged—that is, the formal and material principle of all things. This is **PAN**, or universal nature, produced from the virginal birth of shapeless chaos. And when the philosophers said that the **Tetrahedron** <note>The four-faced pyramid shape</note> was the "first-born" from the cube, they understood that **Fire** or the primary "lucid form" emerged from the immense darkness as if from a massive and most opaque body. For then, formal light immediately appeared in the moist nature; then, I say, the Spirit of the Lord was moved over the waters, imparting a fiery vigor to them. This was followed by the completion of the first day of creation, and thus, according to the wise man, "Wisdom was created before all things" (*Ecclesiasticus 1*). That is, the divine light shone out of the darkness before any other creature. King Solomon also seems to confirm this in these words: "Jehovah possessed Wisdom at the beginning of his way, before his works, before any time: before the beginning of the earth; when there were no abysses I was brought forth (says Wisdom), when there were no fountains, when God strengthened the clouds above, when he fitted the heavens there I was, when he established the circuit on the surfa-"

...the surface of the abyss, when he established the heavens above, etc. <note original: "Prov. 8. 22.">Proverbs 8:22</note>. And so the **Hidden GOD** was made the **Manifest GOD**, the effect of whose divine splendor upon the moist or watery nature was the created light. We have, therefore, from this birth the **Tetrahedron** <note>A four-sided pyramid, which in the Platonic tradition represents the element of fire.</note>, or the first fire, begotten of the **Cube** <note>A six-sided solid, here representing the dark, solid foundation or the "father" of the elements.</note>, its dark parent. Then, from the bowels of the Tetrahedron—that is, from the illuminated spirit—the **Dodecahedron** <note>A twelve-sided solid representing the heavens or the universe.</note> is extracted. For when the lucid spirit was created on the first day, the Heaven or the Firmament was created from its womb or matrix on the second day of creation, as Moses testifies. This Dodecahedron is formed from pentagonal surfaces, and for this reason (as I believe) heaven is called the **quintessence** <term>quintessence: literally the "fifth essence," a refined substance distinct from the four earthly elements</term>, thereby arguing it to be a fifth element distinct from those four sublunary ones. The work of the third day, however, is the gathering together of the thick or sensible waters into a place destined for them by God; their symbol is the **Icosahedron** <note>A twenty-sided solid representing the element of water.</note>, from whose belly the air immediately flew forth, the symbol of which is the **Octahedron** <note>An eight-sided solid representing the element of air.</note>; for air was produced by the refining of water. The remainder of the dark Cube resided in the earth, and thus it now obtained the name of "fertile earth," which was previously called "void earth" by Moses. Therefore, in the image of these three principles—namely, darkness, waters, and light—the entire spirit of the world is divided into three elements, differing from each other in nature and disposition: namely, into **Earth**, into the **Sphere of Moisture**, and into **Fire**, just as has been more than sufficiently explained in the second book of our *History of the Macrocosm*.

From these things which have been explained in this place, such a great discrepancy has arisen among the leading ancient philosophers concerning the principles of natural things; nevertheless, their opinions do not seem to differ much from one another if we consider the matter a little more accurately. For **Thales of Miletus** placed **Water** as the principle of all things; **Anaximenes** said that infinite **air** was the cause of the existence of things, whence **Anaximander** even made air **GOD**. But **Zoroaster** <note>An ancient Persian prophet often cited in Renaissance philosophy as a source of primordial wisdom.</note> asserted that all things were made from fire or light, and the **Pythagoreans** said there was a single fire throughout the whole.

And certainly, as has been said, if we consider the matter well, we shall find that these men did not stray far from the path. For fire, first emerging from the darkness, revealed the unseen waters with a sudden splendor; the vast, subtle part of these waters is the airy spirit, whence both Thales and Anaximenes seem to agree in a certain way. But truly, these two only explained the material or passive principle. But Zoroaster, preferring fire to the rest, rightly called it the primary principle, inasmuch as it preceded the moist matter, just as action precedes passion <note>In this context, "passion" means the state of being acted upon or receiving an influence.</note>, or as an act precedes the thing to be produced into action. And yet he himself erred in a way, because an active principle cannot exist except insofar as it has a relation to a passive principle.

Whence **Saint Peter** said, *the heavens and the earth were made of water and through water by means of the word* <note original: "2 Pet. 3:5">2 Peter 3:5</note>—that is, by the agent or the first act. Hence, **Diogenes** spoke with more mature discourse concerning the principles of things, saying that **air** endowed with divine reason is the principle of things: that is, the created air or moist nature, and the divine light. It is as if he wished to say with Moses, *the spirit of the Lord moved upon the waters* <note original: "spiritus domini vectus super aquas">Genesis 1:2</note>, and with the waters was the principle of created things. And **Zeno the Stoic**, more cautious in his opinion, attempting to make his sentiment regarding the principle firmer, says that the substance of **Fire** converted through air into water is the principle of all things. And **Empedocles**, proceeding in a coarser manner, established the **four elements** as the principles of all things. Finally, the error of all these men in their judgment of principles was immense, because they did not notice that the divine power or the most holy Word was the more ancient beginning of all these things. Indeed, if they had understood this with more mature meditation, they would say with Zoroaster—instructed by *a priori* reasons <term>a priori: reasoning from cause to effect, or from self-evident principles</term>—that the divine light was the **Monad** <term>Monad: the number one, representing unity or the Divine source</term> or primary author of all things, since it is the source and origin of acts and forms, by whose revelation the number **Dyad** <term>Dyad: the number two, representing duality or the first step away from unity</term> was produced: namely, with the light-filled Monad came the dark Monad, which was the water.

### CHAPTER IV.

Concerning qualities of this sort and the reason for their origin, we have spoken quite amply in Chapter 7, Book 1 of our *Physics of the Macrocosm*. Here, however, we think it will be worthwhile to say a few things about them: seeing as by their effects, a progression is made from the aforementioned principles to things "principled" <note>Things that have a beginning or are derived from primary principles.</note>—both imperfectly and perfectly mixed—through both the thickening and the refining of the elements. By these qualities, like-natured things are gathered, digested, ripened, and fixed, and are led to the goal of perfection; and likewise, different-natured things are cut into, dispersed, scattered, driven away, and beaten back. This duty is indeed completed by **heat**, insofar as it is from the most noble and subtle spirit...

### CHAPTER V.

#### On the progression in Nature which was made from these primary principles to the fabric of the three Elements: which are the secondary principles of Natural things.

Once these simple qualities—and those derived from them by the aforementioned principles of Nature—were produced, the movement of nature then immediately tended toward the generation of secondary principles, which are called **elements**. In this state of simplicity, Nature seems to rest in its absolute fabrication of the world, such that it would remain in this condition until the very end without any evident change or alteration. However, those things that follow these in the order of nature—pertaining both to the generation of perfectly mixed bodies and to their corruption in this sublunary <note>The "sublunary" world refers to the Earth and its atmosphere, which ancient science believed was subject to change, unlike the "unchanging" heavens above the moon.</note> world—are subject to daily changes and alterations and can never rest in the same state for long. These are called **meteors** <note>In the 17th century, "meteors" referred to any atmospheric phenomena, including rain, wind, and rainbows, not just falling stars.</note> or *imperfectly mixed things*, which we have not unwisely designated as "third-order principles," as was declared in its proper place in Part 1, Section 1, Portion 1, regarding the physiological discourse of both worlds, and will be explained more copiously below. Therefore, regarding these principles subject to change as well as those simple ones, the Wise Man <note>A reference to King Solomon, traditionally considered the author of Ecclesiastes.</note> was referring to the least corruptible simple principles when he spoke these words: *A generation passes away, and a generation arrives, but the earth stands forever,* <note>original: "Generatio præterit, & generatio aduenit, terra autem in æternum ſtat." Ecclesiastes 1:4</note> arguing from this that the elements are immutable—that is, they are not to be resolved back into their primary principles—but that all "Generable" things (such as meteors and things procreated from them) are subject to alterations. 

Just as in the first moment of creation three principles presented themselves—namely **darkness** (or Chaos), **Light**, and **Water**—so too in the production of these secondary principles, three parts of the said "universal water," distinct from one another in nature and quality, seem to come together. Each of these has a very close relationship to one of the aforementioned primary principles. The highest of these moist portions of the sublunary nature is benevolently set aflame by the light and the action of its heat; and since heat is excited by the vehement motion of light (for light is more mobile than all things, as you will find abundantly in Book 1, Chapter 1 of our *History of the Macrocosm*), and since its nature is to refine and disperse moist nature, it drives the moisture of the waters of that place downward from its own region. From this, it happens that this place becomes very dry. Furthermore, that moist vapor, having been pushed downward toward the dark place of the earth, is naturally denied entry there because it participates in the heat of light, which is entirely contrary to terrestrial darkness and its coldness. 

Consequently, between these two extremes, a very vast **sphere of moisture** is gathered, participating in both extremes in some way. From this, it happens that the base of this sphere, due to its commerce and proximity with the earth, becomes thickened and made visible, and it borrows its cold disposition from the earth. Thus, this portion of the sphere is called **cold and moist**, just as the opposite part, being closer to the bright or fiery orb, is the most refined and is not as moist as the middle portion—which is nonetheless called **moist and hot** along with the whole invisible portion. 

And this is why philosophers, both ancient and modern, have divided this sphere into two distinct elements which they made **Water** and **Air**. However, the purpose of my discourse leads me to consider these two as nothing other than a single **moist element**, which we call the "sphere of moisture." In this way, we can better arrange these three principles according to the pattern and order of those first three. For Moses did not say, "He divided the air from the water," but rather, *He divided the waters from the waters.* <note>Genesis 1:6</note> Therefore, we align this sphere of moisture with the created waters; and just as in the first creation, the Spirit of the Lord (or fiery love) was borne over the waters, so too the bright orb (or fire) is borne over this sphere. Finally, the **Earth**, which is the lowest of the secondary principles, is compared to darkness; indeed, it is the gathering of the darkness itself into the center of the universe. Whence Cold has its offspring ready in its bowels to oppose any invasion of the "son of bright light" <note>A poetic term for heat or solar influence.</note>.

Thus far, then, we have reached the completion of the fabric of the **Macrocosm**: namely, from the circumference of the shapeless shadows divided from the infinite darkness—from which the moist or watery matter of the world emerged—down to the very center of the periphery, in which all darkness resided.

But lest you think these things were invented by me or devised from my own brain—what I have just put forward regarding the production of the first principles and the procreation of the primordial qualities (which serve the principles like handmaidens), and also concerning the origin of the three Elements from them as secondary principles—I would like you to observe with a diligent gaze and somewhat more accurate speculation how these assertions of mine are defended by the consensus of both the **Sacred Scriptures** and those skilled in the mysteries of **Theosophy** and the **Kabbalah**, appearing to be supported by shoulders as if they were those of Atlas.

### CHAPTER I.

#### Concerning mixed principles or meteors: where they arise from, and toward what they naturally tend.

[Decorative initial Q] Just as we expressed two types of principles in our discussion of simple substances—namely, that they are either absolutely simple (which we called primary) or simple things made from those primary simples (which we call the elements)—so in a similar respect we have asserted that among mixed principles, some are primary. These, according to the intention of the Philosophers <note>The author likely refers to Aristotle and the scholastic tradition, which defined "meteors" as phenomena in the upper and lower atmosphere.</note>, are vapor and exhalation. Others are secondary: specifically, those constituted from vapor, from exhalation, or from both joined together. These are called **meteors** <term>meteor: in this context, not a space rock, but any "imperfectly mixed" substance in the air or body, like rain, wind, or bodily vapors</term> or "imperfectly mixed bodies."

And thus it is necessary that, according to the intentions of the philosophers, the final stage of the simple principles—that is, the "simples from simples"—are the immediate principles of fumes or vapors and exhalations. These are likewise the closer beginnings of meteors. Because these are imperfectly mixed bodies, they follow the same progression of nature toward the procreation of all composite bodies (that is, "perfectly mixed" bodies). 

From this, it happened that in the circuit of nature, from darkness, water, and light—acting as primary principles—three elements immediately arose: namely earth, the sphere of humidity (both the visible kind called water and the invisible aerial kind), and Fire. Thus far, the progression has moved toward the complete production of the material and formal world. Because of the simplicity of its substance, the structure of this world will remain firm and unchanged in its state until the last day of judgment.

It follows then that elements of this kind are simple principles. They are the starting point from which nature proceeds into the generation of any composite or mixed creature; they are also the goal toward which nature tends in its progress from generation to corruption <note>In early science, "corruption" simply means the breaking down or decay of a complex thing back into its basic elements.</note>. The middle path is the **meteor**, which is either "waxing" (like the Moon) during generation, or "waning" and scattering the parts of the composite during corruption. 

Thus, the starting point in generation is the "point of elements," while the goal is the **perfectly mixed body**, such as the human body, which is our primary focus here. Conversely, in the corruption of a composite body, the starting point is that perfectly mixed body; the goal toward which nature verges in its decay is the simple element. From this element, progression can begin again toward the generation of either an imperfect or perfect mixture. Beyond the simple elements, there is no further progression of corruption because of the simplicity of those basic principles. The middle point—the path through which this happens—is the **meteor**.

Since it is impossible for any progression to occur from one extreme to another without an intervening middle, it is necessary that between simple natures (where there is no mixing) and composite bodies (where mixing is perfect), an **imperfect mixture** must intervene. This is called a "meteor," named after the place of its procreation, whether in the heavens or in the earth. 

Consequently, it follows that life and death, as well as health and disease, are brought to completion through the mediation of meteors. Just as the meteor is the middle between the point of perfect generation and that of complete corruption, so too is disease in a creature a retreat of health toward the goal of dissolution into the elements. Thus, disease is, as it were, the reduction of a healthy, generated thing back toward a "meteoric" nature—that is, to the middle path of decay. Therefore, that healthy nature which was once perfectly mixed has now become imperfectly mixed, as it is now morbid and situated on the middle path between complete generation and absolute destruction. 

The nature of the earthly creature <note>original: "ternæ creaturæ", likely referring to a "threefold" creature composed of the three aforementioned elements, or a typo for "terrenæ" (earthly).</note> is just as capable, in this middle station, of retreating back toward the point of health from which it departed, as it is of proceeding toward the extreme end of destruction. This destruction moves toward the nature of the elements (especially air) from which it first arose. Therefore, the more nature tends toward simplicity beyond this middle point, the more the composite creature gradually approaches its end; but by taking the opposite path, it begins to recover more and more. 

At this point, we must carefully observe that the conjunction of a "most evil meteor"—that is, a dissolving and destructive nature—with the middle nature of a thing that has reached complete composition, is the cause of death and destruction. This is true unless it receives aid from a **life-giving meteor** through divine assistance, as will be explained more broadly and clearly below. 

That the motion of this "meteorological nature" exists within the composite body is clearly shown by its effects in the heart of the "sphere of humidity" of the macrocosm <term>macrocosm: the universe or "Great World," which reflects the "microcosm" of the human body</term>. Just as meteors—both healthy and poisonous or ill-omened—are frequently produced in the aerial spirit of the Great World, it is certain and beyond doubt that meteors of both conditions are sometimes generated in the spirit of any perfectly mixed being. This is because it is necessary for some meteor (an imperfect mixture) to intervene between any perfectly mixed thing and the simple elements.

# On the Material Cause of Meteors. 17

...it must be necessary: for no meteor <note>In this period, "meteor" referred to any atmospheric phenomenon, including rain, wind, clouds, and lightning, as well as falling stars.</note> can be brought forth unless it exists within the aerial matrix. For the air, by virtue of its spiritual moisture, is said to take the place of a mirror. Inasmuch as it very easily either receives forms or imitates them, it readily represents and receives the likenesses of all figures and colors; indeed, the air is the life, the essence, and truly the "all" of meteors—or rather of "impressions," both visible and invisible. Everything that is present in a meteor, whether it be health-giving or morbid, is drawn and brought forth from the air itself, as if from a storehouse of the hidden spirit of the world <note>original: *spiritus mundi occulti*</note>; or, to speak in the language of the Holy Scriptures, from the secret and divine Ark or perfume-chest <note>original: *myrothecio* — a vessel for precious ointments or incense</note> of GOD. The air, therefore, is the material cause of meteors, but other causes are also required for their generation. Hence it is that in this strict inquiry of ours into these meteorological principles, we shall take care to consider four of their causes first and above all:

The first is that **from which** they are made, namely the **material** cause, as the substantial part of its composition. 
The second is that **through which** they are made, namely the **formal** cause, as the peculiar essence by which one meteorological species usually differs from another, either to the eye or in its effect.
Then follows that **by which** it is led to the completion of its species, as if by a **moving** or immediately **operating** cause. 
And finally, that **for the sake of which** this mixed principle is led to its conclusion by the **efficient** cause, namely the **final** cause.

Regarding these causes of meteors, in order to arrive at a more exact understanding of their formation and their effects (both morbid and healthy), we shall discourse in an orderly and methodical way. In the first place, we shall deal with the material cause of the meteor through the entire treatise of this book.

->### CHAPTER II.<-

### On the material or substantial cause of meteors: What the Author’s opinion is regarding it, and how it is seen to differ in this matter from the sentiment of the ancient philosophers.

The material of Meteors (says Aristotle, along with the other philosophers of that same sect) is clearly the fumes arising from water or earth. Moreover, they make this smoke of a dual nature: either **vapor** or **exhalation**. They assertively say the former is hot and moist, watery and non-inflammable, arising from earth and water; while the latter is hot and dry, earthy, inflammable, and summoned from the earth. For they seem to show by the following reasoning why the remaining elements—namely fire and air—do not yield fumes as thick as the substance of those meteors: specifically, because those superior elements are much more subtle in their substance than fumes. Therefore, they think that air and fire cannot produce such fumes. 

These are their views. But it shall be our task to destroy these arguments of theirs with their own mouths. For every one of them acknowledges in their writings that air, through condensation, becomes water, and much more so **Vapor**, which by its nature and constitution stands between pure air and visible water. Furthermore, they themselves acknowledge, and we have experienced, that this same water is reduced into earth by thickening <note>original: *inspissatione*</note>. Does not Aristotle also refute himself with his own mouth in the fourth book <note>Referring to *De Caelo*</note>, where he says that a stellar body is a denser part of its own orb—that is, a visible substance fashioned out of condensed invisible ethereal spirit? From this, he seems to imply the possibility that a comet, a cloud, or some other meteor can be produced from the condensation of air.

Therefore, this assertion of the ancients—that air cannot be the proximate cause of vapors because it is more subtle than vapor—is invalid. For in the 7th book of my Physics of the *History of the Macrocosm* <note>The author refers to his own major work, *Utriusque Cosmi Historia*</note>, where the generation of clouds is discussed, we have demonstrated by infallible arguments that clouds are made immediately from the composition and condensation of air by opposing winds. Consequently, that cloud, as a middle substance between water and air, takes its origin not from the watery extreme, but from the aerial one as its primary principle. 

Whence we say that the air brings forth the material of the cloud from its own womb, and by the operation of the divine power, administers it centrally to the world by way of rain, snow, or hail. We gather this also from these passages of the Holy Bible (the fountain of all truth), having neglected the writings of the Pagans <note>original: *Ethnicorum*</note> in this matter. For in the Pentateuch of Moses we find these things written: *The LORD shall open to thee his good treasure, the heaven, to give the rain unto thy land in his season.* (Deuteronomy 28:12). And GOD himself, speaking to Job, says: *Hast thou entered into the treasures of the snow? or hast thou seen the treasures of the hail?* (Job 38:22). And a little later he continues: *Who is the father of the rain? or who hath begotten the drops of dew? Out of whose womb came the ice? and the hoary frost of heaven, who hath gendered it?* (Job 38:28).

From these things, therefore, it is clear to the diligent observer that the sanctuary of GOD, in which He hides His meteorological treasures, is the **heavens**; and "heaven" in this place is taken to mean the **air**, for meteors are not birthed in the supralunar regions <note>The regions above the moon were considered eternal and unchanging in older cosmology; "meteors" only happened in the "sublunar" air.</note>. From these passages of the sacred fountain, we gather that **watery meteors** <note>In the 17th century, 'meteor' referred to any atmospheric phenomenon, including rain, snow, and wind, not just falling stars.</note>—such as clouds, rain, snow, hail, and others of this kind—are brought forth from the **Ark of Heaven**, or the treasury/shrine of the mundane spirit or air, by the divine will. This occurs through the winds acting as instruments ordained for this task. Thus, the "meteors" appear to vary according to the different dispositions of the winds blowing from various regions of the world:
*   When **Boreas** <gloss>The North Wind</gloss> blows: snow, hail, and frost are produced.
*   When **Auster** <gloss>The South Wind</gloss> blows: clouds and rain.
*   When **Eurus** <gloss>The East Wind</gloss> blows: heat and lightning.
*   When **Favonius** <gloss>The West Wind</gloss> blows: thin clouds are produced.

All these meteors are procreated from the substance of the air, with those winds blowing in opposite ways and differing from one another according to the wind's disposition, as will be clearly declared in its proper place.

As for the origin of **ignited meteors** <note>Phenomena involving fire or light, like lightning or comets.</note>, which the **Peripatetics** <note>Followers of Aristotle’s philosophy.</note> believed were caused by exhalations sent up from the earth: certainly, if we pay attention to the sacred writings of the Bible, we will observe that their origin is far more abstruse than the common philosophers have dreamed. For first, we read in Leviticus that a fire or flash going out from the presence of Jehovah consumed the burnt offering on that altar, Leviticus 9:24. And in the following chapter: fire going out from the presence of Jehovah killed the sons of Aaron, verse 2. Indeed, God himself is called a "consuming fire." Elsewhere, we read that his ministers are called a "flaming fire," Deuteronomy 4:24. From this it is said that the fire sent from Jehovah consumed those 250 men, etc., Numbers 16. Elsewhere, the fire of God falling from heaven by the power of Elijah's spirit consumed the captain with his 50 men. And in Job we find: "Can you send lightnings, that they may go, and say to you, 'Here we are'?" Job 38:35.

Finally, in another place, it is excellently denoted that the source and origin of ignited meteors arises from that very Author, where it is written: By God’s neesings <note>An archaic word for sneezing; here referring to the violent expulsion of divine breath.</note> a light shines, and his eyes are like the eyelids of the morning; out of his mouth go burning lamps, and sparks of fire leap out. So out of his nostrils goes smoke, as out of a boiling pot; his breath kindles coals, and a flame goes out of his mouth, Job 41:18, where he understands this as lightning. And elsewhere: "By what way is the light parted, which scatters the East Wind upon the earth?" Job 38:19.

By these biblical testimonies, we are taught primarily that the beginning and origin of light and flashing, and consequently of all **luminous meteors**, is very secret and abstruse. It is as far distant from the conceptions of the Ancient Philosophers (who believed their origin was from the earth) as day is from night, or light from darkness. For who among the philosophers will deny that an empty medium <note>likely referring to the 'vacuum' or space between objects</note> has its beginning from the start rather than from its end? Furthermore, since the beginnings of mixed things are simple, why should the most essential meteors be derived from the corrupt and mixed earth, or from an opaque body, or from that which comes after, rather than from the beginning itself? Why should they not be derived from the fire or luminous source suited to their nature? And why should that which is hot be procreated by a natural birth from the cold? For like enjoys like, and like is usually procreated by its like.

Indeed, we can boldly pronounce that if moist meteors are usually made by the compression of the thin substance of the middle air (or the middle sphere of humidity) through the mediation of two winds, much more are ignited meteors materially elicited from the compression of the substance of the **supreme element** <note>The highest region of the atmosphere, closest to the heavens.</note> by winds gently concurring there. For a portion of the supreme sphere of humidity is nothing other than dissolved and expanded fire, or **fiery air**; which, by condensation, appears in the form of an ignited meteor, such as comets, fiery columns, and all those meteors observed to be born in the highest region of the air. Their matter is air contracted by the breath of the winds of Jehovah, but their luminous form is fiery light, in the center of which dwells the power of Jehovah—not otherwise than it appeared to Moses in the midst of the burning bush, or in the pillar of fire that went before the Israelites by night in the desert. For God is clothed (as the Psalmist testifies) with light as with a garment; and according to Moses, He spoke to the Israelites out of the fiery flame. Hence, elsewhere, He is called a "consuming fire."

Therefore, it is a very difficult labor, and the greatest of **Herculean labors**, to discern the source of these meteors unless it be detected by revelation. For this reason, that man of patience <note>Job</note> said: "By what way is the light parted, which scatters the East Wind upon the earth? Where is the way where light dwells?" Job 38. And as **Pagninus** <note>Santes Pagnino (1470–1541), a famous Hebraist and Bible translator.</note> interprets it: "Do you know where the way is by which the exhalation is divided that spreads the wind over the earth?"

If, therefore, the fiery form of meteors goes out secretly from the presence of Jehovah, as we have said above; if by the sneezings of God the lightning or flash or light shines; if from His mouth flames like torches proceed and sparks of fire; if from His nostrils comes smoke like a boiling pot; if His breath kindles coals (Job 41:18); certainly these things are far more occult than that they should proceed from simple warm and dry smoke exhaled from the bowels of the earth.

Who among Christians, even moderately versed in the nature of things, could be so mad as to attribute the immense force of thunder, the admirable power of lightning and thunderbolts—which can melt a sword while the scabbard remains untouched, and can snatch away the life of animals in the blink of an eye even while the body remains unmarked—to a matter of such small importance as an **earthly exhalation**? For what more did that fire do which went out from the presence of Jehovah, by the power of which both the sons of Aaron and the 250 were killed and bereft [of life]...

->### CHAPTER III.<-

->In which the trifling vanity and improbability of the ancient philosophers' opinions regarding the origin of meteors is discussed.<-

**T**o begin with the opinion of the ancient philosophers regarding the origin of winds, they seem to hesitate somewhat and disagree among themselves. Those who embrace the Peripatetic <term>Peripatetic: A term for followers of Aristotle, referring to his habit of walking while teaching.</term> sect and establish Aristotle's opinion in this matter define wind as a hot and dry exhalation, difficult to ignite, raised up to the middle region of the air. From there, it is driven downward by the cold of that place, and then, striving upward again by the inclination of its own nature, it moves laterally over the earth in the lowest region of the air—partly due to its lightness and partly because of other exhalations encountered from below—which air it stirs and fans, lest it should rot from a kind of perpetual idleness. Others (among whom I name Vitruvius) maintain that wind is a "wave of air" with an uncertain redundancy of motion <note>original: "aeris undam, cum incerta motus redundantia"; citing Vitruvius, *De Architectura*, Book 1, Chapter 6</note>, when heat meets moisture and the force of the heat turns the power of the blowing spirit. Therefore, the first group, who sustain the Aristotelian sect, say that a breath, smoke, or a hot and dry exhalation—having no fatness <note>original: "pinguedinis"; referring to oily or combustible matter</note> in it by which it can be ignited—is the material cause of wind. Because it lacks fatness, it can neither be ignited nor reduced into a mist by condensation, much less thickened into a cloud; and they said this emerges from the earth, although Pliny also says some winds breathe out from the waters.

Let us now ask what these Peripatetics (who seem to so excel in the inspection of nature) think about the origin of a Comet? They say this arises from an earthly smoke or exhalation that is thick, fatty, and viscous, and made of densely compacted parts, raised by the power of the stars from the bowels of the earth into the highest region of the air. There it is dilated, kindled, and ignited, etc. Thus, the difference between the windy exhalation and this mother of comets is this: the former is light, hot, and dry, and difficult to ignite because it has no fatness in it; the latter is earthly, thick, fatty, and viscous, composed of densely compacted and easily flammable parts.

Thus these Peripatetics fall into Scylla while wishing to avoid Charybdis <note>A classical metaphor for trying to avoid one mistake only to fall into another.</note> when, in the description of the generation of both meteors, they show that both materials are false and not at all true. For what is the reason that one exhalation—since it is not fit for ignition and consequently less opposed to cold, and since it is lighter in its substance than the other—is nevertheless hindered in its ascent by the force of the cold in the middle region of the air and beaten back down to the place from which it was raised? Yet, meanwhile, the other exhalation—which is thick, fatty, and flammable, and consequently most opposed to the cold of the middle region of the air, and less suited for upward motion because of its heavy thickness—has a path through the middle region of the air into the highest region without any opposition from the cold? How poorly these things agree, and how adverse they are to the laws of Philosophy! Namely, that heavy and more compact things should ascend more easily by natural appetite and tend upward by their nature than those which are light; and furthermore, that those things which are further removed from ignition by their nature should be more infested and attacked by cold than those which are flammable and of a purely fiery disposition? From this it is clear that when they say the coldness of the middle region of the air is the cause of the hindrance to the ascent of the windy exhalation, which is hot and dry but not flammable, they are entirely...

### CHAPTER IV.

->*Where the admirable nature and disposition of the air is clearly discussed.*<-

**S**i <note>This "S" marks the beginning of the chapter, originally printed as a large decorative initial.</note> therefore it is asked by the curious: what is the material origin of meteors—or indeed of all things, whether perfectly or imperfectly mixed—or what is the immediate cause from simple things and of simple things? We say it is the substance of the air itself, altered from its simplicity. For this reason, Anaximenes <note>Anaximenes of Miletus (c. 585 – c. 528 BC), a Greek philosopher who believed air was the primary substance of all things.</note>—and not without foresight—did not blush to boldly assert that air was the cause of all things. Indeed, the air is so ancient a principle that Anaximander <note>Another Greek philosopher, though usually associated with the "apeiron" (the infinite) rather than air, which the author here critiques.</note> did not hesitate to estimate it as God, though in this he was quite inconsiderate. The vast dimension of this our history and its abstruse depth compel me to treat and discourse upon its nature and hidden properties in this place.

Regarding the essence and consistency of the air, it is called *RUACH* <note>Hebrew: רוּחַ, meaning spirit, wind, or breath.</note> by the Hebrews, by which name spirit or wind is also understood. Whence these three also seem to differ very little from one another in respect to the word *Ruach*, which denotes them in many places of the Holy Scriptures, seeing as they all agree in the same essence. Therefore *Ruach*, or Air, is that great spirit occupying the vast cavity of the world with its mass, which encompasses heaven and earth in its embrace and fills all things that are in the world; for it is present in angels, stars, men, beasts, plants, the earth, the water, and stones, permeating all things. Moreover, it is not double or multiple in its substance, but uniform; not divided, but a single spirit, and as it were the one and only perfect life and spirit of the world. In its existence it is thin, slender, subtle, invisible, incomprehensible, impalpable, and spiritual; and in its essence, it is not inaptly compared to the spirit and soul of man. For just as the human soul or spirit (which is also derived from the air) is the tabernacle of the spirit of God, and also of other spirits of God (whence it is called the temple of the Holy Spirit by the holy writings), so also the Air is the habitation of the Holy Spirit of God, and also of other spirits. For we are taught here and there in the Holy Bible that thick clouds are His pavilion, that He rides upon the wings of the wind, and that His spirits or angels are winds and His ministers flaming fires. From this it is clear that the Principle of this world dwells in the air. From the air, therefore, and through the air, all creatures live, grow, and move by means of the Word; for they are primarily constituted of air and filled with air, which rejoices in its own likeness. Hence, those more skilled in Philosophy maintain that air is a spirit of an incomprehensible nature and the most ancient foundation of things, which occupies the vast cavity of the universal world and is observed to perpetually circulate through all things contained under heaven—visiting them, cultivating them, inspiring them, transforming them, binding them, keeping them in vigor, nourishing them, and miraculously sustaining them. Whence the Hebrews did not count it in the number of the elements <note>The traditional four elements were Earth, Water, Air, and Fire. The author suggests some Hebrew traditions viewed Air as a higher unifying force rather than just one of the four.</note>, but rather made it the firm bond and connection of all higher things with lower things. And not far from these is the opinion of the Pythagoreans, who thought that the air was a certain great divine organ or instrument, which perpetually resonates both on earth and in the heavens, and retains the higher things with the lower in union and concord. For this reason, if someone passes through a place where a man was killed, or where a corpse was recently hidden, he is immediately shaken with fear and horror. Regarding the disposition or <term>complexion</term> <note>A person's "complexion" was their specific balance of the four qualities (hot, cold, moist, dry).</note> of this spirit, a huge difference of opinion seems to have arisen among the princes of the Philosophers (Galen, *On the Powers of Simple Medicines*, Book 2, Chapter 20), who are observed to be quite inconsistent with one another in their writings. For Aristotle and those who follow his opinion think the air is **hot**; the Stoics, opposing them, confidently say it is **cold**. But if we explore the matter a little more accurately, we will perceive that it is by itself neither hot nor cold, nor moist nor dry, but consists in a middle state between these qualities. Hence, it is judged to be fit and suitable for receiving any of these accidental impressions, although the air itself exists with no certain or manifest quality. And thus it is observed to be sometimes hot, sometimes cold, sometimes moist, and not rarely dry. Therefore, it is not improperly compared to the celestial **Mercury**, the messenger of Jupiter, as was said above; for Mercury is accustomed to put on the nature of the quality of whichever planet he is joined with. Thus, he is observed to be cold and dry with Saturn, more hot and less moist with Jupiter, hot and dry with Mars, but with the Sun in a more moderate degree, more moist and less hot with Venus, and cold and moist with the Moon. The air is observed to provide this same function, as it desires to receive a varying temperature according to the variety of celestial influences and the difference of the blowing winds. Therefore we say that the air, considered simply and in its own nature, is neither hot, nor cold, nor moist, nor dry. However, insofar as it withdrew from the abyss of dark <term>hyle</term> <note>Hyle is the Greek term for "prime matter," the raw, unformed substance of the universe.</note> in the first creation under the name of "the waters," it is more apt to participate in the quality of darkness (which especially rules in the absence of light), namely **coldness**. But insofar as it participates in the form of light, it is rendered ready to receive hot and fiery influences. From this it is clear that in its own nature, without respect to other influences, its aptitude for coldness is removed by its inclination toward the heat of the informing light; therefore it cannot be called hot or cold originally and in its essence. Since moisture and dryness are simple qualities derived from the primary ones (that is, from heat and cold), it follows that the air by its nature is neither cold nor hot, and consequently neither moist nor dry.
