# On the Material Cause of Weather Phenomena. 23

The potential existence of air within the *hyle* <note>original: "hyla"; a term for the primordial, unformed matter of the universe</note> or the dark chaos was naturally a companion to potential coldness. This coldness later flowed out from the darkness along with the water at the creation of the world. Therefore, the air has a certain hidden inclination toward moisture; however, this is not essential to the existence of air, as it can be converted into an extremely dry nature or condition, as is seen during the summer season. We conclude, therefore, that the air is fit to receive any of the four aforementioned qualities <note>Heat, Cold, Moisture, and Dryness</note>. It is accustomed to bringing this aptitude into actual effect constantly, according to the nature and condition of the wind that happens to be blowing. For example: North winds <note>original: "Aquilonares"</note> render it cold and dry; South winds <note>original: "Australes"</note> make it warm and moist; the East wind and the Southeast wind <note>original: "Eurus"</note> make it warm and dry; and the West winds make it cold and moist. From this, it follows that the quality of the air can change at any moment according to the ordination of GOD, who disposes it according to His will; indeed, the air itself receives whatever is poured into it, yet it nevertheless retains and preserves its own spiritual and uniform essence.

### CHAPTER V.

->*Where the active method of changing air from one quality to another is explained. Here also is treated how air itself is accustomed to be altered and changed daily from a thin to a thick and visible constitution.*<-

Although the air (as has just been said) is unique and simple in its own nature and existence, it is nevertheless moved from one quality to another through the mediation of the Word and the angelic ministers who blow the various winds. Consequently, it is accustomed to migrate from a dense substance into a thin or moderate one, and conversely from a thin substance into a dense one, and this happens daily. For who, being practiced in common experience, does not see that clouds are thickened out of the air? And who does not see the very substance of the air condensed into hail, ice, and hoarfrost by the northern cold? The Holy Scriptures teach us that this cold gushes forth from the divine breath. For (as it says in Job, chapter 37, verse 10 <note>The text cites verse 9, but the quote "By the breath of God frost is given" is verse 10</note>): *The mighty GOD produces ice by his breath, and by the breathing of GOD the frost grows.* And elsewhere it is said: *He sends forth his command to the earth, his word runs very swiftly; he gives snow like wool, and scatters hoarfrost like ashes; he casts forth his ice like morsels; who can stand before his cold?* (Psalm 147, verses 15–17).

Therefore, it is clear from this that thin and invisible air thickens into dense and hard matter through the mediation of the word of GOD producing His cold. This word (as the fountain of truth testifies in Psalm 104) is carried out by angels who are most powerful in strength. Again, when heat is sent out through the mediation of the Word with the angels administering it, the air—having been reduced by contrary blasts into vapors and watery clouds, and changed by the cold blast into snow, hail, ice, and hoarfrost—is again dissolved into drops of water. This is clear from the conclusion of the last testimony cited from the Psalmist, for it follows in verse 18: *He sends out his word and melts them; as soon as he breathes his word, the waters flow.* From this, he argues that by the sending out of the word (that is, of divine light) and by the blowing of the South Wind by His power, with the Angels ministering, those things which the cold North wind congealed, the South wind dissolves back into what they were before.

Moreover, no one commonly practiced in the boiling of liquids can deny that watery vapor is dissolved into air by the action of heat, as if into the "first matter" from which it originally arose. Therefore, cold condenses the air, while heat refines it. However, the cause of this condensation and refinement is always achieved with the assistance of the winds and their qualities. By the opposition of these winds, the air in between is compressed and reduced first into the form of vapor, and then later into watery smoke or a cloudy substance. This occurs especially if a warm and moist wind (the South wind) contends against a cold and dry wind (the North wind). For it is necessary that the watery or moist mass of air—from which rains are generated, or the dry mass that gives birth to hail and snow—be procreated in the gap or middle space of the air between these opposing blasts, according to which opposing wind dominates. 

But where the North wind blows and the South wind offers little or no opposition, there ice, frost, and hoarfrost are produced from the condensation and constriction of the air and waters. Likewise, when the South wind blows, if the North wind does not oppose it, we see that the sky does not abound so much with clouds, nor is the air so damp; but since the northern wind rarely rests, there are also rarely southern winds that are not associated with clouds and rains. 

We say, therefore, that the uniform nature of the air is accidentally suited to take on whatever disposition the winds provide. Thus, when the North wind <note>Boreas</note> blows from the North, it congeals and thickens the air itself; it gathers and glues together its dispersed parts with its dryness, and the coldness coagulates and thickens it, converting it (as is evident in snow, hoarfrost, and hail) into an earthy condition. But when the South wind <note>Auster</note> blows from the South, that wind conversely converts that portion of the air which the North wind made earthy back into water, because the works of cold are destroyed and dissolved by heat. Again, the warm and dry spirits of the East wind <note>Eurus</note> convert that water into an airy or fiery disposition, which the West wind nourishes and refreshes with its breath. Are we not taught by the testimony of all truth that winds of this kind have power over the air? ## CHAPTER VIII.

### On the three stages in the movement of increase and growth between simple air and meteorological bodies (or imperfectly mixed things), and on their mathematical ratio.

In the final chapter of the previous small book, you have seen it declared that a progression was made from nothing—or from the <term>womb of matter</term><note>original: "hylæ gremio." In Renaissance philosophy, "hyle" refers to the formless, primordial substance from which the world was created.</note>—through the emanation of light toward unity. By the revelation of this light, another "potential unity" was produced with an opposite disposition: namely, darkness. From there, the progression moved from the <term>monad</term> to the <term>dyad</term>, and from the dyad to the <term>triad</term><note>The author uses Pythagorean numerology: 1 (Monad) is divine unity; 2 (Dyad) is division or darkness; 3 (Triad) is the reconciliation of the two.</note>, through the introduction and production of the humid spirit. This spirit acts as a "glue" between these two, joining both extremes together just as a soul is joined with a body. Finally, the progression of all these things reached the <term>quaternary</term> number (four), which serves as the completion of the simple world. This produced the four elements, differing from one another in their actual existence. These elements are the immediate beginnings of all mixed things, just as in geometry, squared surfaces are the immediate principles of a cubic body. We have depicted this arithmetic order in the following way:

In this order, **h. 4.** relates to the **perfectly mixed body** just as **1. a** (or the light of simple progression) relates to **e. 4.** (the four elements). Furthermore, just as **b. 2.** represents <term>prime matter</term> <note>original: "materiam primam" — the formless "stuff" of the universe before it is given shape</note> and **form**, from which the four elements proceeded through multiplication, so indeed do **e. 4.** (or the four elements) denote matter and form in the simplicity of the elements. From these elements, through further multiplication, bodies emerge that are more profoundly and perfectly mixed the deeper the **unity** immerses itself into the **multitude of matter**. 

Therefore, just as the luminous unity **1. a.** is the most simple source of all <term>simples</term> <note>original: "simplicium" — pure, unmixed substances like the base elements</note>, so also **e. 4.** (or the four elements) are the most simple origin of mixed bodies. In this progression of mixtures, the order of **5** (the <term>quinary</term>) relates to the others as **2** relates to nothingness (or darkness) among the simples. Similarly, the order of **6** relates to **5** as **2** relates to **1**; and **7** to **6** as **3** is to **2**; and finally **8** to **7** as **4** is to **3**. 

As we see in the first progression, where **2** was created as **1** shone forth, so also the four elements, by clustering together within the "womb" of the single **Air**—which is their parent and the universal spirit of the world—produce the first species of mixture. From these come the winds and invisible <term>meteors</term> <note>In the 1600s, "meteor" referred to any atmospheric phenomenon, including rain, wind, or lightning, not just falling stars.</note>, both fiery and watery. These gradually thicken through the force of the winds and visibly take on a fiery nature (represented by the 6th order). This has a relationship to the **3** of the simple progression, in which either water is abundantly illuminated by light (denoting fiery meteors in the second degree of mixture), or water prevails over the light (indicating thunderous meteors). 

Finally, the **septenary** <note>the number seven</note> degree shows more dense and dark meteors, such as clouds of hail, snow, and rain, and others of that kind. If these proceed further into composition, they coalesce into **perfectly mixed bodies**. For this must be known for certain: all bodies—whether animal, vegetable, or mineral—are nothing other than **clouds or meteors** brought to a state of perfect mixture. For who can doubt that any perfectly mixed thing was first imperfectly mixed? It is necessary for imperfection to come between the simples and those things completely composed of simples; it is impossible to find two extremes where the "middle" between the starting point and the destination is missing. We observe this even in the movement toward generation: **sperm** is a kind of imperfect mixture, a "little cloud of generation" <note>original: "nubeculam generationis"</note> which proceeds steadily by natural motion until it reaches the complete production of the fetus or the perfect mixture.

We say, therefore, that a **meteor** is called "imperfectly mixed" because it is "on the way"—a natural motion arising between the simple elements in the womb of the air. It moves toward the goal of perfection for whichever species it tends toward. If it fails in its motion due to some impediment in its path, so that it cannot progress further toward perfection, it gradually returns to its simple nature from which it was first derived. 

If it is procreated by poisonous winds or malevolent spirits blowing together, it usually infects the air and brings a bad omen. But if it is procreated by benevolent breaths by divine power, it sometimes purges and cleanses the air, bringing a good and propitious omen to the earth and its fruits; it is even proven to be healthy for the lives of animals, if God so wills. We should not doubt that meteors contribute to the production of perfectly mixed bodies, since we are taught by experience that **frogs, worms, and monstrous animals**—as well as flesh, blood, grain, and other crops, and even stones, sand, and dust—have fallen from the clouds and the air by the blast of the winds. <note>The author refers to "prodigies" or "blood rain," which historical observers often interpreted as spontaneous generation occurring in the atmosphere.</note> It must be understood, therefore, that there are meteors of both generation and corruption.

# **BOOK THREE**

## **Section I**

### *Concerning the formal cause of Meteors.*

#### **Chapter I of Section I**

->*Precisely treats the formal cause of the Meteors of both worlds, as well as their differences.*<-

Since in the preceding book we have discussed enough—and more than enough (as it seems to us)—the material origin of the meteors <note>In the 17th century, "meteors" referred to all atmospheric phenomena, including rain, wind, and rainbows, not just falling stars.</note> of both worlds, it is my intention in this place, for the sake of a more certain method, to discuss their formal cause <note>The "formal cause" is a philosophical term for the essence, shape, or design that makes a thing what it is.</note>, though briefly and succinctly. Therefore, just as we declared in the aforementioned sections that the material cause of meteors is that from which all meteors are fashioned as a substantial part—namely, from a thinner substance of air, more or less contracted and compressed according to the condition of the meteor—so we also affirm that their formal cause is that by which those meteors, as far as their material existence is concerned, are thus sculpted or delineated from the universal and invisible mass of the world’s air. That is, they are brought into visible action and claim for themselves a particular name and essence; for this cause is what is accustomed to adorn and clothe, or figure, this or that aerial vapor with various and diverse shapes, differing from one another.

Indeed, this diversity of likenesses or images is shown to proceed from the hidden and internal form of the meteors, not otherwise than as the external image or figure of a man proceeds from his internal essence (which is appropriated to him alone), making his structure differ from that of other animals and plants, by which we recognize from afar that this or that person is neither a beast nor a plant. By a clearly similar reasoning or distinction, we gather and distinguish a dark meteor from a bright one—that is, species from species—and again, in a more particular respect, one bright thing from another bright thing, and one opaque or dark thing from another dark thing. For example, we observe a comet, or lightning, or a spear, or a burning column to be distinguished and differ from a cloud, a mist, a halo, or dew; and even in the same region or species, we see a comet vary from a burning column, or from lightning, by the same formal difference. Similarly, in a dark <insert>region</insert> <note>The original text contains a struck-through word here, likely a printer's correction.</note>, even the common eye discerns that a cloud differs from a mist, and a mist from dew, and rain from frost, and so on. Hence it is that in this treatise of ours, by means of formal causes, we distribute meteors first into their genera <term>genera: broad categories or families</term>, then those into their species, and those finally, through various subdivisions, into infinite individuals; not otherwise than we see the trunk of a tree divided into branches, and those again into subdivided twigs, which finally end in little shoots, so that by an easier method you may arrive at the goal of our intention.

And since our purpose in this present treatise leads us to compare the meteors of the greater world <note>The Macrocosm: the universe.</note> with those of the lesser world <note>The Microcosm: the human body.</note>, or man himself, so that we might more clearly demonstrate the reason for his health or sickness through the effects of the good or bad meteors generated within him; therefore, through the whole thread of this progression of ours, after each chapter concerning the meteors of the Macrocosm, we have made a correlation and comparison between the members of the preceding chapter and those of the Microcosm or man—namely, by applying the meteors, humors, and properties of the one to those of the other, as the subject and the occasion to be treated presents itself.

We find it written, not without wise counsel, by **Hermes Trismegistus** <note>original: "Mercurio Trismegisto." The "Great World" or the universe at large.</note>.

Indeed, since both the spirit and the body of the "lesser world" (man) are derived from those of the "greater world" (the universe), it must infallibly follow that the airy and ethereal spirit in man, as well as his dark body, is sustained and nourished by the world. At every moment, man remains in his state and existence through this connection. He adheres to the worldly parts, both spiritual and bodily, by an unbreakable bond, such that they cannot be separated from each other even by death or the dissolution of the physical compound. For this reason, it has been so from the beginning: when the elements of the greater world fall ill, the airy and terrestrial parts of man are very quickly infected, as will be described more accurately in the chapters to follow.

Wind is a spirit or invisible air, animated and quickened by divine light from the face or sight of Jehovah, like a breath proceeding from his nostrils, to execute his pleasure both in the heavens and on the earth.

Wind is a certain angelic spirit; or subtle air inspired and animated by the fiery spirit of Jehovah, sometimes visible and manifest, as in lightning and flashes, sometimes invisible and hidden, like that which is heard but not at all seen, sent forth from some quarter of the world in a divine and secret manner to execute the divine will, whether for salvation and benevolence, or for punishment and a curse upon the earth.

Wind is an angelic spirit, breathing here and there secretly and invisibly according to the hidden good pleasure of the creator; though its noise may be heard, the limit of where it comes from or where it goes is unknown to mortals. *John 3:8. This is proven because everything is resolved back into that from which it was originally created. Wood, wheat, and the animal body are reduced by the violence of fire into smoke or thick vapor, almost like a cloud, which is also gradually dissipated into invisible air, from which all things are seen to depart. Since no creature can grow or live deprived of air, we say therefore that the whole composite body is nothing other than air of various conditions, fashioned into that which it is.

## Chapter I. Of Part II.

### Where meteorological bodies procreated from winds are treated in general.

The condition of meteorological bodies, in both substance and form, is the same as that of perfectly mixed things. These were previously bodies imperfectly mixed during their movement away from aerial simplicity; in that state, they took on the form of meteorological bodies. This happens, specifically, between the "limit from which" <note>original: *terminum a quo* — the starting point in Aristotelian physics</note>, which is the purely aerial state, and the "limit to which" <note>original: *illum ad quem*</note>, namely, perfect composition. You have already seen this sufficiently demonstrated in the preceding sections.

From these points, it seems clear enough that everything that exists is originally, regarding its consistency, only one and the same thing—namely, air. There is no composite thing in the world that is not either a meteor or made from a meteor. I say "a meteor" if it is an imperfect body; and "from a meteor" because it is through the nature of a meteor that the transition must be made from a simple nature to one that is perfectly mixed. 

For it is impossible for a progression to happen from a starting point to an ending point without a middle stage being interposed. In the number two <note>the binary</note>, no perfection is found, since it has only two limits; for this reason, the Pythagoreans <note>Followers of Pythagoras who believed numbers were the ultimate reality</note> quite reasonably called it a "confused and imperfect number." Therefore, they most rightly attributed the dignity of perfection to the number three <note>the ternary</note>, because in it three terms are found: the beginning, the middle, and the end. These terms in a composition are like an imperfectly mixed or meteorological body. 

Thus we see dough being formed from impalpable flour as if from air; the dough acts as the middle term or the composition-in-motion between the bread and the flour. Then, by the reduction of moisture and by cooking, that imperfect composite is strengthened and reduced into the perfect form of bread. Does it not also appear in the testing <note>original: *examine* — referring to a metallurgical assay</note> of wood, or animal bodies, or even metals like lead, iron, copper, etc., in the hearth or cupel <note>a shallow vessel used in refining precious metals</note>, that those bodies are first turned by the violence of fire into thick smoke or a cloud...

Since it is certain and beyond all doubt that two things are required for the constitution of bodies—both those of a meteorological nature and those perfectly mixed (which also stem from the meteorological)—I believe it will be worthwhile to diligently inquire into the nature of those two things. But because it is impossible for anything in the nature of things to be performed without action (which comes from the <term>Form</term><note>In this context, "Form" refers to the organizing principle or "soul" of an object, not just its shape.</note>) and passion <note>original: "passione" – here meaning the capacity to be acted upon or shaped</note> (which comes from the <term>Matter</term>), we must inspect the natures of these two in their composition, as without them nothing in the world can exist. We find that **Form** is a single, simple thing—the primary, central act, the offspring of the primary light. It forms and effects all things; it is supernatural and uncreated in its origin, yet clothed in a natural spirit and effect, making it natural and created. Hence, the Book of Ecclesiasticus <note>Also known as the Book of Sirach</note> says: *Wisdom is the first creature* <note>original: "Sapientia est prima creatura." Ecclus. 1:4</note>, and that light was created on the first day. Thus, in one respect—namely, regarding the garment of the spiritual world which it puts on—it is called an **Angel**. In respect to the purely formal soul, or the great name of **GOD** inscribed in the Angel, it is **Jehovah**, or the immediate emanation of GOD (the fountain of light) into the world, through which His spirit, existing only in potential, was informed. And so it is said that light was created on the first day; that is, the spirit shining with divine light—either the light itself or the divine act—clothed in the spiritual substance of the world and illuminated by its presence. Hence it was said by David, *GOD is clothed in light* <note>Psalm 104:2</note>, which is to say, in an illuminated spirit; that is, the glory of GOD shines in His creature. So also in His wrath, GOD is called a *consuming fire*. And this light or form sometimes assumes the name of its "garment." Thus we find it written, *Wisdom was a covering for the Israelites by day and the light of the stars by night* <note>Wisdom of Solomon 10:17</note>, and elsewhere, *I, Wisdom, came out of the mouth of the most High, and like a mist I covered the earth; my throne was in a pillar of cloud, etc.* <note>Ecclesiasticus 24</note>. This **Divine Wisdom**, therefore, is the act of acts and the central mover in every creature; whence the wise man said, *the incorruptible spirit of GOD is in every thing* <note>Wisdom of Solomon 12:1</note>. This same luminous spirit of GOD is its central power, without which it can neither live nor exist.

That this spirit of Wisdom is the innermost light and "soul of souls" of meteors—and indeed the mystical, secret soul of every substance, whether imperfect or perfect—is evident from several points. First, in its perfection it surpasses all things, insofar as it is divine, incorruptible, and uncreated. Second, it is more mobile than all moving things, simpler and more subtle than any spirit, and more powerful than any act. Third, it is in every thing, as has been said—that is, in every element and every thing composed of elements. We can also very easily gather this from the words of the previously mentioned passage: *I, Wisdom, covered the earth like a mist; my throne is in a pillar of cloud; I alone compassed the circuit of heaven, and walked in the bottom of the deep; in the waves of the sea and in all the earth, and in every people and nation I have taken rest.* Therefore, it is Divine Wisdom—which the wise man clearly describes with these words—that is the *holy spirit of understanding, unique or simple, manifold, subtle, undefiled, certain, sweet, free from passion, acute, kind, human, possessing all virtues, overseeing all things, containing all intelligible spirits, more mobile than all moving things, reaching everywhere because of its purity, a vapor or emanation of the power or brightness of God; since it is one, it can do all things, and remaining in itself, it renews all things, and passes through individual nations.* <note>Wisdom of Solomon 7</note>. This, I say, is the central life or principle and the most internal being of every thing that exists in this world. It is not that **fictitious or imaginary form of Aristotle**, who attributes everything to its own nature and not immediately to GOD. *By the Word,* says the Evangelist, *all things were made, and without him nothing was made; in him was life, and that life was the light of men; the world was made by him, and the world knew him not.* <note>John 1</note>. How foolish, therefore, is that distinction of the "Christian" philosophers, by which they wish to distinguish and separate GOD from His power and virtue, saying that GOD is everywhere "virtually" (by His power) but not "essentially." This is as if any sane or consistent person were to say that the power of GOD could be separated or divided from His essence, any more than solar rays could be separated from the sun itself, which are in every way inseparable. Even **Hermes Trismegistus** seems to confirm this in his *Pimander*, Chapter 12: *Mind is indeed of the very essence of GOD—if indeed He has an essence—and it is born from it; wherefore it is by no means divided from the essence of GOD, but rather connected to it in the same way that light is connected to the body of the Sun.* This "World-Mind" is that immediate emanation, the brightness of eternal light, the spotless mirror of the divine majesty, and the image of His goodness. It is through this that we know GOD "from behind" <note>original: "à posteriori" – meaning by observing the effects or the created world rather than the cause directly</note>—that is, in His creatures. It is that very Wisdom which we described above by the testimony of Holy Scripture <note>Wisdom of Solomon 7</note>.

### CHAPTER III.
### Concerning Universal Water and its species, and how it is the passive matter of anything whether perfectly or imperfectly mixed.

Just as the "form" <note>The "form" is the active, shaping principle in Aristotelian philosophy.</note> of all things, whether mixed or simple, is an internal, uncreated light or a certain incorruptible spirit implanted in them by God from the creation (without whose presence they could not live or even exist), so also that spirit is the garment or the immediate <term>vehicle</term><note>A "vehicle" (vehiculum) is a medium through which a higher power acts on a lower substance.</note> of this light, by which the invisible air (namely, the wind) is moved at the command of this God-like spirit dwelling in the center. From this it follows that all things in the world were created primarily from water and through water, by the operation of that central spirit; but secondarily from the "heaven" (as the internal and spiritual part) and the "earth" (as the external and physical part), since these two are what fill and complete the vast cavity of the world. And this is confirmed by St. Peter, in a passage often cited by us previously, who says: *That the heavens were of old, and the earth consisting of water and through water by the word of God.* From which it follows, that those things which are immediately forged from the mixing of heaven and earth are originally made from and through water—not, however, from waters alone, which are the **passive parts** in the composition, but by the mediation of the active divine Word, without which (according to John) nothing was made, as the life of the creature is in it. Or, as said before, it is through the mediation of Wisdom, *which was the brightness of the eternal light emanating from the mouth of the Most High before any creature, and which (by the testimony of the wise man) was assisting her Father in his works,* or as the leader Moses holds, *by the mediation of the spirit of the Lord, which was carried over the waters,* giving them fiery vigor or life.

We see, therefore, that the waters created first among worldly things are all that which is now called "heaven" and "earth," and consequently, it is certain that they fill the vast concavity of the world. Whence also, just as the heaven or air expanded everywhere in its spiritual nature is of an invisible consistency, so the "thin earth" is visible water, and the thick part or the dregs (the "dead head," so to speak) of the whole is the opaque earth itself—both of a more humid substance like the mud and mire of the earth, and of a drier and harder substance. Thus we think it is not absurd to distinguish between visible and invisible waters: namely, into **celestial** and **earthly**. ### CHAPTER III.

#### The first part: Concerning dark, watery meteors in the Macrocosm.

| | | |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Dark meteors in the Macrocosm of a watery consistency are either** | **Thin & vaporous**, such as: | **Halo**, **Fog**, **Cloud**. |
| | **Thick**. | See section O. |

Dark meteors of a watery consistency are substances that are either thinner or thicker. We call those meteors "thinner" which are more spread out, softer, and less compact in their parts; these are halfway between simple, invisible air and common water. We call those "thick" which are either liquid water or frozen, or which are compacted with earth, about which we will speak below. Watery meteors of a thinner consistency are various degrees of vapors or fumes, where one is denser or heavier than another, or closer to the water toward which they tend. These include the **Halo**, **Fog** <note>original: "Nebula"</note>, and **Cloud** <note>original: "Nubes"</note>, which we will deal with here in more detail—first by explaining Aristotle's opinion on the origin or generation of such meteors, and then how that opinion either agrees or disagrees with the testimony of Holy Scripture.

Aristotle, along with the rest of the Peripatetics <note>The "Peripatetics" were followers of Aristotle's philosophy.</note>, defines the **Halo** as a whitish circle with a black edge appearing around the Sun, Moon, or a bright star. It is formed from moist vapor rising from the land and waters, condensed into a very thin cloudlet or cloud, which creates a circular shape in the eyes of the observers beneath the star. This is usually a sign of rain if it gradually turns black and becomes thicker throughout; but if it breaks with a large gap on one side, it portends winds from that region where it first opens and bursts. These are his views. Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, a Roman natural philosopher.</note> also recognizes that the circle of a Halo is sometimes the color of blood because of the density of the cloud surrounding the sun (Pliny, Book 2, Chapter 30).

**Fog** <note>original: "Nebula"</note>, according to the opinion of the Peripatetics, is a kind of "sterile" cloud—that is, one without rain—which remains from the residue of vapor gushing from the earth and waters that could not be raised high enough or condensed into a cloud. Or it can be defined thus: Fog is vapor drawn upward from the waters and earth by the heat of the sun; however, because the solar heat is not strong enough to lift that vapor into the middle region of the air to be contracted into a cloud by the cold of that place, the heat allows it to descend gradually back to the earth after a small amount of condensation.

A **Cloud** <note>original: "Nubes"</note> (which is the most general category for the others mentioned above) is vapor raised from the lands and waters into the middle region of the air by the force of solar heat. There, it is contracted and, as it were, "frozen" into the consistency of a cloud by the power of extreme cold. Afterward, it is driven here and there through the middle region of the air, partly by the heat of the sun and partly by the force of the winds.

Finally, they define a **small cloud** <note>original: "Nubeculam"</note> as a tiny cloud contracted into a huge magnitude by the union or addition of vapors flying successively into the heights; hence the common proverb: *A great storm can often arise from a small cloud.*

In conclusion, all these meteors seem to differ not only in their material cause but also in their external form, as some are more or less compact than others, and some are smaller or thinner in quantity than others. Therefore, once the matter and form of one have been investigated with diligent intuition, the others will reveal themselves more clearly by that light, since they are all of the same nature and condition.

In the definition of the condition of any such meteor, three things are worthy of observation: namely, the **matter**, the **place**, and the **efficient cause**.

Aristotle makes the matter of the halo, the fog, and the cloud the same: namely, moist vapor gushing from the earth and water as the places appropriate for its generation. But let us hear what the Sacred Page <note>A traditional term for the Bible.</note> tells of the origin of such small clouds and clouds, so that we may see by the testimony of the whole truth...

<meta>This page continues a philosophical and scientific inquiry into meteorology, specifically the formation and movement of clouds. It transitions from an observation of low-hanging storm clouds to a critique of classical Aristotelian theories regarding atmospheric regions.</meta>

60 Section I. Portion IV. Part II. Book III. Member I.

And sometimes, when summer thunderstorms occur, clouds are observed to almost touch the tops of tall trees; therefore, it is clear that clouds do not consist of vapor raised from the earth or waters by the force of solar heat into the **middle region of the air** <term>The "middle region" was a concept in early meteorology describing a layer of the atmosphere believed to be perpetually cold, where vapors condensed into clouds.</term> and then condensed and frozen by the intense cold of that place, as those **Pagans** <note>original: "Ethnici." This refers to ancient Greek and Roman philosophers, specifically Aristotle and his followers, whose natural philosophy dominated European universities for centuries.</note> claim.

Then, afterwards, he proceeds to the **efficient cause** <term>In Aristotelian philosophy, the "efficient cause" is the primary agent or force that brings something into being.</term> and the procreating cause of the cloud, which he says is solar heat. By the power of this heat, such vapor is not only lifted from the earth and water, but it is also moved here and there, partly by the sun’s power and partly by the winds. However, he identifies the cold of the middle region of the air as the cause that constricts the vapor. From this, two agents—contrary in their nature and condition—seem to work together to complete the formation of a cloud: namely, the heat of the sun and the cold of the middle region of the air. Yet, he provides no internal cause for the movement of the cloud, as if it were by its very nature formless and inanimate. In this part of the definition, therefore, many doubts arise for the careful observer that must be resolved. As a result, they should produce either no clouds or at least thinner ones than the other winds. Yet experience teaches us it is far otherwise, for those winds are noted for thickening the air and producing clouds far denser and wetter than the others. Indeed, these winds so thicken the middle air that they usually make objects appear larger to the eyes than other winds do, as **Isidore** <note>Isidore of Seville, an influential medieval encyclopedist.</note> testifies.

If, therefore, we agree with the Pagan, the doctrine of the Holy Page must be rejected, and thus falsehood embraced instead of truth.

Indeed, they falsely attribute to created things what Holy Scripture teaches us is derived most closely and immediately from the **Creator**. As far as the consistency of the Halo is concerned, it exists in the form of a transparent <term>mist</term><note>The author uses "nebula" to mean a low-level atmospheric mist or fog.</note>, through whose vaporous substance the stellar rays can most easily penetrate. This consistency is applied to it in a denser or thinner measure according to the will of divine wisdom, in whose power it is *to give weight to the air, and to weigh out the waters or vapors by measure, Job 28:25.* Thus it happens that, according to the diversity of quantity in density and thinness, He produces various effects according to the creator’s will, as will be more clearly explained in our treatise on the final cause. It is necessary, therefore, that the consistency of this kind of meteor is not of the purely natural constitution of the air, which is invisible and consequently cannot visibly receive such impressions; nor is it of a dense mist or cloud, because a stellar body <note>A "stellar body" refers to any celestial light source, like the sun, moon, or stars.</note> could scarcely—if at all—be seen through such bodies, and consequently could not print its own circular image upon it. Instead, it is a medium between a bodily darkness and that incorporeal state in which air is rendered invisible; it does not so obscure the light with darkness that it is not somewhat transparent. Yet, certainly, this transparency must not be without some darkness, because otherwise the reflection of the "species" <note>In medieval optics, a "species" is the visual image or form of an object traveling through a medium.</note> cannot occur, and consequently there will be no visible impression of the rays or the received image, just as one may see clearly in glass and in the air itself. Hence **Algazel** <note>Al-Ghazali, a 12th-century philosopher.</note> rightly says in *On the Nature of the Mirror*: *That no part of the celestial sphere is an object for the power of sight, nor capable of receiving and retaining the light of the sun, except for its denser part, which we call the star itself; because,* he says, *those other parts of the sphere, being more rare, do not become bright when light is cast toward them, because they are not subject to color, for they are not visible.* This also seems to be confirmed by **Haten** <note>Alhazen (Ibn al-Haytham), a foundational figure in optics.</note> in Book 1 of *On Optics*, saying that what has no color is not visible, because (he says) a thing is not visible except according to the light in the thing seen; for visible light occupies only that which is colored. From this it is clear that the substance of the Halo must be misty, and of a consistency between an invisible spirit and an entirely opaque body, so that it may better receive the forms of the stars within itself. Whence **Albertus** <note>Albertus Magnus, a 13th-century polymath.</note> says that the images of bodies can be most easily expressed in moist air, no differently than in a mirror or in its reflections. For this reason, it is even recorded that a certain person, due to the weakness of his sight, found that the nearby air in a time of humidity served him as a mirror; the rays could not perfectly penetrate through it but were partially reflected. The same thing also tends to happen to those afflicted with the most destructive and dangerous illnesses and pestilential fevers; they, looking at their own faces in the air because of the weakness and lack of their visual faculty, think they are looking at demons and foul forms, struck with fear. But I shall proceed to the description of the Mist.

Mist is a transformation of air from its natural and invisible consistency into a visible and thick vaporous substance, by the light of wisdom acting centrally—that is, contracting the air into itself from the inside on all sides—and by its windy ministers lightly compressing it with contrary blasts from the outside.

Mist is therefore of the same matter as its body: and of the same form as that of the Halo; the only difference is in thinness and density: that is, in the formula of its composition.

Regarding the matter of this subject, although we have spoken quite abundantly in the preceding sections, something nevertheless remains to be explained in this place that was not fully demonstrated before: We have said, therefore, that air is the immediate origin of the first grade of <term>meteors</term> <note>In the 17th century, "meteors" referred to all atmospheric phenomena, including rain, wind, and clouds, not just shooting stars.</note>, namely of vapor, which, thickening more and more, is reduced into the consistency of a cloud. Christus Iesus factus est nobis sapientia à DEO"</note> Therefore, the Apostle also says elsewhere, *From him, in him, and through him are all things; to him be praise and honor, verse 36.* 

But this same point is also excellently expressed by the mystical Doctors and <term>Cabalists</term> <note>Followers of the Kabbalah, a tradition of Jewish mysticism often adapted by Christian scholars during the Renaissance.</note>. For Rabbi Bahir says, *That there is no beginning except wisdom:* which, contracted in darkness or invisibly, or in an invisible spirit (according to that saying of Hermes Trismegistus: *The Monad generates the Monad and reflected the heat back into itself* <note>original: "Monas generat monadem & in seipsam reflexit ardorem"</note>—that is, it shone back upon itself), remained as if idle and devoid of action, having respect for "nothing." In such a state, it is called by the Hebrews **Ein** <note>original: "אין" (Ain), meaning Nothingness or the Infinite.</note>, that is, "nothing," or "non-being," and "without end." Our apprehension is so sterile, and our capacity in the contemplation of divine objects so meager and powerless, that we judge those things which do not appear at all as if they do not exist. But truly, when it appears in reality in some form or subsistence, then the Cabalists say that *the dark Aleph is converted into the bright Aleph.* <note>Aleph is the first letter of the Hebrew alphabet. Here, it represents the move from the hidden God to the revealed God.</note> And as the letter **Aleph** is held by them to be a hieroglyphic for God, representing unity and simplicity, so they understand by that "dark" one the hidden GOD, and by the "bright" one the manifest GOD. Hence they also call the bright Aleph **Beth**, which is the second letter in the Hebrew alphabetical order, just as Aleph is the first. Therefore, if Beth is added to the letter Aleph, it is read as **AB**, which is interpreted as "Father," who always has a relation to a "Son." Thus **אב** (AB) denotes the father of all generation, where Aleph is the sign of the father, and Beth of the son, proceeding from the father by divine emanation. 

And this order is esteemed by the Cabalists as the first deduction in the divinity and the primordial beginning of all alteration, which Moses called **Bereshit**, that is, *In the Beginning,* or the immediate emanation of light from infinity. This is the second Cabalistic numbering called **Chochmah** or Wisdom, over which the benevolent name of GOD, **IAH**, presides. Job 38:22.* And elsewhere, *He brings forth the wind from his treasures, Psalm 148.* And elsewhere, *He opened the doors of the heavens and as it were the air, raining down manna etc.* 

From these words of Holy Scripture, the place [of origin] is generally gathered. But truly, what that thing is which is enclosed within the hidden recesses of that treasury chest of GOD is beyond the grasp of the common man to understand—except that it is in the power of divine wisdom to detect and reveal the things reserved and hidden in that secret way according to her good pleasure; to bring the seeds (I say) hidden in the air, which are in potential only, into visible act regarding us. That the matter of mist is air, condensed into a thick vapor, is clear from what has gone before. And although someone might object that the vapor leaping up from the earth's surface is the cause of mist, we have declared in the preceding sections that the earth itself is necessarily filled with air, no differently than a man or any other body—whether animal, mineral, or vegetable. The earth continually breathes this air in through its pores, like an animal or plant, for its own sustenance; for in the air is the hidden food and spiritual nourishment of every creature. Here also, when wisdom is at work with its ministers in the earth (*for the spirit of discipline fills the world, and the incorruptible spirit of God is in every thing,* Wisdom of Solomon 1:7 and 12:1), it is seen to occasionally procreate smokes, vapors, clouds, and waters in the earth through various degrees of condensation. For *wisdom prepares the weight for the air according to its desire and weighs out the waters in measure, both in the earth and in heaven,* Job 28:25. Whence the earth enjoys all its "meteors," and even the human body does as well, no differently than the <term>Macrocosmic</term> <note>The "Great World" or the universe as a whole, as opposed to the "Microcosm" or the human being.</note> heaven, insofar as air is present in them, which is of the same nature as the worldly air, as we have disputed more fully in the preceding pages.

From this, therefore, we discern that there is another species of mist besides that which rises from lakes, rivers, and valleys—namely, that which is suddenly formed from the coagulation of the universal air in a wondrous and occult manner by the operation of wisdom, which fills the entire lower region of the air. Hence it is written in the sacred source: *I came out of the mouth of the most High, and covered the earth like a mist; I had my tent in the highest places, and my throne was in a pillar of cloud; I alone compassed the circuit of heaven, and walked in the depth of the abyss, in the waves of the sea, and in all the earth; and in every people and nation I took rest,* Ecclesiasticus 24:3. Furthermore, wisdom, which made the cloud its tabernacle (no differently than the body is held to be the tabernacle for the soul, whence "man" is understood as soul and body, and in the sacred pages "living soul" is sometimes taken for the whole composite), is sometimes itself called "cloud." Whence it is said, *wisdom was a covering for the Israelites* (that is, the pillar of cloud) *and a light of stars by night,* Wisdom of Solomon 10:17. But in the Psalms it is said, *That God led the Israelites with a cloud by day, and all the night with a light of fire,* Psalm 73:15 <note>Psalm 78:14 in modern numbering.</note>. And in Exodus: *God went before the Israelites in a pillar of cloud by day,* Exodus 13:21. And yet God said, *Behold, I send my angel before you: beware of his face and listen to his voice, for he will not bear your defection, because my name is in him,* Exodus 23:20.

This is my essential power. Therefore, those versed in the <term>angelic mysteries</term> <note>Refers to the study of the hierarchy and nature of angels, often associated with Dionysian or Kabbalistic thought.</note> say that an angel is composed of air and fiery light; hence it is called a duality, since there concur in its composition a created spirit (which is its external part, serving in place of a body) and uncreated light (which is its internal part, acting in place of a mind). Thus, in respect to its external part, it is called an angel or creature in that same chapter, but by reason of its central internal part, it is there called **Jehovah**. This angel was called **Metattron** <note>Metatron, a high-ranking angel in Jewish mystical tradition often identified as the celestial scribe or the "Lesser Yahweh."</note> by the Cabalists and the **Soul of the World** by the Platonists; it was that wisdom proceeding from the mouth of the Father. This uncreated emanation, insofar as it was mixed with the worldly spirit, is called a "creature." The words are as follows: *The Creator created wisdom before the age in the beginning, and she shall not fail in the ages to come; she ministers in the Holy tabernacle before him,* Ecclesiasticus 24:10. From him, in him, and through him are all things.*

By means of its central soul residing in every thing of this world, it brings about the blending of elements and impresses upon them a form suitable to their species. Through this form, one thing is distinguished and separated from any other. This hidden nature possesses no specific color of its own, yet it shares in and creates all colors; it has no weight or quality, yet is ultimately the source of all weights, qualities, and the fertile mother of all things.

### CHAPTER VII.

***On the difference of clouds, according to the testimony of the Philosophers, the Pagans, and the Christian followers themselves, as well as the testimony of Holy Scripture.***

Those who were well-versed in Aristotelian Philosophy proposed many differences between clouds. Specifically, they made some differ from others primarily by a general distinction, namely in *substance* and *quality*. Then, they divided each of these members into their own species. For they distributed their *substance* into the "dense" and the "rare," insofar as thick, heavy clouds and thin, subtle clouds are created in and from the spiritual medium of the lower world. They claim that the former are composed and forged from many thick terrestrial "smokes," <note>Aristotle distinguished between "vapors" (moist) and "exhalations" or "smokes" (dry/earthy).</note> while the latter are from a more subtle and less dense vapor. In this opinion, regarding the difference of clouds in density and thinness, they did not err at all, as they were well-acquainted with the varying consistency of clouds through common experience. 

But truly, in their claim that the material cause of the clouds' density is a thick and terrestrial smoke, they are entirely deceived. This is because the consistency of a cloud, in both its thinness and its density, is actually <term>homogeneous air</term> <note>Air that is uniform in its nature throughout.</note> accumulated in a greater or lesser mass and bound together in a more compact order. For do we not see that the rainwater from the blackest and densest cloud is of the same homogeneity and clarity as that from a thinner, whiter cloud? Therefore, an earthy disposition of "smoke" is not the cause of a cloud's density or gloom, but rather the density of the air itself, or rather the gathering of its vaporous consistency into a deep mass. For in a mist, we see the matter of the mist is the same—namely, condensed air—but its diversity lies in the depth of its composition and its compact union. 

But let us proceed. They were also accustomed to distinguish clouds according to their colored *quality*. Thus, they said black clouds arose from terrestrial smoke, or from something bolted and compact. We, however, confess they arise from air that is strongly and deeply thickened. Those clouds that are reddish or yellowish mixed with blackness, they said arose partly from stellar light or fiery exhalation, and partly from thick terrestrial smoke. We, on the contrary, affirm they are made by the various spirits of the winds compressing the air together with <term>luminous seeds</term> <note>Original: "seminaria luminosa." A concept in vitalist philosophy where "seeds" or formative powers are spread through the atmosphere.</note> or fiery elements expanded everywhere through the air, without any exhalation from the earth. Furthermore, they say that those red clouds with a greenish-black tint are created from exhalations mixed with thick and copious vapor, along with a great quantity of water and moisture. We assert they are born from various vapors or air gathered into one mass according to the various winds blowing from different quarters of the world for their creation. For we see from this that opposing winds tend to produce clouds and lightnings of various colors. Finally, they say white clouds are made from a scarcity of vapor, whereby it happens that, besides the thinness of the subject, the stellar light very easily penetrates the mass and makes it bright.

They also have another distinction for clouds, for they make some "void" and almost empty—namely those which are dispersed through the sky like flocks of wool <note>Likely referring to cirrus clouds.</note>. These the Aristotelians claim are forged more from hot and dry exhalations than from moist vapors or those drenched in wetness. But we, along with the Holy Scriptures, say that luminous clouds are purged of their liquid substance by a passing wind. For Holy Scripture speaks thus of them: *And now men do not look at the light when it is bright in the higher clouds, which the passing wind has cleansed. Job 37:21.* <note>Original: "Iam vero non respiciunt homines lucem, cum nitida est in superioribus nubibus, quas ventus transiens purgauit." The text cites this as Job 37:38, though modern bibles list it as 37:21.</note> From this passage, that opinion of Aristotle regarding the winds (mentioned above) is also refuted—namely, that the matter of the winds, which he calls "exhalation," does not penetrate the middle region of the air. Yet, by this testimony, the wind seems to blow in the highest part of the middle air, specifically where the higher clouds have their positions. 

Others, however, are overflowing with water—those which dissolve into rainy matter. But we, following in the footsteps of the Holy Bible, divide clouds first by their different positions into *higher* and *lower*. Hence it is said: *Men do not look at the light when it is bright in the higher clouds. Job 37:21.* And elsewhere: *The higher clouds gave a sound. Psalm 77:17.* <note>Original: "sonum ediderunt superiores nubes."</note> And elsewhere: *He commanded the higher clouds from above, and opened the doors of heaven.* And elsewhere: *The higher clouds were strengthened from above. Psalm 78:23 & Proverbs 8:28.* <note>Original: "Nubibus superioribus cœli præciperet... Nubes superiores superne fortificata."</note> and in many other places. By this, it is signified that there are also lower clouds, which are coarser and denser in their substance.

Furthermore, clouds appear to be distinguished from one another by sacred authority in respect to their substance—namely, into the *dense* and the *thin*. Into the dense, I say, because we find it written in that place: *With dense clouds God covers the heavens, which prepare rain for the earth, etc. Psalm 147:8.* <note>Original: "Nubibus densis obtegit DEVS cœlos."</note> And elsewhere: *Dense clouds are his pavilion. Job 22:14.* <note>Original: "Densæ nubes tugurium eius." The text cites Job 22:15.</note> And elsewhere: *Dense clouds are the chariot of God. Psalm 104:3.* <note>Original: "Densas nubes vehiculum DEI."</note> And elsewhere: *Jehovah binds the waters in the dense clouds, so that the cloud is not torn under them. Job 26:8.* <note>Original: "Iehoua ligat aquas in densis nubibus." The text cites Job 26:9.</note> Furthermore, this passage argues for the thinness of a cloud: *Behold, the Lord ascends upon a light* [cloud]...

In the preceding pages, it has been demonstrated how necessary the relationship is between the Macrocosm and the human Microcosm; because the latter is formed according to the pattern of the former, just as the former is made in the image of the Creator. Both of these are said by those most skilled in both theosophy and philosophy to be created in the divine image. For just as the world was created by God out of the dark void, and was divided into heaven and earth by the mediation of the spirit of God which moved over the waters, and was distinguished into four elements; and finally, by the inspiration of that universally breathing and acting spirit, <term>meteors</term> <note>In this context, "meteors" refers to any atmospheric phenomenon like rain, wind, or clouds, not just falling stars.</note> of every condition are procreated in both heaven and earth; similarly, man was formed by God in the image of the world—and consequently in the image of God himself—from the mud of the earth. He is inspired by the Creator himself and divided into heaven and earth—that is, into spirit and body—which are again distinguished into their own particular elements. Within these elements, meteors both bad (intended for punishment) and good (salutary/health-giving) are produced, namely in his "airy heaven" as well as in his earth or body.

Therefore, just as meteors, both wet and dry, are found in the middle air of the earth in the Macrocosm, as well as in its lowest heaven; so also are similar things found and created both in the body and the spirit (the "airy heaven") in the Microcosm. But truly, since man, considered in his integrity, is "a composite of a composite"—that is, made from the parts of the already composed world—it follows that man has immersed himself more deeply into a multitude of compositions than the world has. Thus it happens that his elements, as well as his meteors, are far denser and more compacted in a glutinous substance than those of the wide world, which are simpler. For example: blood, which is the airy element of man (in which that worldly spirit hides), is visible because of its density; as is that <term>bilious humor</term> <note>Also known as "choler," one of the four bodily humors, associated here with the element of fire.</note> which is related to fire and is the natural receptacle for the world's fire. For (as was said before) the spirit of the world exists in man as his "heaven," in the center of which nevertheless dwells the divine spirit. This provides man with reason and intellect, which the worldly spirit cannot achieve on its own; hence it is written: There is a spirit in man, but the inspiration of the Almighty gives them understanding, Job 32:8 <note>Original: "Iob. 9." The quote is actually from Job 32:8.</note>. By this we see that the divine spirit is the central actor within both the worldly and the human spirit, breathing and inciting the created spirits of both wherever he wills, making them forever ready and prompt to perform his pleasures; it is not the heat or cold of the creatures, which are merely the effects of divine action or inspiration, as will be declared elsewhere.

### CHAPTER VIII.

### On the Halo, the Mist, and the Cloud.

Since air is the medium in which watery meteors <note>In this era, "meteors" refers to all atmospheric phenomena, including clouds, rain, and halos, rather than just falling stars.</note> are produced—both in the macrocosmic heavens and everywhere upon its earth—it follows that such meteors must also be produced in every part of the "human air," whether solid or fluid. Indeed, every degree of cloudiness can be found there. Because the eyes in the "highest heaven" (the head) of the Microcosm <note>The human body viewed as a miniature universe.</note> have a direct relationship to the two great lights of the larger world [the Sun and Moon], and because the rays of the human spirit emit their sight through them, every species of cloud—such as the Halo, the mist, or the little cloud—can be very easily discerned there by their effects.

Just as we sometimes see a Halo or a very thin mist interposed between our eye and the Sun or Moon in the larger world—and sometimes a denser mist, or even a very thick cloud that the solar rays cannot penetrate—so too do we sometimes see such meteors mixed between our visual rays and the objects we see. These occur within the ocular medium, whether in the fluids <note>humors</note> or in the membranes <note>tunics</note> of the eye. Specifically, these are mists, white spots, and "suffusions" or cataracts. 

Mists in the eye are said to be thin, superficial whitenesses or "darknesses" of the eye's membranes. Such a disease is called a "little cloud" <note>original: nubecula</note> because a thin fluid exists there like a tiny cloud impressed in the air, clinging to the corneal membrane. Because of this, the sufferer thinks they see all things through a mist, vapor, or smoke. However, if this fluid or vapor thickens further, it coalesces into the second degree of cloudiness and is called "Albugo" <note>A white opacity of the cornea</note>. In this state, the clear sharpness of vision is blunted, and everything is seen as if in a dark shadow—just as in the densest mist of the larger world, we see the image of a previously visible object completely taken away from our sight. 

Furthermore, sometimes vision is rendered dark due to the excessive density of the corneal membrane, an occurrence called "caligo" <note>dimness of sight</note>. There is also another species of cloud produced in a deeper place, namely in the "crystalline" or vitreous humor. This causes that fluid to change into a bluish-gray or dark color, leading those affected to believe they are seeing through smoke or mist; this alteration of vision is called Glaucoma. 

Finally, we have another species of these meteors which produces the effect in the eye called a "suffusion" or cataract. This is produced by the thickening of misty air, either in the seat of the pupil, or between the grape-like membrane <term>Rhagoides: the uvea or iris</term> and the crystalline humor. This happens gradually and bit by bit, so that in the beginning it can hardly be discerned at all. We observe these same various stages in the creation of a celestial cloud: a progress from air into a barely perceptible vapor, from there into a very thin mist, then into a denser one, which finally hardens into a thick cloud. 

Moreover, when the air is condensed into the first degree around the circumference of the pupil—while the center remains untouched or clouded only by the thinnest smoke—it is observed to take the form of a Halo. Whatever the case may be, we see here that the process of air turning into thin or dense mist, or into the consistency of a cloud, is the same as the process we have in the world's atmosphere. Indeed, we have even observed that when such air is compacted into a dense vapor and condensed into dew, it preserves and nourishes the watery fluid of the eye when it is decreasing, keeping it in its full state. 

That this created vaporous substance was originally air is proven in two ways: first, because it proceeds gradually from invisibility to being visible to the onlooker; and second, because it could not have penetrated through the spongy and porous substance of the optic nerve unless it was in an aerial and "spiritual" condition. The reason why such aerial substance sometimes thickens in these places is due to the nature of the air penetrating that seat. This is caused by its central force, which can be changed into various dispositions by a "constricting wind" <note>A metaphorical way of describing cold or contracting physiological forces.</note>. Through this, it gradually contracts itself into a mass. Air from a wind of the opposite nature, however, remains dissolved in its own nature, so that it may better perform the roles and duties of the watery fluid according to the laws of Nature.

Within the ventricles of the brain, whirlwinds of air, vapors, mists, and clouds are also generated, either by the natural path or by laws beyond nature. Just as the vapors of the air drawn in through the nostrils are condensed into a sweet and natural mist by the urging of the good and healthy spirit of nature, they circulate and lightly condense—partly into the dewy moisture of the anterior ventricles, and partly into the invisible spirit dispersed through the passages of the choroid plexus <note>A network of blood vessels in the brain that produces cerebrospinal fluid.</note>. These are called the "animal spirits." Their superfluous parts are contracted into the form of thick water, which is excreted through the funnel <term>infundibulum: the stalk of the pituitary gland</term> and the pituitary gland, and finally through the openings of the wedge-bone <note>the sphenoid bone</term>, distilling down into the palate. 

In this same way, air filled with the "seeds" of unnatural meteors is drawn in and out through the "mammillary processes" <note>the olfactory bulbs</note>. Sometimes, by an unnatural process, this air is seen to be reduced into a misty or cloudy substance. From this, Catarrh, Darkened Vision <term>scotomia: dizziness with dimming of sight</term>, Vertigo, and other such effects of "meteors" are produced in the brain's ventricles. These occur with their various symptoms according to the aerial substance and the qualities of the "winds" predominating in them, as well as the position and place in which they are formed...

**CHAPTER IX.**

**CHAPTER X.**

***Concerning the watery meteors descending from the heavens. And first, concerning those of a more liquid consistency.***

**P.**
Watery meteors descending from the heavens are:
— Liquid, such as:
—— Dew.
—— Rain.
— Frozen: See **S**.

Those watery <term>meteors</term> <note>atmospheric phenomena</note> which are of a dense and more compact consistency than clouds or mists differ from one another according to the place or "seat" from which they arise. Indeed, some of these descend from the heavens, some rise up from the bosom of the earth, and others derive their origin and growth from the sacred sanctuary <note>original: "sacrario"</note> of both—namely, from both heaven and earth.

Those which descend from the heavens are observed to differ evidently in their consistency: some take on a liquid and flowing form, while others are frozen by the Northern cold and are rendered, as it were, fixed and not at all fluid. Those which fall from the heavens in a fluid and liquid form are Dew and Rain, which are the primary subjects we intend to treat in this section. In the first place, therefore, we shall express the opinion of Aristotle and the <term>Peripatetic sect</term> <note>The followers of Aristotle, known for walking about while teaching.</note> concerning the arrangement of these two meteors; and then afterwards, we shall briefly declare what the opinion of the Holy Scripture is concerning them.

According to the opinion of the Peripatetics, therefore, Dew is defined as a vapor, mixed with a small amount of earthy matter, condensed in the lowest region of the air; they assertsively say that it dissolves into water as soon as it settles. Alternatively, they define it thus:

Dew is a vapor which, in the spring and autumn seasons, is drawn upwards by the power of the sun during the day; but because it does not reach the middle region of the air, it is frozen by the cold of the night in the lowest region of the air and is forced to descend in the form of drops of water. Or thus: It is that which is generated from a weakly warm, thick, and moist vapor, not elevated far from the earth in the lowest part of the air, condensed by the nocturnal cold and resolved into water. Rain, however, they define as a liquefied cloud, resolved into water, dripping drop by drop. Or otherwise thus: Rain (they say) is a warm, smoky, and thick vapor, elevated from moist bodies by the heat of the sun and other stars as far as the middle region of the air; it is condensed there by the cold of that region and converted into a cloud, which cloud is then liquefied again and resolved into water falling to the earth for the health of living and growing things.

Rain that falls more copiously and with force they call a Heavy Shower <note>original: "Imbrem"</note>.

From these definitions of Dew, the Aristotelians seem to place no difference between the matter of a cloud and that of dew: for they assign a warm, moist, and sufficiently compact vapor to the composition of both, arising from the earth and water and attracted upward by the force of solar heat; hence they have not hesitated to attribute the same "agent" <note>the cause or force behind the action</note> to both. Therefore, they placed the entire difference which they make between the constitution of each in the diversity of their locations—namely, in the varying arrangement of the cold found in them. For if that vapor had been elevated into the middle region of the air, it would follow from their doctrine that it would have turned into the consistency of a cloud by the vehement cold of the place... <margin>K 3</margin>

...it would be condensed by the cold; but in truth, since it is not raised beyond the peak of the <term>middle region of the air</term> <note>The "middle region" was believed in pre-modern meteorology to be the cold layer of the atmosphere where clouds form.</note>, it is elevated only by the slight cold of that place and of the nighttime through a gentle constriction. Falling back down little by little due to its own weight, it is transformed into drops clinging to the plants. From this, they have concluded that dew is nothing other than a "small rain," but without clouds.

To be sure, those men assign a very beautiful and, at first glance, a quite probable description to the atmospheric phenomenon of dew. But indeed, if we look a little more deeply into the matter, we shall perceive it to be otherwise—and as far as possible from how they imagined it. For first, we consider those things which were said concerning the origin of clouds, and we shall discern that this whole theory from its origin, as put forward by the Philosophers, is closer to external probability than to central truth. Furthermore, we add in this place that the cause of dew is not originally from the earth, but from heaven or the lowest part of the air; and if any air or vapor is exhaled from the earth, that is only by way of "expiration" <note>original: expirationis</note> after the "inspiration" of the common air. It does not follow, however, that the air exhaled by a living creature must be condensed into a dewy substance by the night cold during the night—even if this sometimes happens when a chilling or northern blast blows. By a similar reasoning, we affirm that although vapor sometimes exhaling from the bowels of the earth may be frozen into dewy drops, it does not follow from this that all dew is created from vapors rising out of the earth.

For just as air is accustomed to penetrate everywhere, even to the very center of the earth—since it provides life and spirit—so it is necessary that, since it is of the same nature as the universal world, it has the capacity to be condensed or refined by that "aerial sea." Indeed, let us boldly affirm that the treasury chest of dewy substance is the universal sea of air. Thus, there is no need for it to be exhaled out of necessity from the cavities of the earth, since the "greater" contains the "lesser" within itself, as you will have confirmed below by the testimony of the Holy Font. The reason for its condensation is the will of **Wisdom**, which moves and contracts from the center; at her command the winds—namely the North and the South—blow most sweetly and lightly (the latter more strongly, the former more weakly), and by a light compression, they very easily condense the nocturnal air. This air, thus condensed and drawn in by the pores of the earth through "inspiration," clings to herbs and grasses and appears in the form of little droplets. 

Does it not seem that Aristotle, contrary to the goal of his own description of dew, acknowledges a great thing—though hiddenly—when he says that the blowing of the South Winds concurs in the constitution of dew? There, he says, taught by experience, that "there is no dew unless the South Wind blows." Upon these words of the Philosopher, Bartholomew concludes thus: *Since* (he says) *dew is a tiny rain, and rain is a great dew*, and in this respect he concludes that the southern wind generates dew because of its humidity, just as, conversely, the northern wind "licks up" and consumes dew with its dryness, or condenses and freezes its substance by means of its cold. Furthermore, in this doubtful resolution—namely, what is the origin of dew?—many have written many contrary things. For Ambrose attributed the generation of dew upon the earth to the constitution of the "moist moon," *since* (he says) *the Moon is the mother of dew.* In these things, one may see that the Philosophers are by no means consistent with themselves regarding the procreation of dew, inasmuch as various men have spoken of it in various ways.

What the Holy Scriptures think about dew and its origin, we shall now show in a few words. We find the Holy Scriptures speaking thus about dew in general, in the person of **GOD** to man: *Gird up now your loins like a man* (says Jehovah, speaking to Job in the whirlwind) *and make known to me that which I shall ask you, etc. Has the rain a father? Or who begot the drops of dew? From whose womb did the ice come? Or who begot the frost of heaven?* <note>original: Job 38:28-29</note> arguing from this that it is beyond human grasp to explain such mysteries without the revelation of the divine spirit. And yet, the Peripatetics <note>The followers of Aristotle.</note> nevertheless seem to answer Jehovah’s objection boldly, asserting that the "womb" or "matrix" of dew is the earth with water; and its "begetter" is the solar rays, by means of the nocturnal cold and humidity. 

But we shall approach a more particular explanation of this matter: We have observed from a twofold consideration of the Holy Letters that there is a twofold difference of dew in the world. Namely, we gather that one kind springs from the earth, whence it is said: *No vapor had ascended from the earth to water the whole surface of the earth. Genesis 2.* But Jerome has it: *A fountain ascended from the earth which watered the whole surface of the earth.* But let the exposition of the text be made in the following manner: we say (as in the preceding pages) that atmospheric phenomena are generated in the spirit or air enclosed in the earth no differently than in the open air. We have also said that **Wisdom** is everywhere—in heaven, on earth, in the depths of the sea, etc. And we say that the earth, at the command of that "Terrestrial Wisdom" (which is a unique and simple spirit, existing everywhere through the world, enclosed nowhere), has its own expirations and inspirations, which we call vapors. 

Nevertheless, that vapors of this kind are condensed into dew is a mystical and secret work of Divine Wisdom, not something that requires matter from the earth. For in His hands are the spirit of the universal world and all bodies that are animated by it; whence it is said: *GOD of the soul and the body, the strong GOD of spirits, the GOD of all flesh. Numbers 16:22.* But since, at His command and breath, the air—both celestial and terrestrial—is changed into this or that disposition: so we say that heaven is the father of the earth, inasmuch as the earth was procreated by it from the beginning; whence it is said, *GOD created the heaven and the earth* and not the earth and the heaven—arguing from this that after the perfection of the Heavens, the earth was created. But truly, just as God is said to be in heaven, so we acknowledge Him to be in the earth; and consequently, it is certain that "heaven" is found in the "dark earth," which is also God’s tabernacle. We conclude, therefore, that the matter of dew is principally from the celestial spirit, although that spirit is also inspired and expired by the earth for its quickening. Therefore, the air is the treasury chest of God...

"Do you know about the balancing of the thick cloud, the wonders of God, who is perfect in knowledge? Have you entered the storehouses of snow, or [have you reached] the inspection of the storehouses of hail?"
