<meta>This page continues the discussion on the causes of atmospheric phenomena, moving from a general discussion of efficient causes to a specific definition of hail and hoarfrost based on both Scripture and classical philosophy.</meta>

->**On the Formal Cause of Meteors. 85**<-

It will be explained more fully in the treatise on the supernatural efficient cause of <term>meteors</term> <note>In the early modern period, "meteor" referred to any atmospheric phenomenon, including rain, hail, and snow, not just falling stars.</note>. We conclude, therefore, from the doctrine and testimony of the Holy Scriptures, that hail should be described in this manner:

**Hail** is a certain hard and icy phenomenon. Its matter is extracted by the mighty God Jehovah from His treasures or His treasury—namely, the hidden bosom of the air. By His cold spirit or breath, He separates, freezes, and compresses that matter into infinite "water-stones" in the heavens, forming and massing them together. Finally, to fulfill His will, He drives them down and casts them to the earth, either by themselves or accompanied by lightning and rain.

In this definition, the "mine" of its matter or substance first presents itself; according to Holy Scripture, it is extracted from His treasures, which we have previously explained are the heavens or the air. From this it is clear that the substance of the air is the material not only for hail, but for all other meteors. Next, it is explained that its form is received from the divine breath or inspiration as the efficient cause; for it is said, *that the mighty God produces ice by His breath and by God's command the frost is frozen. <note>original: "quod DEVS fortis edat glaciem flatu suo stante DEO concrescat gelu"</note> Job 37:9.* And elsewhere, *He casts down His ice like morsels; who can stand before His cold? <note>original: "Deücit gelu tanquam frusta, coram frigore eius quis consistat?"</note> Psalm 147:16.* In this passage, "morsels of ice" can be understood as hailstones. Consequently, it is confirmed that such hailstones are formed by the cold of Jehovah’s breath in the shape of little stones made of water. This extraction of the matter of hail and ice from the dewy bosom of the air is verified elsewhere: *The ice comes forth from the womb of the dew, and the waters are hidden like stone, and the surface of the deep is frozen. <note>original: "Glacies egressa est ex utero roris, & instar lapidis aquæ absconduntur, & superficies abyssi congelatur."</note>* This can be understood both as ice in the clouds of the middle region of the air, and as the surface of terrestrial waters; for elsewhere in the Bible, clouds are called "the deep" <note>or "the abyss"</note>, *Job 38:28.* Finally, the final cause is explained there—namely, to accomplish the divine will. Hence it is said elsewhere, *Cold, ice, frost, clouds, lightning, whatever God commanded them to do upon the face of the world, whether for a scourge or for mercy, they perform it immediately. <note>original: "Frigus, glacies, pruina, nubes, fulgur quicquid præcepit DEVS istis faciendum in superficie orbis terrarum siue ad flagellum siue ad beneficentiam id protinus perficiunt."</note> Job 37.* Furthermore, God sent or produced hail from heaven to strike and destroy the men, cattle, herbs, and trees of the Egyptians, *Exodus 9* <note>The text incorrectly cites Exodus 19.</note>. Likewise, *Jehovah sent down great stones of hail from heaven, with which He killed the enemies of the Israelites, Joshua 10:11.* 

Therefore, we gather from our description that the material cause of hail is extracted from the air; for in its substance it is nothing other than air, thickened into a cloudy consistency by contrary winds. Next, we have the formal cause in that it is reduced into the form of water-stones, either round or angular in shape. Hence Joshua says, *Jehovah sends great stones of hail from the heavens.* From this it is also clear that the place where the thick air is reduced into such an image by means of the divine breath is the sky or the air. Furthermore, the efficient cause is the cold, freezing, and hardening breath of God. Finally, the final cause is mostly punishment and a scourge or penalty; for the earth is rendered far more fertile by rain than by hail, the nature of which is to harm fruit, trees, and crops rather than to bring them any advantage or profit.

But now we reach the third type of such solid meteors: **Hoarfrost**, which does not seem to differ much from the others regarding its efficient cause, as it is the cold breath or inspiration of Jehovah.

**Aristotle**, along with the Christians of his sect, defines this as a certain phenomenon arising from a moist and cold vapor rising from the element of water, which is not gathered into the thickness of a cloud. This phenomenon is frozen in the middle region of the air by the coldness of the place (in which no heat is present) and the coldness of the time, and is brought into the form of hoarfrost.

Others (among whom I name **Bede**) <note>Venerable Bede (c. 673–735), an English monk and scholar.</note> wish for this kind of phenomenon to be nothing other than frozen dew, which, in its descent toward the earth, drinks in and receives into itself the nocturnal coldness; by means of this, it puts on such a white, hard, and cold appearance as hoarfrost has.

We turn then to that Aristotelian description, and we say that if its first part were true—namely, that the matter of hoarfrost was a cold and moist vapor springing and exhaling from the nourishment of water and earth—it would follow that the frost would diminish and decrease more and more every day. This is because, in the weather of hoarfrost, the "gates of the earth" are closed by the freezing cold, so that neither plowshares nor other iron instruments can penetrate it. Furthermore, the waters are mostly shut up by ice so tight that we see fish dying in great numbers for lack of penetrating air. But everyone will admit that air is thinner than vapor. Since this is proven false by its effect, we say that Aristotle’s opinion on the substance or matter of hoarfrost is erroneous. We do not see the frost decreasing daily from its state; rather, we observe it growing stronger for the most part from day to day, and the earth and trees putting on a "swan-like beard" <note>A poetic term for thick, white rime frost.</note> more and more.

The same must also be said regarding the material cause of hoarfrost explained in the second description—namely, that it is not made of the substance of dew, if we assume it arose and was created in the Aristotelian way from vapor exhaled from the water and earth. However, Bede’s opinion will be probable if he agrees with us that the entire matter of meteors consists in the potential of the air.

But we proceed to the efficient cause of both, which Aristotle believes to be the cold of the middle air, in which he recognizes no heat; Bede, however, says the coldness of the night is the cause of both the freezing and the white form of the same.

Therefore it is clear that the breath of the mighty God Jehovah is the most ancient and primary cause of this birth; for the mighty God produces the ice, and the instrument by which he produces it is explained in that he produces it by his breath, and also forms it and reduces it into its icy substance; for by the breath of God, the frost congeals. Furthermore, that it is accustomed to be frozen on the surface of the waters is explained both by the place previously cited and by common experience.

**On the Formal Cause of Meteors. 91**

Even if we grant that air might multiply, it still does not necessarily follow that wherever air is contained within the cold earth, vapors and springs must also be produced. For beyond all controversy, it is certain that there is no pore or cavity of the earth that is not filled with air. Air is so subtle and penetrating that it acts as the life and spirit of every thing; indeed, even in water, the particles are not so tightly joined or constricted that air is not scattered throughout its members. Furthermore, even if we allowed for the free passage and movement of air through the earth’s pores, it would not follow that it would first change into vapor and then later into fluid humor or moisture. We have demonstrated by experience that if a tube of any substance is passed through a jar full of water, the simple air enclosed in the tube is not observed to convert easily into vapor, much less into water. This is even truer for air enclosed in the "veins" of the earth, since the dryness of the earth is more opposed to such a function—namely, the condensation of vapor into fluid water—than water itself is. But if the cause of vapor turning into the nature of water in the earth’s caverns were indeed water (which is resolved into vapor by the force of heat), then that labor would be in vain; it is entirely possible for the water itself, in its complete form and nature, to be raised from the bowels of the earth (which the abyss of the sea constantly refills) up to the level of springs through the earth's veins, without such a reduction. This fact is explained primarily by the two clear demonstrations that follow, and is further supported by the authority of Holy Scripture. As for the first ocular experiment <note>An "ocular" experiment is one intended to be seen or observed directly with the eyes.</note>, it is described in Heron's *Pneumatics* <note>original: "Heronis spirital." refers to the *Pneumatica* of Heron of Alexandria, a 1st-century Greek mathematician and engineer known for his work on pressure and steam.</note>, Book 1, where he discusses the bent siphon, illustrated thus:

[An illustration of a siphon mechanism. A large vessel labeled 'D' and 'E' contains water up to a level marked 'F' and 'G'. A bent tube (siphon) is inserted into the vessel. The tube is labeled with points A, B, C, H, K, and L. Point A is the submerged end, B is the highest point of the bend, and C, K, L are points on the descending arm outside the vessel.]

A. B. C. is the bent siphon; A. B. is the leg of the siphon inside the vessel, D. E., which is full of water. The surface of the water in the vessel is at the straight line F. G., and the leg of the bent tube A. B. is filled with water up to the line F. G. That is to say, let the part of the leg A. H. be full of water, while the part of the bent siphon H. B. C. is full of air. If, therefore, we draw out the aforementioned air with our mouth through the opening C, the liquid will follow at the same time, because a place cannot be entirely empty <note>This refers to the classical concept of *horror vacui*, or the "abhorrence of a vacuum," the belief that nature will pull in any available substance to prevent an empty space from forming.</note>. If the opening of the siphon C is level with the line F. G., the siphon will be filled with water but will not flow; it will remain full so that the part of the siphon A. B. C. is replenished with water, even though the part of the water between H. and C. is carried upward against the laws of nature. Rather, like a certain balance or scale in equilibrium, the water will remain held up according to the part H. B. and suspended downward according to B. C. However, if the outer opening of the siphon is below the straight line F. G., such as at point K, the water flows. This happens because the part of the "scale" or leg K. B. becomes heavier than the part B. H.; thus, by its own weight, it overcomes and pulls the water in a fluid motion, first upward from H. to B., and then downward from B. to K. But it does not pull more than what reaches the surface of the water A. If that leg is even deeper and longer, namely at point L, then that leg will pull to itself all the water between A. and H., gradually elevating it to the height of B, and then falling downward through the leg B. L., it exits through the orifice L; in this way, it will empty the water entirely.

From this, we see that wonderful connection and contiguity <note>A "contiguity" is a state of being in direct contact or touching.</note> that exists primarily between water and air: once the air is drawn out, the water must necessarily follow so that no vacuum is admitted, which is a thing utterly abhorrent in the nature of things. Furthermore, we see that firm continuity that exists between water and water, such that one part enclosed cannot flow without the other closely adhering to it, whether flowing upward or downward, for the same reason of avoiding a vacuum.

The second experiment is expressed in the second place by the aforementioned Author <note>Heron of Alexandria.</note> and in Treatise 1, Book 7, Chapter 9 of our *Physics of the History of the Macrocosm* <note>original: "physices nostræ macrocosmi historiæ" refers to Robert Fludd's own massive encyclopedia of the universe, *Utriusque Cosmi Historia*.</note> (where the origin of winds was discussed by us). Its visual depiction is of this kind: Let A. B. be a vessel full of water, through the bottom of which a tube C. D. is narrowed into the bottom itself and extends into the lower part. Its opening C does not communicate with the mouth of the vessel A. B., but an outer tube E. F. surrounds it on all sides, so that they are equally distant from one another. The upper part of the outer siphon E. G. must be exactly closed and fixed, while its lower foot...

# Universal Experiment

## THE SECOND PART OF this Experimental BOOK.

### CHAPTER I.
#### Concerning the primary nature of condensation and freezing.

As we have abundantly declared to you in the preceding sections that heat and its effects flowed from the **manifest God** <note>Latin: *Deo patente*; the aspect of the divine that reveals itself through light and creation</note>, so too have we shown that cold and its effects took their primordial origin from the **hidden God** <note>Latin: *Deo latente*; the divine in its unmanifest, restful state before creation</note>. Yet cold—though it was born from the womb of darkness and <term>hyle<note>from the Greek *hyle*; referring to primordial, unformed matter</note></term>—was not actually prior in place or time to heat establishing its essence in the world. For cold is only known to exist in the world insofar as its nature and properties are completely opposed to heat. 

Nevertheless, from our human perspective, the hidden God is thought to be older in time than the manifest God, since before the creation of the world He was unknown and, as it were, inactive relative to human understanding. For this reason, He is called **Ayin** <note>original: *AEN*; a Hebrew term meaning "Nothing" or "The Infinite Void"</note> by the Cabalists and Hebrew Rabbis—that is, "nothing" and "non-being"—because He was known only to Himself and existed only within Himself. Indeed, those more skilled in the <term>occult philosophy<note>The study of the hidden laws of nature, including alchemy, astrology, and magic</note></term> described such wisdom existing before the construction of the world: namely, a dark principle, possessing action only in potentiality.

<summary>This page introduces the second part of the work, explaining that while heat comes from the manifest God, cold originates from the 'hidden' or unmanifest aspect of God (Ayin), though both properties emerged simultaneously within the created world.</summary>

**Correlative from Demonstration.**

All these things, which have already been described concerning cold and heat, are most clearly shown through their effects by means of our experimental machine. For regarding what primarily pertains to the nature of cold, we observe that when it prevails in the open air or within the body of a <term>matrass <note>original: "matracci"; a long-necked glass bulb or flask used in early scientific experiments.</note></term>, the water is raised higher and higher. We have an explanation for this phenomenon ready at hand: namely, that the trapped air, which was previously expanded by external heat, is now—due to the arrival and onset of cold—contracted more and more in proportion to the intensity and dominance of that cold. This contraction occurs out of necessity and natural instinct; however, since a vacuum is not permitted in the nature of things <note>original: "vacuum in rerum natura non admittitur"; this refers to the traditional Aristotelian belief that nature abhors a vacuum, which was the standard explanation for suction and fluid movement before the understanding of atmospheric pressure.</note>, it is necessary that the water touching this trapped air fills that space which the air had previously occupied because of its expansion. Thus, the water is visibly raised upward due to the presence of intense cold; and the more that cold dominates, the higher the water will be gradually lifted. Conversely, when heat prevails in the external air or on the surface of the vessel

...it crosses the limits of the equinoctial line <note>The Equator</note> and seeks the northern parts in a violent manner; from this, those Southern winds are generated, whose blasts are usually accompanied by rain. This is because that air, receding from the Antarctic region toward the Arctic, carries within itself a solar soul <note>original: "animam solarem"; the vital heat or life-force attributed to the sun's rays</note>, by means of which it is carried. Thus, these winds are warm. However, this rarefied air, mixing itself with the dense northern air, immediately increases the quantity of that air by its presence. From this, the resistance of the wind blowing in a hidden manner from the North thickens it, and thus the "soul" dissolves the thickened air into droplets of water. But more on these things below.

Do we not see all of this expressed through the contemplation of our machine? <note>This refers to a "weather glass" or early thermoscope, a glass instrument used to demonstrate how air expands with heat and contracts with cold.</note> Where the enclosed air is condensed by cold, but made thinner by heat; and in its rarefaction, it compresses the waters and requires a more spacious place.

As for the Northern wind, the reasoning is the same as its opposite. For when the air is heated in the southern parts during the night by the clear and powerful presence of the sun—multiplied by the power of reflection or by the alignments of certain planets—it seeks the Northern part: first the Torrid Zone, then the Temperate, and finally that frigid zone where our antipodes <note>People living on the opposite side of the globe</note> dwell. This happens in the form of a southern wind, always pushing the dense air before it in its expansion toward the Arctic point, just as we see in our machine: the air enclosed in the concavity of the <term>matrass<note>A glass vessel with a round body and a long neck, used here to demonstrate air pressure.</note></term> pushes the dense waters before it as it expands.

Then that air, following in the form of the South Wind, is so animated by the solar rays that it is violently driven from the Northern part back toward the equator—partly by the extreme cold of the pole, partly by the compression of the space, and partly by its own heat. If it is strongly reinforced by rays and spirits together with the planets aligned with them—especially if it be Mars—that blast occurs with lightning and thunder, such as we very often see happen in summer. But if the enclosed animating spirits are weak, then they come with snow and extreme cold, such as we see in winter.

But here we make it known above all: if that Southern wind happens among the Antipodes in the summertime, and especially while the sun is in Cancer or near that tropic, then we are taught by experience that the air—driven from the South by rarefaction and passing through Arcturus <note>A bright star in the northern sky, used here to denote a celestial position</note>—creates not snow nor hail from the North, but mostly cold rains due to the nature of the place. This happens because the solar rays, having become more powerful in the Northern parts due to the direction of their reflection and mixing themselves with the expanded air (animating it and pushing it toward the North), act strongly against the cold nature of the pole and loosen it.

Do we not perceive this very thing with open eyes through the properties of the preceding machine? Indeed, that which was cited above from the Wise Man <note>Referring to King Solomon, traditionally the author of Ecclesiastes</note> seems to confirm this more than sufficiently. *The sun rises,* (he says) *and after it sets, it pants again toward its place where it may rise; it hastens to the south so that it may circle to the North; circling in its circuit, the air (or as others prefer, the wind) hastens on, and according to its circuits it returns.* <note>original: Ecclesiastes 1:5-6</note> By which he seems to hint that the winds are animated by the solar spirit, whose internal spirit is the uncreated light itself, which placed its tabernacle in the sun. As it is a spirit, it breathes centrally within itself and circumferentially in the air—whether in the created spirit or the external wind—that is, outside itself to fulfill the will of its Father.

Hence the Prophet said, *The wind performs the command of GOD* <note>original: Baruch 5:6 [Vulgate numbering]</note>. And the Evangelist: *The spirit (or wind) blows where it wills* <note>original: John 3:8; the Greek and Latin words for "spirit" and "wind" are the same</note>. And the royal Psalmist: *Who brings forth the wind out of his treasures—that is, from the hidden bosom of the air or heaven* <note>original: Psalm 135:7</note>. So also it is said, *that Jehovah brought an east wind into the land all that day and night; and Jehovah turned a very strong west wind, etc.* <note>original: Exodus 10:13, 19</note> And elsewhere: *He impels the South Wind into the heavens, and by his power he brings in the South-West wind, when he rained flesh upon them* <note>original: Psalm 78:26-27</note>. And elsewhere: *God fits a weight for the wind (or air) and weighs the waters in a measure* <note>original: Job 28:25</note>. From which it is manifest that God—or the Word, or Wisdom—beholding Himself from His palace, or leaping forth according to His pleasure, gives a soul to the winds; indeed, He is even present in the winds, which is confirmed in *Psalm 18:10: Jehovah, sitting upon the Cherubim, flies upon the wings of the wind;* and elsewhere, *who makes the winds his angels and his ministers a flaming fire;* and elsewhere, *by the breath of God, ice is frozen, etc.*

Here, however, it must be understood that the southern wind, violent among the Antipodes, is the cause of the Northern wind among us, and vice versa, for the reasons we cited above.

->### CHAPTER II.###<-
->*Concerning the origin of Clouds and consequently of rain.*<-

The procreation of clouds and rain occurs by plainly the same reasoning. For air is dissipated in the equinoctial parts by rarefaction proceeding from the solar rays, near or beyond the line where the solar rays strike perpendicularly. These dissipated parts are forced toward the Temperate Zone, which is already chilled and consequently condensed due to the long absence of the sun. Thus it happens that this rarefied air—driven by the rarefaction of the South and animated by the thinning solar spirit—mixes itself with the air of the Temperate and Frigid zones. By the compression of the parts, it changes into dense vapor, which migrates into the substance of a mist, a small cloud, or a great cloud. This, in turn, is ready to be liquefied into water droplets and converted into the nature of rain because of the central heat of the rarefied air inspired into it by the sun. But if, while this rarefied air seeks the northern part, a stronger wind blows from the Northern region, then by an overabundance of dry cold, they are converted into snow...

Therefore, the entire creation of clouds in and from the air—if we seek the primordial and supernatural principles—is usually accomplished by the divine wisdom dwelling in the sun, perfecting all things in the heavens and on the earth according to its will. Hence the Prophet Moses says: *The Lord will open to you his best treasure, the heavens, by giving rain to your land in its season (Deuteronomy 28:12).* And the royal Psalmist says: *God covers the heavens with thick clouds, which prepare rain for the earth (Psalm 147).* And the wise man says: *By his wisdom the depths broke open, and the heavens drop down dew (Proverbs 3).* And elsewhere: *I came out of the mouth of the most high, and like a mist I covered the earth (Ecclesiasticus 24).* And elsewhere: *It happened immediately, that the heavens were darkened with clouds and wind, from which came a great rain (1 Kings 18).* And elsewhere: *God makes a weight for the air and weighs the waters by measure, he makes a law for the rain (Job 28).* And elsewhere: *Who made the sapphire clouds by wisdom? and who tilts the bottles of heaven? (Job 38).* But it is said that God placed his tabernacle in the sun—that is, in the uncreated light-spirit proceeding primordially from Him, flowing into the sun as if into a tent—from which he sends out rays of life everywhere through the world, by which the world lives and is sustained. The secondary principles, however, are the rays of the sun, which lead the air everywhere according to the will of their internal source, rotating it, and continually ruling and preserving it in the world. We observe this same luminous soul in every composite thing to be the leader and governor of its own spirit (which is its nearest vehicle or tabernacle). This is what the wise man intended through the words brought forth earlier, which in Jerome’s translation are as follows: *After the sun sets, it pants again toward its place, from where it rises; it hastens to the south, and circles the North; and the spirit goes on, surveying all things in its circuit.* Or, as Tremellius <note>Immanuel Tremellius (1510–1580) was a prominent Jewish-Italian convert and Hebraist whose Latin Bible translation was highly regarded for its accuracy.</note> prefers: *In its conversion, the air hastens, going around.* Or, as Pagninus <note>Santes Pagninus (1470–1541) was a Dominican friar and leading philologist who produced a literal Latin translation of the Bible from the original languages.</note> prefers: *The wind goes on, constantly circling, and the wind returns to its circuits.* From these, one may gather how great is the obedience and fitness of the air, or spirit, or wind, for receiving the impressions of the sun. Finally, the earthly principles of clouds are the winds, which by their various blowing gather and accumulate mountains of air, and this through the way of compression and condensation. And yet all these principles have a sincere relation to that unique, uncreated Principle of principles, who placed his tabernacle in the sun; for without Him all things are nothing, and with Him everything that exists is exactly as it truly is, according to that saying of the Evangelist: *Christ is all and in all.* And elsewhere: *Through that Word all things were made, and without it nothing was made that was made (John 1).* For what is a cloud without wind? What is wind when no consideration is given to the sun? What, finally, is the sun if its luminous soul were extinguished? Who, then, is the first mover of this soul? What is its inward life if he is absent who placed his tabernacle in the spirit of the sun? From Him, this divine and central Apollo <note>The author uses "Apollo" as a classical metaphor for the sun, identifying the Greek god with the divine light of God/Christ.</note>—the lovable and gracious desire of the whole world—disperses life and being everywhere to his creatures. This is the uncreated light of the world, the invisible Son of God, holding his seat in the visible Son of God (as Plato says), to whom be praise, honor, and glory. Amen.

We have seen in our experimental instrument <note>Likely referring to a "weather-glass" or primitive thermoscope.</note> that the air itself, enclosed in a matrass <note>term: matrass (a round-bottomed glass flask with a long neck, used in alchemy and early chemistry)</note>, expands itself by the contact of heat; and in its expansion, it requires a larger and more spacious place. From this, it tends downward against the quarter of the heat expanding it—with a motion so strong, indeed, even against the nature of its own bodily lightness—that it compels and urges even a dense mass of water before it. By these things we are taught that air expanded by solar heat is moved in the world mostly to the right or to the left, and it recedes from the seat of heat (namely, the place of the sun) to other light places. This happens many degrees faster than in the glass, both because of the immense motion of the sun in the open air and because the expanded air is not as strongly opposed or repelled by thickened air as it is by thick and dense water. It follows, therefore, that if air applied or joined to air usually produces denser air, it is necessary that such a thickening of the air creates a middle composition between water and earth, of a moderate substance. For it is necessary that there be a medium between two extremes: namely, water and air. Indeed, those more skilled in natural philosophy have frankly recognized the condensation of air into water, and again the thinning of water into air. Therefore, the medium between such a starting point and ending point is vapor; and a denser or looser vapor usually produces such a cloud as it is itself, which cloud is finally resolved into drops of water. Therefore, thinned air, mixed with thick air, passes into a cloudy vapor, which is finally seen to distill into rain. And this we can prove by ocular experience—even if some were ignorant of the opposite—by moving from the lesser to the greater in this way: If a portion of the air's subtlety is usually transformed into the substance of water, how much more so when that air is joined to thicker air? That a portion of thinned air usually migrates into an aqueous substance is the "major" evident point; the "minor" point is explained by the following experiment.

This happens even more so because of the abundance of material to be condensed, since the aforementioned experiment shows that this same effect is usually achieved by the simple condensation of air.

But if by chance the thinned air is gathered together by contrary winds and moves into the existence of a cloud, it is then mixed with such great fiery spirits for the most part that thunder and lightning flashes arise from it.

### CHAPTER III.

#### On the origin of springs and consequently of rivers.

From the preceding sections, supported by both philosophical speculation and experimental practice, we consider it more than sufficiently demonstrated that the air filling all things in this world is expanded in its regions by the power of heat (the common source of which we have said is the sun itself). By this expansion, the air requires a larger space to receive its expanded substance—moving upward and downward, as well as to the right and left, and forward and backward. 

But conversely, we have explained that this same air, which is universally spread out, is condensed by the presence of cold (to a greater or lesser degree according to the dominance of that quality), and is gathered and contracted into one. We also noted that just as expanded air requires a larger space, so too, when its members are contracted, it is content with a narrower place. 

Since this is the case, it follows that the reason for the diminishing and drying up of springs and rivers in the summer time is not due to the evaporation of their water into the air, as is the opinion of the **Peripatetics**. For if this were so, it would follow that solar heat was not the cause of the thinning of the air, but rather its thickening. If the aquatic substance of the springs and rivers were evaporated into the air, then it would be necessary for the air to be thicker in the summer time; consequently, the sun, by its proximity and the direction of its rays, would not be rarefying the air, but rather making it thick. Yet we are taught that the property of heat is to rarefy and not to thicken—a fact we draw from the property of our aforementioned experiment, since the air contained in the <term>matrass</term> <note>a long-necked glass flask used in early scientific experiments</note> is expanded by the presence of heat, just as it is thickened again by the assault of cold.

But to investigate this further, let us see, I pray: if the substance of rivers and springs is converted into air during the summer, what finally becomes of that superfluous air, since the extreme heat of the sun always tends toward the thinning of the air? Certainly, it is not converted into clouds, because in the summer time—and especially when the sun is heating in an extreme way—clouds are not so frequent, nor is rain in such abundance. Indeed, as it says in the **Holy Scripture**, the heavens are "brazen and dry" <note>A reference to Deuteronomy 28:23, describing a drought where the sky yields no rain</note>, and whatever clouds might be present are sterile. 

From this it follows that, contrary to the doctrine of the ancient philosophers, there is another cause for this flowing away of rivers, springs, and pools, and another path for them, though it be invisible and quite hidden. Namely, the air of the hemisphere, being greatly thinned and requiring a wider and vaster place for its existence, pushes the waters of the springs downward into their depths and causes the moisture to descend into the innermost parts of the earth. 

Is this not indicated by the ocular demonstration of our machine? In it, we see that in the presence of heat, the air contained in the matrass requires a larger place for itself through expansion. There, the heat in its expansion does not convert the nature of the lower vessel's water (which was raised through the neck) into dense air—since such a sublimation would be entirely against the laws of the nature of heat—but visibly thrusts it downward toward its deep hiding places and recesses, from which it had first been raised upward by the effort of the cold. 

But perhaps someone will ask about the location: where does that water, so depressed among us in the summer time, move to while its waves are hidden from us? For without a doubt, it is necessary that the waters of springs always be in motion. To this we respond with the **Holy Bible**: they return to the sea from which they previously departed <note>A reference to Ecclesiastes 1:7: "All the rivers run into the sea... unto the place from whence the rivers come, thither they return again."</note>. Yet the sea does not seem to grow, because the sea distributes that portion of water which the more summery quarter of the world refused to the winter quarter of the world. For beyond any controversy, by as many degrees as the Northern <note>original: "Borealibus"</note> hemisphere of the world excels in heat and dryness, by just as many degrees the Southern <note>original: "Australe"</note> hemisphere prevails in coldness and moisture.

And yet, nevertheless, their Christian followers or disciples are so intoxicated by the "magical cups" of these pagan philosophers that they eagerly prefer these false opinions over the true and infallible spirit of all truth.

This is why, in all the sciences dependent on natural philosophy—and even in commonly taught Theology—we find so many contradictions, so that truth itself seems to be imprisoned by us Christians in deceptive clouds and darkness.

**But** let us return to the matter at hand. It is most certain, contrary to the doctrine of the Peripatetics and confirmed by the sacred page, that the nourishment of springs comes from the sea, and not from vapor or air enclosed in the earth and condensed there by cold, as they claim. For why is there a need for many operations when nature is accustomed to perfecting things through fewer? Indeed, this is an invincible axiom published to the world by those very people: *It is vain to do with more what can be done with fewer.* <note>A version of the principle known as Occam’s Razor.</note> For without the conversion of air into vapor and vapor into water, water—by its simple nature, through the inner recesses of the earth and the hidden veins of its bowels—is carried upward from the deep abyss of the sea through the pores and veins of the earth. This is driven by its own astringent nature and its tendency to gather air in the cold. This is demonstrated exactly both by philosophical reasons and by this practical experiment of ours. For unless there were such a close continuity between the elements of water and air that one could not be separated from the other, that monster in the nature of things—namely, a **Vacuum**—would be admitted. From this, it necessarily follows that where air retreats through vessels closed on all sides, water follows, because of the natural embrace of one with the other.

This has been exactly demonstrated by us in the conclusion of *Rule 7, Treatise 2, Part 7, Book 3 of the Technical History of the Macrocosm*, where the movement of elements is discussed. The rule is as follows: *The substance of the element of water is contiguous with air, joined by a tenacious mixing so that there is no distance between them.* <note>original Latin: "Substantia elementi aquæ contigua est aeri..."</note> From this, it happens that water is raised upward with the air. At the end of that rule, an experimental demonstration follows, which we have expressed in this place.

But indeed, we have said that the universal source of these waters is the sea, which also seems to be suggested by the Holy Bible in these words: *Let the waters which are under the heaven be gathered together into one place, and let the dry land appear, and it was so. Whence it happens that the springs of that place are pushed down toward the bowels or center of the earth. But indeed it is certain that water cannot be raised by the northern cold more than in that proportion by which the southern heat pressed it into the earth; if it happened otherwise, then a vacuum would be left in the nature of things, which is most absurd and abominable to nature itself. And hence it is that, although the rivers (according to the word of the wise man) flow into the sea, yet the sea does not overflow, <note>A reference to Ecclesiastes 1:7: "All the rivers run into the sea; yet the sea is not full."</note> nor is it fuller at one time than another: for there is a circular motion in nature, but she admits no increase or decrease.

### Corollary.
What need is there for more words? Do we not see in the observation of our present machine <note>This "machine" is likely a thermoscope, an early instrument used to show changes in temperature through the expansion and contraction of air.</note> that upon the approach of heat to the matrass <note>original: "matraceum"; a long-necked glass bulb used in chemistry.</note>, the air is dilated, and that in this dilation it requires a larger space for its existence? This is proven by the fact that we perceive with our own eyes the water—which had been raised many degrees into the neck of the matrass by the presence of cold—being gradually driven downward by the expansion of the air. 

Indeed, this experience has been very costly and laborious—and truly even quite dangerous—for some common chemists. For in the making of <term>strong water</term> <note>original: "aquæ fortis"; nitric acid.</note> from saltpeter and vitriol, the spirits leaping out from the small mass contained in the retort, due to the dilation of the nitrous air, could not be contained even by a very large glass receiver. Instead (and I speak from experience), they wretchedly tore that vessel into infinite particles, accompanied by a horrendous sound like a shotgun, so that they might acquire a wider field in the air for their existence. 

From this, therefore, we find the reason for the diminishing of springs in the summertime: namely, because the air in our Zone is thinned by the presence of solar heat, as can be seen by a diligent look at the properties of our machine. Therefore, the dilated air does not pull the terrestrial waters upward to itself, but on the contrary, thrusts them downward. We see the same in paralytics, where the nerves, relaxed by thinning, do not stretch or pull the limbs to perform their functions, but conversely, we note them falling toward the earth—that is, being pressed downward toward the ground. Do we not observe this very same thing in the action of this instrument of ours, whose water, raised by the cold, is driven gradually downward by the presence of heat and the rarefaction of the air? 

In like manner, during the winter time, we see the air contracted by the cold, and in its contraction, the springs overflowing with water and the rivers swelling with fluids. We have said this happens because of the constriction of the air, which moves the water itself according to its own motion; the water is, as it were, the servant and handmaid of the air. The air moves the water, I say, either by driving it from the center toward the circumference (in its hot and dilated condition) or by drawing it from the circumference to the center (in its cold, contractive, and gathering nature). Behold the proof in our machine: where by the contact of cold, the air contained in the matrass is so condensed that it lifts the water many degrees high into the neck of the matrass, through which the cold is intensified in its nature. From this it is clear that this is the reason why waters are elevated on high from the central depths of the earth: namely, by the presence of winter’s cold.

### CHAPTER IV.
### On the origin of Luminous Meteors, and how they are procreated in rarefied air.

Since, therefore, visual experience teaches us that the more the air is heated, the rarer and thinner it becomes, it follows conversely that the rarer and purer the air is, the closer it approaches the nature of the element of fire, or the luminous and fiery spirit. On the other hand, it is clear that the more the air cools, the more dense it is rendered. Thus, the first degree of condensing air is into the consistency of **vapor**; the second into the consistency of **mist**; the third of a **cloud**; the fourth of **rain**; the fifth of **snow**; and the last of **hail and ice**. 

Such is also the relationship of the degrees in the thinning of the air from its middle state up to the very sphere of fire: namely, **wind**, **will-o'-the-wisp** <note>original: "ignis fatuus"; a ghostly light seen over bogs.</note>, **falling star**, **lightning**, **flash**, **pillar of fire**, and the other kinds of **comets**. All these fiery meteors <note>In this period, "meteor" referred to any atmospheric phenomenon, not just space rocks.</note> have as the basis of their existence air that has been rarefied by fiery heat. 

However, we think it must be diligently observed by us that the "hidden" part—that is, the greatest spiritual part of the air—is **Light**. This light vivifies the air itself, not otherwise than a soul vivifies an animal, moving it everywhere according to its will. Therefore, the hidden or internal part of the air, which dwells in its center, is pure fire; just as its manifest or external part is a certain humid substance, covering and enclosing that hidden light no differently than a body encloses a soul. A thick cloud is the lightning-maker; for the fiery or central substance of the air is pure fire, which God, in the first creation when He said **"Let there be light"** <note>original: "Fiat lux."</note>, breathed into the universal spirit of the world. Therefore, by stripping off its humid garment—or by manifesting the hidden and hiding the manifest—the humid, invisible air is changed into invisible fire. 

But truly, just as we see the external and manifest (yet invisible) air first take on the appearance of visible vapor and then a dense cloud through contraction, so also we perceive the hidden or fiery invisible air change first into the substance of a flash and lightning, and then, in a tighter contraction, into a visibly fiery meteor, such as a comet, a falling star, a will-o'-the-wisp, and other things of this kind. 

The "starting point" from which air tends away from its middle nature through thinning is fiery existence; but that toward which it usually migrates from its middle nature is the nature of a dense cloud. From this it is clear that in ordinary air there is an aptitude either toward a dark nature (by virtue of thickening) or toward a luminous existence (by way of rarefaction). In this way, both dark and luminous meteors are produced in the world, from which afterward both the internal and the external—that is, both the soul and the body of any thing, whether simple or composite—is derived.

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the nature of meteors, transitioning from a critique of Aristotelian physics to a Hermetic and Neoplatonic comparison between the "Great World" (Macrocosm) and the "Small World" (Man/Microcosm), specifically regarding the origin of breath and spirit.</meta>

**On the Efficient Cause of Meteors.** [page] **195**

How ridiculous then are the schools of the <term>Peripatetics|Followers of Aristotle’s philosophy, who often explained natural phenomena through physical "exhalations"</term>, who invent so many fantastic efficient causes for the winds—namely, a hot exhalation seeking only to rise, the heat of the sun lifting and summoning it from the earth, and the intense cold of the middle region of the air. I leave this for you to consider, you who are lifted up on the more exact wings of doctrine and the knowledge of truth.

->***A comparison to man, in which it is proved that GOD is also the sole and only author of the winds produced within the Microcosm.***<-

It was not without wisdom that man was called the *microcosm* <note>original: "ὁ μικρόκοσμος"</note> by the Philosopher, insofar as he has the greatest similarity and analogy with the great world. For he enjoys the same elements as the world, which are accustomed to act and suffer among themselves with similar actions and passions, both in the one world and the other. Indeed, it seems the "lesser world" received the parts of its substance and essence from the "greater world," if we consider the matter a little more accurately; for in time and order, the latter preceded the former. Hence, <term>Hermes Trismegistus|A legendary figure representing the fusion of the Greek god Hermes and the Egyptian god Thoth, credited with ancient wisdom on the connection between the divine and the material</term> did not hesitate to repeatedly call man the "son of the world," just as the world is the "son of GOD." And indeed, if we carefully weigh the words of the Prophet, we will find them relevant to the Philosopher’s purpose, where he speaks thus regarding the resurrection of the bones: *Come from the four winds, O spirit, and breathe upon these slain, that they may live: Ezekiel 37.* By these words, he seems to hint that life comes from that spirit which God imparted to the world for its existence and vivification. But however certain and well-worn this truth is—that just as God created one world by his breath of life, so he created the other—it means that just as the spirit of the Lord, which was carried over the waters in the great world, provided them with fiery vigor and created and animated its moist spirit, so indeed at the creation of man He breathed the breath of life into the created spirit of man, *whence man was made into a living soul. I, says God, creating the heavens and establishing the earth and what germinates from it, give breath to the people who are upon it, Isaiah 42:5.* From these things, we gather that the life not only of the world but also of man took its beginning from the wind or divine inspiration.

Furthermore, just as we see the common spirit of the world divided into four elements, so not only the human spirit (which we also call air) but also the body participates in these elements. Indeed, we see that the air of both worlds enjoys its own sun: for the heart performs its duty in the human spirit no differently than the macrocosmic sun does in its own. But we see with open eyes that, just as man’s first power was from his inspiration—by Him who "placed a tabernacle in the sun"—and he received the parts of his constitution from the air and elements of the world, it is necessary that there be a continuous relationship. This exists both between the incorruptible spirit in the sun and that in the heart (as both are but one thing in essence), and also between the air of the world and that of man (which both come from one and the same source). Both enter into this same common duty: namely, that the bright spirit of the Creator flies upon the wings of both winds or spirits, and is carried as if by a vehicle or chariot. And just as in the world that airy spirit is divided into three regions, of which one is placed above the others in dignity and purity, so indeed is this spirit in man: divided into the **animal** <note>From 'anima,' referring to the soul's governance of movement and sensation</note> and **intellectual** in the brain (the "highest heaven" relating to the Empyrean or Angelic spirit of the world); the **vital** in the heart (compared to the ethereal region of the world); and the **natural** in the liver (having regard to the sublunary or earthly region of the world). 

From this it arises that there is such proximity—indeed, continuity—between these two spirits and bright souls (which in effect are of one essence governing them) that the Microcosm cannot exist without the assistance and presence of the Macrocosm. For this reason, Heraclitus said not unwisely: if you take the Sun from the world, what is our little body? If the soul is missing, no pulsing vein is found there, no vital breath, and no respiration at all. And from this it is that the Philosopher <note>Referring to Aristotle</note> argued that man cannot be generated by man unless the sun assists. Hence his axiom: *The Sun and man generate man.* 

For this reason, then, man (for we are now discussing his sympathy with the mundane spirit) is said to live as long as he breathes. Therefore, antiquity rightly ascribed the "spirits"—which the most excellent physicians consider to be the "innate heat" moving the body, exciting the senses, and nourishing thoughts—to the sun. The sun moves all things as an instrument and is the "organic cause" of all living things through that incomparable spirit which dwells in its center. According to Homer <note>original: "teste Homero"</note>, such spirits are said to be in us daily as the mundane Sun, the Prince of planets, breathes out, moves, irradiates, and prepares, refines, and elaborates through the middle sublunary air. Because of this air—as Hippocrates and experience itself testify—we are forced to breathe continuously and necessarily whether we wish to or not. We draw it in by the aid of the lungs through the mouth and the windpipe <note>original: "asperam arteriam"</note>, and from there it is sent into the left chamber of the heart, which is full of the body of spirits that give life and nourish animal power. Moreover, it is received into the brain through the nostrils and into the entire body (which is entirely "breathable") through the connections and pores of the arteries. # Concerning Fire

Fire is most frequently used to represent the **wrath** and **fury** of God. <margin>Psalm 17</margin> For smoke rose from His wrath, and fire broke out from His face; coals were kindled by it. <margin>Psalm 104</margin> He makes His angels spirits, and His ministers a burning fire. <margin>Job 38</margin> For the fire of God’s wrath is often compared to a tempest. <margin>Psalm 18</margin> He rained snares upon the wicked: fire, sulfur, and the <term>spirit of storms</term> <note>original: "spiritus procellarum"; often interpreted as a scorching or destructive wind.</note> are the portion of their cup. <margin>Psalm 79:5</margin> How long, Lord? Will you be angry forever? Shall your jealousy burn like fire? <margin>Psalm 17</margin> Fire shall go before Him and burn His enemies round about. <margin>Genesis 19</margin> For He rained sulfur and fire upon Sodom and Gomorrah. <margin>Leviticus 10:12</margin> Thus fire came out from the Lord and consumed the sons of Aaron. <margin>Numbers 16:35</margin> And fire went out from the Lord and consumed the two hundred and fifty men.

In Fire there is a **dual power**: the power of **heat** and the power of **light**. <note>This distinction was central to natural philosophy, separating the physical "burning" (heat) from the spiritual or intellectual "revealing" (light).</note> The power of heat is for burning and consuming; the power of light is for illuminating and nurturing. For fire, through its heat, dries out the earth, consumes moisture, and <term>hardens</term> <note>original: "induret"</note> what is soft; yet through its light, it dispels darkness and grants the faculty of sight.

Fire is the <term>most refined element</term>, <note>original: "elementum subtilissimum"; in the four-element system, fire was considered the "thinnest" and most spiritualized material.</note> for it is light and agile. It moves itself with great speed and always seeks to ascend toward the heavens. It does not rest until it reaches its proper place. It penetrates all things with its heat—even causing a <term>burning blight</term> <note>original: "urigine"</note> where it is too intense—and transforms whatever it touches into its own nature. 

When it is heard, the sound <note>original: "auditum"</note> of its crackling manifests its strength. It is a force that where <note>original: "vbi"</note> it finds fuel, it thrives, but where it lacks it, it dies away.

On the Efficient Cause of Atmospheric Phenomena. 201

The Wise Man says that the upper clouds distill dew by wisdom, <note>Proverbs 10: The author refers to the biblical Book of Proverbs, though modern numbering may vary.</note>. From these things it is sufficiently clear, against the false assertion of the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle’s philosophy, who sought naturalistic rather than purely divine explanations for weather.</note>, that neither the vapors emerging from the earth or waters, nor the cold of the middle region of the air thickening and sustaining that imaginary vapor, is the material or efficient cause of a cloud. Instead, it is the air itself, compressed and thickened by the opposing or transverse breath of God; that is, by the ray of wisdom of the angels, who are moved and agitated to carry out the will of their Creator.

The matter is the same regarding the generation of snow, hail, and frost, except that in such a creation the North wind <note>original: *Ventus septentrionalis*</note> holds dominion. Its nature is to constrict the air into a cloud—air which had been reduced by the South wind <note>original: *flatu Australi*</note> (though blowing in a milder degree)—and to harden it. For just as it is the nature of the South wind to soften, liquefy, and dissolve, so it is the nature of the North wind <note>original: *Aquilonis*</note> to harden and constrict. Moreover, that God alone, through the mediation of his angelic ministers, is the producer and effector of these kinds of <term>meteors</term> <note>In this period, "meteor" referred to any atmospheric phenomenon, including rain, snow, or lightning, not just falling stars.</note>, is proven by these testimonies drawn from the sacred font: "Who has fathered the frost of heaven?" God says in Job 28, 19. It is as if by such a question he proves that no one does so except himself alone. And elsewhere: "God sends snow like wool, and scatters the frost like ashes; he casts down his ice like morsels; who can stand before his cold?" (Psalm 147:16). By these words he seems to suggest that God, through his winds—and especially the North wind <note>original: *Boream*</note>—begets snow from the air gathered by the milder breaths of the South wind. Hence it is said: "The strong God by his breath produces snow and ice" (Job 37:9). <note>The text cites Job 27:9, but the content matches 37:9.</note> And elsewhere: "The North wind produces cold." Furthermore, ice and frost are produced from the curdling of dewy air by the breath of God from the north; hence we read that "ice comes forth from the womb of the dew" (Job 38:28). And elsewhere: "By the breath of God, ice is congealed like a stone of water, etc." (Job 37:10). In this speech, the matter of ice, its form, and its author are explained along with his instrument: namely, the dewy matter, the watery form of stone, and God as the agent working through his windy instrument. From these things, therefore, the error of the pagan philosophers regarding the matter and efficient cause of these types of atmospheric phenomena is evident.

-> CHAPTER XX. <-

-> On the single efficient cause of flashing, lightning, thunderbolts, and thunder; similarly of the actor of sulfurous smoke and flames. <-

Just as the Creator of all things "makes his angels winds," so also he makes "his ministers a burning fire or flame," as witnessed by the Royal Prophet <note>King David</note> in Psalm 103/104. We call thunderbolts and flashes of lightning the air animated by their presence and clothed in their fiery form. Indeed, we gather this from the consequence of such speech: "God fits a weight to the air, and weighs the waters by measure, and makes a way for the lightning of the thunders" (Job 28:25), where he seems to fit the air in its weight so that through it, as through a medium, his fiery spirits may make their way to fulfill the will of the Creator. Job seems to suggest this in another place: "The clouds scatter his light, by which they illuminate all things round about, wherever the will of the Creator drives them, for everything he commanded them upon the face of the world, whether for a scourge or for mercy" (Job 37:11-13). <note>The text cites Job 28:25 and Job 37.</note> And "God extends his light over the clouds, and covers the roots of the sea" (Job 37:30); and elsewhere: "Will you send forth lightnings, and will they return and say to you, 'Here we are'?" (Job 38:35). Are we not also made certain of the efficient cause of lightning from these words: "Fire coming out from the presence of Jehovah consumed the sons of Aaron" (Leviticus 10:2)? And elsewhere: "Fire going out from Jehovah consumed the 250 men who had offered incense" (Numbers 16:35). Finally, in the Apocalypse <note>The Book of Revelation</note>, we have it that "lightnings, voices, and thunders proceeded from the throne of God." By these things it is clearly denoted that flashes and lightnings proceed immediately from God.

This discourse is to be understood in this way: the Divine Essence, in its wisdom or emanation, agitates its likeness in the fiery spirits (by means of which a fiery angel exists and remains just as he appears in the air during the time of lightning; for the incorruptible Spirit of God is in every thing, but more abundantly in the angels). He urges and moves a part of himself, as it were, to perform those things ordained by the moving Father. These fiery spirits in their motion disturb the air, crowding and constricting it into dense clouds. Conversely, spirits of an opposite nature, breathing from the contrary region of the world and waging an impetuous war, violently break out from their damp embrace and the dense prison surrounding them. This is not something those fiery or watery spirits or demons do on their own, but rather what God is accustomed to effect by a double ray emitted from his essence acting within them. And this is the reason why many thunders are heard at the same time, arising from different corners of the world; hence Daniel says that "the four winds of heaven strove upon the great sea" (Daniel 7:2), that is, in the open air. By "winds," the Prophet understands the angelic intelligences who preside over the four corners of the world. But we shall discuss these things more clearly, God willing, in the second book of this section. We also have other testimonies of the sacred page scattered everywhere to prove this our single efficient cause of all things, especially that God alone (with no other subordinate efficient cause mediating) is the author and actor in thunder, lightning, and all other luminous phenomena whatsoever. For in one place it is said: "Smoke went up in his anger, and fire from his face glowed, coals were kindled by him... At the brightness in his presence the clouds passed, with hail and coals of fire, and the Lord thundered from heaven, and the Most High gave his voice, etc." (Psalm 18:8-13). <note>The text cites Psalm 17:9, following the Vulgate numbering.</note>

— From this discourse it clearly appears that God does all these things. Although we may say in our common speech that lightning and thunder happen, or in a more mystical sense, that angels set the air on fire with their own fiery presence, nevertheless in truth it is God within the fiery angels, and God within the thick clouds or watery spirits, who brings all these things to their conclusion to fulfill His commands. Whence the Holy Scripture rightly said **that in God all things live, move, and have their being** <note>original: "quod in Deo omnia viuant, moueantur & ſint." A reference to Acts 17:28.</note>. **Acts 17:9.** And elsewhere, **God works all in all.** **1 Cor. 12.** And again, **God the Father from whom are all things.** **1 Cor. 8.** 

Therefore, I leave it to be judged by you—looking into this matter with upright eyes and weighing it in the scales of justice—how foolish, tasteless, and over-subtly presented is that opinion and assertion of the <term>Peripatetics</term><note>The Peripatetics were followers of Aristotle's philosophy, who sought to explain natural phenomena through physical causes rather than divine ones.</note> (both of the Heathen and the Christian order). They presume to assert that lightning consists of hot and dry exhalations springing from the earth, which are raised by the sun's power into the middle region of the air; there, being enclosed in a cloud and driven by the force of the local cold, they catch fire, and so forth. 

Is this matter—namely lightning and thunder—truly a thing of such small importance (as those Aristotelians think), or is it of a far higher depth and inscrutability? In the Holy Scriptures, these are called the fires of God leaping from His mouth and throne, and the voices and sounds of God everywhere. 

For this reason, some philosophers, considering the wonderful operation of the lightning-bolt, judged it to be no work of nature, but the immediate effect of the Supreme God. Indeed, this work seemed so marvelous to the Heathen that they doubted greatly concerning its origin and disputed among themselves. For Empedocles thought that lightning and flashes were fire generated by the rays of the sun descending downward and intercepted by clouds. Anaxagoras claimed that this fire was a portion of the ether, which he says is sent down from on high and strikes the place where the clouds stay. Although Aristotle himself and Seneca attempted to refute these opinions, they nevertheless seem far more probable and relevant to the matter than those of Aristotle and his sects. 

This is also declared clearly enough by arguments drawn from experience itself. For, good God! How lacking in reason are those who are accustomed to attribute the wonderful effects of thunders to the power of an earthly exhalation, or to the weak faculty of earthly fire? For by the action of a lightning-bolt, we see wine drawn out of a jar by a sudden force without the vessel being touched at all; a sword broken in its scabbard; gold and silver melted in a purse; and the bones crushed within the fleshy home of a person. We see sudden winds created in the air, forests burned, stones crushed, and huge towers suddenly torn up, along with infinite other wonders performed, for which it is most difficult to give a ready explanation. 

Indeed, there seems to be sense and reason in the lightning, by which they offer obedience to the Creator. They are said to bless Him in the Holy Scriptures, thereby indicating to us Christians that there is within them a certain Angelic virtue very close to divinity. They are governed by these virtues, and **when sent forth they go out violently, and returning they say to their creator, "Behold, here we are."** <note>original: "emiſſa violenter exeunt, & reuertentia dicunt creatori, en adsumus." A reference to Job 38:35.</note> **Job 39:35.** 

Indeed, its spirits are so subtle and its life so agile, as we find written by one skilled in these mysteries: "Angels are much clearer and more splendid than spiritual bodies—which a man can hardly admit or comprehend—for by reason of their subtlety they can pass through and penetrate all things without any hindrance and without their own corruption, like lightning. Similarly, the human soul can do this, since God likewise created it from the same [substance] from which the angels were created." Thus he says in the *Book of the Secrets of Creation*. 

By this, he seems to hint that the substance of an angel, of lightning, and of the human soul are of the same matter, which he is pleased to call the "sixth essence" in many places. And in truth, just as the substance of an Angel is not seen at all except in its airy garment (which it illuminates in the manner of the sun's spirit, which is illuminated by its own internal soul), so indeed the internal part of lightning is an Angelic force and essence veiled in airy clothing. From this, then, it arises that so many wonders are performed by lightning, far surpassing the deaf nature and disposition of a mere "exhalation."

For experience has revealed here in England that in the county of Devon <note>original: "prouincia Deuienſi"</note>, thunder coming from the North cast a fiery stone into a certain nobleman's kitchen. Rolling from that place into the hall of that house and passing between the feet of a certain man of that household, it rendered him for a time insane and a raving madman. Passing from that place into a chamber, by its mere sight, all the window glass of that part was perforated in infinite places as if they had been pierced with needles. And so, penetrating through a thick wall and leaping out of the house, it buried itself in a hard rock in a marvelous manner. 

Furthermore, in Ireland, two women seeking a forest and traveling through a field were delayed on the road by a certain horrendous thunder. One of them was struck with fear and terror, and crying out to God, she hurried toward a tree. The other appeared not at all disturbed, but behaved in an impious manner, holding the voices of the thunders in derision and contempt. Striking her backside <note>original: "anum ſeu podicem"</note> with her hand, she turned it toward the place from which the sounds were being emitted. Whereupon it happened that the first woman, moved by the fear of God and His voice, escaped safe; but the other's buttocks and entire backside were immediately torn and mangled by the thunder, and so that blasphemous woman died miserably. 

But to come closer to the foolish assertions of those Aristotelians: one day certain merchants and others were in the company of a certain <term>Peripatetic</term> (a youth of good character who lived in the city of Shrewsbury <note>original: "Salopienſem"</note> and devoted himself to literary studies there, and was held in high esteem by all of that place for his knowledge of philosophy). As they were traveling together through the wide plain of Shrewsbury, they noticed thick clouds with sounds and thunder approaching them, and the greater part of them began to be vehemently afraid.

But that young man, wishing to show himself well-versed in the knowledge of **Peripatetic philosophy** <note>The school of philosophy following Aristotle, which dominated universities at the time.</note>, advised them and persisted in boldly persuading them not to fear. He affirmed that the phenomenon was common in nature and happened by chance as an external occurrence. He argued it was created through that **antiperistasis** <term>antiperistasis</term><note>An old scientific theory where a quality, like heat, intensifies when surrounded by its opposite, like cold.</note> which he said existed between the coldness of the place and the heat of the received exhalation. In this way, the blasphemy of this man—deceived by **Aristotelian arguments**—was judged by the righteous judgment of God.

In the year 1623, near the town they call **Croydon**, located only 8 miles from the city of London, around the month of July, certain people were preparing hay in the field of a nobleman. As they were drying it in the sun, they noticed voices and thunder approaching with horrendous lightning. Consequently, they divided themselves into two groups or pairs, gathering together not much more than two cubits <note>About three feet or one meter.</note> apart from each other, so they might remain safer from the rage of the storm. Under one tree sat three young women with a certain boy; under another sat two or three men. 

As the storm approached (marvellous to say!), the thunder could do nothing against those under the first tree while one of the aforementioned young women remained under it—as if she alone had been marked on her forehead by God so that the evil spirit might not bring her any harm. However, moved by some internal instinct, while the thunder continued and a great rain was falling, she proposed to leave that tree and hurry to the other. Addressing the others, she said, "I am going to hurry to the other tree; do you want to leave with me?" <note>original: "Ego ad arborem alteram properabo, vultisne mecum decedere?"</note> But when the others refused, she had only gone five or six paces when immediately the other two women and the boy who remained under that tree—refusing to leave with her—were struck by lightning and killed. No other sign appeared on them except for a small scraping of the bark. The woman who left escaped safely to the men sheltering under the other tree. 

But what seemed an even greater miracle was a fire in the shape of a globe descending from the top of that tree to its root; it rolled upon the ground like a wheel and passed near the other tree where the woman stood with the men. By its presence and passage, those standing there were not only alienated and astonished by stupor and fear, but the tree itself seemed moved by a certain remarkable reverence, appearing to bow and humble itself toward that wheel. It was such that a robust man leaning against the trunk felt his back broken by the great leaning of the tree. From this it is clear that there is a greater mystery in lightning and thunder than the **Peripatetics** <note>Followers of Aristotle.</note> could ever comprehend. Therefore, true Christians ought to apply themselves to the sense of the **Holy Scriptures** rather than to the vain and scarcely probable imagination of the **Pagan Peripatetics**, since the certainty of the former and the vanity and absurdity of the latter has been clearly declared in the preceding pages.

Furthermore, another wonderful example of this astounding natural meteor presented itself in this past year of 1624, in the month of July, near the town of **Windsor**, where one can see a royal and well-fortified palace or castle, only eighteen miles from the city of London. For as two women with three girls were gathering ears of wheat scattered everywhere through the field after the harvest, a stupendous thunder suddenly came upon them. The eldest of the girls, seeing the lightning flying everywhere through the air and appearing before her eyes in an oblong shape with sharp tails, was moved and disturbed in spirit beyond all the others, crying out to her mother: "Fie on this lightning and thunder! I cannot endure it; I wish I were home!" <note>original: "Phy de fulgure isto & tonitru non possum perdurare, utinam essem domi"</note> When she was admonished by her mother and another honest woman (who before her marriage was a servant or maid in my house) to leave off such frivolous and contentious talk and call upon God, she nevertheless neglected prayers to God and continued her exclamations against the annoying appearances of the meteor. 

Consequently, the others attempted to protect themselves from the violence of the storm under the wings or branches of two tall trees. But that girl, with a joking and cheerful face, leaning her back against the trunk of a very tall oak, said she was placed as if on a **royal throne** above the others and was safe from the storm. The other woman, formerly my servant, had her arm resting in the girl's lap, and her younger sister was not far from them, while the girl’s mother was under another tree five or six paces away. It happened suddenly that a certain ball of fire fell from a cloud into that huge tree, stripping its bark in three places from the top to the root with a most violent and sudden force, without any interruption of the parts, scattering fragments of it everywhere for almost a mile. Meanwhile, the substance of the trunk and inner body was not immune from that triple wound, but was hollowed out to the depth of a finger with long and continuous wounds inflicted from the highest branches to the root, as if by plowshares—the finger of God or some administering angel undoubtedly at work. Thus it happened that the girl who thought herself most safe and protected from all violence was suddenly killed in the blink of an eye by a force beyond words. The woman who was once my servant was deprived of the use and feeling of the arm that had been resting in the girl's lap, and ran in a frenzy through the street or road, crying with a loud voice and looking at the clouds: "Holy God, open your clouds and your gates that I may enter!" <note>original: "Deus sancte aperi nubes tuas, atq; ianuas tuas, ut ingrediar"</note> nor for herself...
