**Correlation to the Microcosm.**

We have learned from the teachings of both the most learned Theosophers and Philosophers that there are four things in the world procreated according to the likeness of the Archetype and the First Idea. Two of these were created by the natural path by the best and greatest Creator—namely, the World and Man—while the others were fabricated by the craftsmanship of a human creature—namely, the Ark or Tabernacle of the Covenant built by Moses, and 그 that distinguished Temple built by Solomon. Just as those natural things were created according to the image of the Archetype, so indeed were the artificial things fabricated according to the example of the natural ones. For thus in the world we have three regions, one of which excels the others in dignity:

1. The **Supreme Region**, which is the most excellent essence of all, called the **Empyrean** <note>From the Greek 'empyros,' meaning fiery; the highest heaven in ancient cosmology.</note> because of its fiery nature. Indeed, just as fire is the element more eminent in dignity, purer, and simpler in essence than all others, so for that same reason the Empyrean heaven is the head and Prince over the other two lower regions. From this, it is assigned as the seat for the purest and simplest of all creatures—namely, the Angels and the Intelligences shimmering with divine splendor.

2. The **Middle Region** follows, participating in both extremes; it is called the **Aether**, because it seems to be composed of the supreme fire and the lowest air. Therefore, it is not as pure as the supreme region, nor so impure, thick, and unclean as the lowest, but consists in a middle state.

3. Finally, the **Lowest Region** is thicker in quantity and more imperfect in quality than the higher ones, and is subject to all changes—namely, the agitation of winds, the procreation of clouds, the shouting of thunders, and the inflammation of lightnings, fire-storms <note>original: "praesterum," a term for a whirlwind or fiery waterspout</note>, and other glowing meteors <note>In this period, "meteor" referred to any atmospheric phenomenon, including rain or snow.</note>, the soaking of rains, the flooding of waters, the insane and raging violence of winds erupting from the earth, the power of whirlwinds, and infinite other accidents occurring outside the laws of placid nature.

Furthermore, in Man—who was fabricated in the image of the world (whence he is called the "Son of the World" by Hermes Trismegistus)—we have an **Intellectual Heaven** assigned to the divine mind and its angelic sparks; hence his head is the seat of the Holy of Holies. In the **Middle Region**, or the celestial spirit, is the seat of life and the living soul. Finally, the external seat of this human temple—namely, the **Body**—is composed of thick air and is subject to so many and such great changes and the effects of "meteors" (tending toward both generation and corruption) that it should most aptly be compared to the lowest region of the world.

Indeed, Moses in his method of constructing the Tabernacle, and Solomon in his building of the Temple, confirmed this same thing. For the **First Part** of them is uncovered and left open to the common air, subject to winds, rains, hail, snow, and other impressions of the air that are observed to form beneath the circle of the Moon; finally, it is subject to all alterations and changes. Therefore, common men of every kind approach this part, along with animals, where by reason of continuous sacrifices there is an unceasing alternation of life and death. From this, it follows that this part is appropriately applied to the disposition of the elementary world, which is composed of water as a fluid and unstable substance; thus the world is truly called a place of shadows and obscurity. For this reason, the Tempter is sometimes called the "Prince of Darkness," sometimes the "Prince of the World," and sometimes the "Prince having power over the air."

The **Second Part** of the Tabernacle or Temple is covered, and it shines on the inside with gold and is illuminated by a candlestick with seven branches, which without doubt denote the seven planets. Thus, this region of the Tabernacle undoubtedly represents the Celestial World in the Macrocosm, participating in both light and darkness—namely, fire and thin water. For this reason, the heavens were called *Eschamaim* <note>original Hebrew: שמים (Shamayiim)</note> by the Hebrews, from *Esh* (fire) and *Maim* (water). From these things it is clear that the substance of the heaven is indeed a body, but incorruptible, imbued with a certain intellect by which it is governed and to which it is annexed, so that this matter is neither free nor wandering. The rational soul in Man (the Microcosm) has a similar relationship to his body.

The **Third Part** of the Tabernacle or Temple was the **Holy of Holies**, presenting a likeness or image of the Intellectual World. This is the seat and domicile of the fiery angels and the abstract or separate Intelligences (who are the ministers of the living God). This is also signified within it by the two golden Cherubim who, with wings extended at length, cover and overshadow the Mercy Seat.

Furthermore, in the human temple, we have all these regions, differing in every way by purity and impurity. Thus it happens that, as in the Greater World, we receive all influences from GOD through the most pure and fiery world into that which lies closest beneath it—namely, by means of the Sephirot <term>Sephirot: The ten attributes or emanations in Kabbalah through which God is revealed.</term> through the angelic or Empyrean region into the Aethereal, and likewise from the Aethereal into the sublunary region, called the elemental...

The intellect is set apart—not from matter, but from the Divine nature—insofar as the Divine is unity, while the essence of an angel is <term>alterity</term> <note>original: "alteritas." In Neoplatonic philosophy, this refers to "otherness" or the state of being distinct from the absolute oneness of God.</note>, as will be explained more clearly below. Moreover, by "intelligence" and "set-apart intellect," we mean an intelligible substance that is free from any heavy or decaying physical mass; it is immortal, insensible, present to all things, and influencing all things. Here used in the classical sense of a tutelary spirit or supernatural being, not necessarily an evil entity.</note>, and the Spirit are of the same nature and condition.

Names have also been assigned to them based on their origin and dignity—namely, "Holy Ones," "the Wills of God," and "Divine Faces." Indeed, they are even called "Gods," and "Angels" is interpreted as a term for "Gods." Furthermore, Dionysius calls them <term>agalmata</term> <note>original: "agalmata" (Greek: ἀγάλματα). Dionysius the Areopagite used this term to describe angels as "divine statues" or "splendid mirrors" that reflect the light of God.</note>, that is, distinguished and polished mirrors in which the divine glory and splendor are received. On account of the omnipresence of such forms, the Platonists said that all things were full of gods—though they referred these back to a single Jupiter as if to their own parent—for they sprang from an uncreated lineage and received their own shining glory from him. As for the names imposed upon them because of the names of the men they assisted, we read in the Holy Scriptures that such names were given: for instance, in the book of Esdras, the name of the Archangel Jeremiel comes from the Prophet Jeremiah; Zachariel from Zachariah; and Uriel from the Prophet Uriah, whom Jehoiakim killed. Thus Samuel, Ezekiel, and Daniel are names for both prophets and angels. Furthermore, Phaniel is the name of both an angel and the place where Jacob wrestled throughout the night. From these examples, it is clear that the names of spirits are sometimes taken from the very things they oversee, whether stars, men, or places.

Finally, they are called "good" or "evil" based on the contrariety of their natures. However, since we shall make broader mention of these matters in what follows—where we will discuss the differences between angels—we shall now descend with a light leap to their actual composition.

### CHAPTER II.
### *On the Essence and composition of the Angel: what is its external,*
### *and what is its internal?*

A great dispute and discrepancy has arisen among the more skilled philosophers and theologians regarding the "consistancy" of angels. Some (among whom I name Damascene, Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas</note>, and Dionysius) affirm that an angel is something absolutely incorporeal. However, Basil, Origen, Gregory, and Hermes Trismegistus, along with the entire School of the Academics <note>The Platonists</note>, wish for them to be a corporeal substance. Augustine, in his commentary on Genesis, says in express words that without error, angels can be called "bodies," and that demons are aerial and fiery animals. Consequently, he seems to assign aerial bodies to them; for elsewhere he does not hesitate to assert that from the beginning of their creation, angels had aerial bodies, formed from the purer part of the upper air, suited for acting but not for suffering. He claims the evil angels were changed by their fall, such that their bodies took on the quality of thicker air, so that they might be able to suffer and be tormented by fire. Basil teaches us what kind of bodies were assigned to angels by God at creation: namely, when he says they are thin, aerial, and pure spirits. Artesius, in his *Key of Wisdom*, says that the "external" of the Devil is air, but his "internal" is fire; for this reason, he teaches it is very easy for the Devil, by means of his external part, to join with the aerial spirit in a human being, and in this way produce burning diseases.

As for our own opinion, it is most certain and proven by clear reason that Basil, Gregory, Origen, and all the Academics do not deviate from the truth when they say that demons or angels are, in their external part, incorporated from the air. Hence, according to the variation of the air’s thickness or thinness, different orders of demons are found in the world, differing in nature and condition. For just as it is observed in the order of nature that subtle air is nothing but mere fire, and moderate air is nothing but wind, and thick air passes into the nature of water—the density of which is finally earth itself—so, for this very same reason, some demons are fiery, others aerial, others watery, and some earthly. Consequently, all of them, in respect to their external part, are purely aerial—that is, subtly corporeal—insofar as they are made of air.

For who, having been somewhat practiced in philosophy, can be ignorant of the fact that rain-water was previously a dense cloud, and a dense cloud was previously derived from a type of misty vapor? And that misty vapor, which is visible to the eyes, was once an invisible vapor, which is the first step in the progression from moderate, invisible air to that which is thick and visible. This alteration happens through degrees of thickness. Reason must therefore allow that we have a regard for the varied constitution of angels, and from this arises the mystery of angelic mutation from one species to another, from a visible form to an invisible one, and vice versa. Thus it is certain that angels, insofar as they are aerial, are to that extent corporeal; for unless air in its invisible nature were corporeal, it would be impossible for it to be condensed into a visible body. For that which makes something a certain way is always "more so" in its own beginning; certainly nothing can give what it does not possess. But air, by addition, creates clouds, water, and earth through the path of condensation; therefore, it undoubtedly possesses a corporeal nature within itself, otherwise it would be impossible for it to be altered into the form of a body. This, then, was the reason why some demons are fiery—namely, those who are clothed in the thinnest and rarest air...

In this figure, therefore, it is clearly explained that proportion by which any order of angels abounds as much in matter as in form, and also by what proportion the divine emanation immerses itself into the multitude—that is, into the depth of the formal pyramid. Also, in the contemplation of this image, you will see with open eyes how all things have proceeded from God, and how they shall return to God, according to that saying of the Apostle: *And consequently how one is all, and all in the end are nothing but one.* <note>original: "iuxta illud Apostoli... vnum sit omnia." In conclusion, we can perceive that creation is nothing other than the mingling of the divine emanation with that which is to be created, since without this it could not persist for even a moment of time. Hence, it is said that *All things are made by the Word*, and *without Him, nothing was made*; hence we say that God fills all things everywhere; and hence the Apostle said, *In God we move, and in Him, through Him, and from Him all things exist*, etc. <note>original: "In Deo nos mouere," a reference to Acts 17:28.</note> But truly, the Angels are called the creatures of the "first composition," because their matter, being the thinnest of all, first received the effects of the creating emanation, which is therefore called by the wise man "the first of all creatures."

But lest you misunderstand me when I mention pyramids, because the word "pyramid" seems to sound like a mathematical term, and moreover I have described them in a mathematical fashion—namely, with a base and a cone <note>the "cone" here refers to the apex or point of the pyramid</note>—I wish you to understand that I mean a **physical pyramid** and not a mathematical one. Although I am forced to describe the former by the latter (as the mathematical is more commonly known), by a physical pyramid I mean the **world-spirit**, which, ascending from the earth to the periphery of the world, always gradually renders itself thinner and more subtle in its ascent, until it reaches the extreme perfection of rarity at its apex, beyond which boundary matter cannot ascend. But that which is beyond the capacity of matter must necessarily belong to the divine essence. Does not experience itself seem to declare this same thing, since all—both physicists <term>physici: natural philosophers who studied the physical laws of the universe</term> and those more skilled in theology—agree on this: that water is more subtle than earth, air than water, fire than air, ether than fire, and the Empyrean spirit than ether? This spirit also has its own degrees up to the "cone" of the physical pyramid. Here, therefore, we have expressed the material pyramid both physically and mathematically, so that what has been said by us might be more easily conceived by you.

### **On the Efficient Cause of Meteors.** 217

...can a visible body be produced by adding parts? Whatever, therefore, can be understood within the laws of rarity and density can be called a body (and not without justice). In the same way, since a cloud is dense air, why should its rare form not also be granted the name of a body, especially since that which easily becomes a body is itself a kind of body? What then? Because it is a natural body, is it therefore not a spiritual body? "The body," says the Apostle <note>A reference to St. Paul in 1 Corinthians 15:42-44.</note>, "which is sown in corruption rises in incorruption; the natural body will be changed into a spiritual body." It is therefore no more impossible for a sublunary or ethereal spirit, or even one of the empyrean or angelic realm, to be a "rare" <term>rare: in this context, meaning "subtle" or "thinned out," the opposite of dense</term> body—and consequently for angelic creatures to be rendered corporeal by their presence—than it was for that physical body of our Savior. After His passion, His body became incorruptible, and through its purity and subtlety, it was raised and exalted even to the throne of God, where in the covenant He is said to sit at the right hand of the Father; yet, nevertheless, He did not lose the name of "body." For this reason, we should not be faulted for assigning an external corporeal nature to angels of any order, because all matter—whether subject to corruption or of a heavenly and incorruptible nature—is contained within the limits of corporeal substance. For who can rightly deny that water reduced to vapor is a body just as much as it is in the form of water? Or that the point of a material pyramid is any less a body than its base? The entire difference lies in rarity and density; but truly, because a thing is dense and a body, it does not follow that something rare is excluded from being a body. Therefore, I hope it has been explained more clearly than light that angels, as far as their external aspect is concerned, are corporeal and not incorporeal, as some have thought.

But as for their internal nature, we say that it is uncreated light, such that the exterior of angels is like a highly polished, very clear, and stainless mirror, receiving within itself the ineffable likeness of God. For in it, as if in a clean and pure mirror, the divine splendor shines, emanating directly from the divine majesty. For this reason (as was declared in the preceding pages), angels are called *Agalmata* <note>original: "Agalmata," a Greek term for "cult images" or "statues," used here to mean "most clear mirrors."</note>, receiving the light of God. On account of this, an angel is said to be an image of God, a revelation of hidden light, a most polished and pure mirror without a stain.
*Dionysius, On the Divine Names, chapter 6.* <note>Dionysius the Areopagite, a highly influential early Christian theologian and philosopher.</note>

For they receive through influence the light of the Deity, which in itself is incomprehensible and invisible, and they show it, emit it, and reveal it to others of a lower order. The angel is called a mirror because it is able to receive light, and is called a "most polished mirror" because of the complete purity of its substance. Another author says that angels are "intellectual lights" receiving light from the First Light. That emanation, descending both into the bodies of angels and into other creatures through their mediation, is what the Kabbalists call *Hochma* <note>original: "Hochma Sapientia" — Hebrew for Wisdom.</note>, which the wise man therefore calls the "first creature," inasmuch as it proceeds immediately from the Father like a son, from a luminous source. Solomon describes this as a holy spirit of understanding, more mobile than all moving things, reaching everywhere because of its purity. He says that it is, in its essence, a vapor of the power of God, and a certain pure emanation or flow of the brightness of the almighty God, and the whiteness or splendor of eternal light, and the spotless mirror of God's majesty, and the image of His goodness. *Wisdom 7.* <note>Referring to the Book of the Wisdom of Solomon, Chapter 7, verses 22–26.</note> Hence, according to the doctrine of the Kabbalists, this spirit is that great angel Metatron <note>original: "Mettatron."</note>, whose role is to animate the entire universe, and whom the Platonists frequently called the "Soul of the World." But they understood that divine brightness as it is mixed with created spirit. We say, therefore, that this brightness, first striking the angelic spirit, informed it by its presence. For this reason, it is also said that the Name of God is in the angel—that is, the Divine light or the Word that gives life to all things, moving first within the angelic composition. From this, angels are ministers through whom, as instruments, the Word of God is perfected in this world. Therefore the Psalmist says: *Bless the Lord, you his angels, mighty in strength, who perform his word, listening to the voice of his word; his ministers who do his pleasure, Psalm 103.* And elsewhere: *Behold, I send my angel before you... listen to his voice, for my name is in him, Exodus 23.*

We conclude, therefore, that an angel is composed of "created spirit," which is its external part and serves as its body, and "uncreated light" shining directly from God, which is its internal part by which it is animated. By means of this composition, an angel is sometimes called "angel" or "alterity" in Holy Scripture with respect to the whole composition of the two (the internal and external); yet in another place, the angel is called "Jehovah" with respect to the internal part alone, which is the emanation of God. Thus it is sometimes said that an "angel" was in the bush, and sometimes that "Jehovah" spoke to Moses from the bush. For this same reason, the name of God is assigned to the angels of God, as in Gabriel, Michael, Raphael, etc. <note>The suffix "-el" in these names is the Hebrew word for God.</note>

### B
**Super-celestial Angels** are divided by:

**More recent Theologians** into three distinctions which they call **hierarchies** or **choirs**, of which:
*   The **Highest** is called **Epiphany** <note>original: "Epiphania," meaning "manifestation" or "appearance from above."</note>, whose order is threefold:

    *   **Virtues**
    *   **Powers**
    *   **Dominions**
*   The **Lowest** is called **Ephionia** <note>original: "Ephionia," referring to the rank closest to the human world.</note>, which is divided into:

**The more ancient Hebrew Doctors** into nine orders or ranks, which they call:
1.  First: **Haioth Kadosh** <note>original: "Haioth Kadoſh," from Hebrew *Chayot HaKodesh*.</note>, that is, **holy animals** or **living beings**.
2.  Second: **Ophanim**, meaning **forms** or **wheels**.
3.  Third: **Aralim**, meaning **strong and robust angels**.
4.  Fourth: **Chasmalim** or **Hashmalim**.
5.  Fifth: **Seraphim**.
6.  Sixth: **Malachim**.

8.  Eighth: **Ben Elohim**, that is, **sons of Gods**.
9.  Ninth: **Cherubim**.

Theologians have placed the **Seraphim, Cherubim, and Thrones** in the higher distinction or Hierarchy as super-celestial spirits looking directly upon the grade and condition of **divine providence**. The highest of these orders reflects God's **goodness and fiery love**; the second reflects His **essence and wisdom**; and the third reflects His **prudence and justice**. **Isaiah** mentions the Seraphim in chapter 6, and Holy Scripture mentions them in many other places where they are described as spirits closest to God in rank. To the **Cherubim** is assigned the guardianship of **Paradise**; and elsewhere, *God ascended upon the Cherubim, and flies upon the wings of the wind* (Psalm 18 <note>The text cites Psalm 17 following the Vulgate numbering; in modern Bibles, this is Psalm 18:10.</note>). Many holy biblical passages also speak of the **Thrones**, namely **Ezekiel** chapter 1, the Apostle in **Colossians** 1, and **Revelation** in many places.

In the **second Hierarchy** are placed the **Virtues, Powers, and Dominions**, acting as spirits of the world whose duty is more closely adapted to the **governance of the world**. The highest of these commands and gives orders to the inferiors; the second administers in the heavens and organizes the **laws of fate**; the third strives with great effort to prevent those things which presume to disturb the **divine law** in any way. The Apostle speaks of **principalities, powers, and Dominions** in the place cited above, namely Colossians 1:16.

In the **lower Hierarchy**, they identify **Principalities, Archangels, and Angels**, whose duty it is to descend to care for **lower things**. For the first order of this distinction cares for **public affairs**, namely **Princes, Magistrates, and Provinces or kingdoms**, each for their own. Among these, **72** are numbered by the **Cabalists** <note>Followers of the Kabbalah, a school of Jewish mysticism.</note>, to whom 72 portions of the earth (which are therefore called kingdoms) have been committed by Divine providence.

The **second order** is concerned with **sacred matters** and assists upright men on earth; they are said to offer **prayers and sacrifices** to **GOD**. Furthermore, seven of them are dedicated in heaven to the **governance and direction of the wandering stars** <note><term>wandering stars</term>: The planets, which were historically distinguished from the "fixed stars" because they moved across the sky.</note>, as will be discussed more broadly below. Finally, it is the duty of **Angels** to handle those matters which are of lesser inter— <margin>Ee 2</margin>

From this, it is clearly established that each of these hierarchies has a relationship to a specific person in the Holy Trinity: the highest relates to the divine essence; the middle to the emanation, or the Son, regarding the monarchy and management of the heavens; and the lowest has regard for <term>sublunary</term> <note>the region below the moon, i.e., Earth</note> things, as it is present for the forms and virtues of lower things and is seen to administer to them.

The royal Psalmist <note>King David</note> seems to speak on this sense in very few words, saying: *By the word of the Lord the heavens were made firm, and all their power by the spirit from his mouth* <note>original: "Verbo Domini firmati sunt cæli, & spiritu ab ore eius omnes virtutes eorum"</note>; where the Lord (or Father) created the heavens by the Word (or Son), and every power and influence by the Spirit from both.

According to the division of the ancient Hebrews, we see the same orders of angels—both in number and effect, though varying in nomenclature—following the series of the "gates of light" or <term>Sephirot</term> <note>the ten attributes or emanations in Cabala through which the Infinite reveals itself</note>, or the "numberings" of the Cabalists, through which various influences of divine properties descend to lower things. For as I have declared elsewhere, the influences of *Kether* <note>the highest Sephirah, "The Crown"</note> (over which the name of GOD *Ehieh* <note>meaning "I Am"</note> presides) descend through the order of the Seraphim according to the teaching of Dionysius. Thus, according to the sense of the ancient Hebrew Doctors, God *Ehieh* is said to grant the gift of "being" through the order of angels known as the *Haioth Kadosch* <note>Holy Living Creatures</note>; through the *Ophanim*, God <term>Elohim</term> <note>a Hebrew name for God often associated with creation and justice</note> distinguishes the Chaos; through the *Aralim*, <term>Jehovah</term> provides the forms of universal matter; and so on with the rest, as will be clearer in the following sections. Other Hebrew Doctors have given almost the same names to these angelic orders, though the sequence is changed: namely, *Chashmalim, Cherubim, Tarshishim, Aralim, Seraphim, Malachim, Ophanim, Ishim, Elohim*, to which they also delight to add the *Bene Elohim* <note>Sons of God</note>, who oversee both good and evil spirits (about which see below). All these names were drawn by them from the sacred fountain of the holy pages. For Ezekiel speaks of the *Chashmalim*; Genesis, Exodus, and the Psalms mention the *Cherubim*; Ezekiel also names the *Tarshishim* (though common interpretation calls them "angels" or "messengers"); Ezekiel also has the name *Ophanim*; the *Ishim* are expressed by Solomon; they took *Elohim* from the first book of Kings, where the Medium <note>the Witch of Endor</note> said to Saul: *I saw gods ascending from the earth* <note>original: "Vidi Elohim ascendentes è terra", that is, "Gods" according to the common edition</note>. Mention of the good *Bene Elohim* is made in Job, and of the evil ones by Moses and also Job in another place.

It is not irrelevant to note that although only nine orders of angels are noted by the wise or the secret theologians, there is nevertheless an innumerable multitude of individuals of each of those species, which they have called "armies." They divided each of these orders, primarily according to the partition of the celestial Zodiac, into twelve parts, the first member of which they called <term>Mazzaloth</term> <note>the constellations</note>. Then they divided each of these twelve members into thirty portions, which they called "Cohorts." This subdivision consequently contains thirty cohorts for each of those twelve, making a total of three hundred and sixty cohorts of Angels.

Then they assign another subdivision which multiplies that 360 by 30, producing the number 10,800; they call this subdivided member a "Legion." They multiply this number again by 30 and produce a <term>Ribaton</term>, consisting of 324,000. Further, they multiply this number by 30, and the result is a number they call <term>Chitton</term>, which is composed of 972,000. Finally, they multiply that product again by 30, and the resulting number will be 29,160,000. Thus, the sum of all these is one million, six hundred and fifty-five thousand, one hundred and seventy-two <note>The author's total here does not mathematically match the sum of the preceding multiplications, reflecting a specific symbolic or Cabalistic calculation</note> according to the doctrine of the Cabalists, who made all these angels "ministering spirits," of whom more will be said in the following pages. The Platonists, however, maintain that there are as many legions of lower spirits as there are stars in the sky, and they say there are as many spirits in each legion as there are stars in the sky. Some Cabalists strongly defend the idea that angels not only agree with humans in many natural things but also in number, asserting that as many humans must be saved as there were rebel angels who fell from heaven in the conflict between Michael and Lucifer; and again, as many will be damned as there were angels on Michael's side who obtained victory over the fallen angels.

But whatever the opinion of the Cabalists and Platonists regarding the number of angels may be, we also gather from the sacred scriptures that there are many myriads of angelic spirits. This is seen in several places: "The chariots of God," says David, "are two myriads, many thousands of angels; the Lord is among them, the Lord of Sinai, dwelling in the Sanctuary" <note>Psalm 68:18</note>. Furthermore, Christ speaks of many legions belonging both to his Father and to Satan. Augustine and Gregory maintain that the number of good angels transcends all human understanding; to which respond the innumerable "unclean spirits," there being as many in the lower world as there are world-spirits in the upper world. Celestial demons are called **Mundane** <note>original: "mundani"; spirits belonging to the world/cosmos.</note> by the more secret theologians. Furthermore, they are also called **Olympic**—those who dwell in the firmament and its stars. Their duty is to decree the fates and to administer fatal events to those below, according to the will and permission of God. Whence it happens that neither an evil demon nor an evil fate can harm one who "sits in the help of the Most High." <note>A reference to Psalm 91:1.</note>

Moreover, it is decreed for each of these spirits to carry out that which the star to which it is attached has portended. However, they can bring nothing from potentiality into action without divine permission. For it is God alone who grants the power and the execution, since He is the creator of all, and it is granted that super-celestial, celestial, sublunary, and even infernal things must obey and submit to Him.

Regarding the demons presiding over the fixed stars: those who hold their kingdoms in the Zodiac preside either over the **triplicities** (namely Fire, Air, Water, or Earth).

Thus, from Aries comes **Ariel**; then Telechiel, Suriel, Tommiel, Sartamiel, Betuliel, Mafniel, Acrabiel, Chefitiel, Gediel, Deliel, and Dagymiel. It is as if we were to say in Latin letters: Ariel, Tauriel, Geminiel, Cancriel, Leoniel, Virginiel, Libriel, Scorpiel, Sagittariel, Capriel, Aquariel, and Pisciel. 

In any case, it is certain that each of these signs has its own particular overseer or angel. The **Cabalists** <note>Followers of Jewish mysticism or its Christian adaptations.</note> believe that John intended this in the **Apocalypse** <note>The Book of Revelation.</note> where, in the description of the **Heavenly Jerusalem**, he mentions the twelve gates of the city. By the twelve gates, he understands the twelve celestial signs, which **Plato** calls the "gates of heaven." The Apocalypse says that in each of these gates there is an angel, for it explicitly assigns twelve angels to the twelve gates of the heavenly city. 

Just as there are three Eastern signs, three Western, three Southern, and three Northern according to the doctrine of the astrologers, so the revelator recognizes and assigns three gates to the eastern region, three to the western, three to the south, and three to the north.

According to their opinion, every angelic triplicity <note>a group of three signs belonging to the same element, such as Fire or Water</note> also enjoys its own angelic prefect.

The Abbot Trithemius <note>Johannes Trithemius (1462–1516), a famous Benedictine monk and occultist</note> testifies in a particular treatise dedicated to the Emperor Maximilian that every sphere of the planets possesses a presiding spirit or intelligence. Through these spirits, the world is governed in a successive order. By their agency, all things—those in the heavens and the air, as well as those that inhabit and grow upon the earth—are fatedly arranged according to the will of the Creator. The Prince or superior prefect destined for the governance of **Saturn** is called *Zabkiel* by the Magi (as some wish), while others call him *Oriphiel*. He is succeeded by *Zadkiel*, or *Zachariel*, who presides over **Jupiter**. *Zamael* or *Samael* (or as others prefer, *Camael*) presides over **Mars**. *Michael* presides over the **Sun**, although some appoint *Raphael* as its prefect. *Haniel* or *Anael* governs **Venus**, *Raphael* governs **Mercury** (though some attribute *Michael* to it), and *Gabriel* governs the **Moon**. These princes or prefects have many cohorts of inferior spirits under each of their commands. These spirits, according to the will of their leader (and in accordance with God’s mandates), flow diligently into the lower realms by way of "influence." They do so more abundantly according to the dominance of the star in the heavens which they are said to inhabit. These lower angels or spirits <term>demones; in this context, the term refers to "daemons" or spirits in the classical sense, not necessarily "demons" in the modern evil sense</term> receive their general names from their star. ### CHAPTER IV.
## On the difference between wicked and malignant Demons.

Just as God, who is the Emperor of light, is the Emperor of goodness, so also the Devil, who is the great Prince of darkness, is the author and worker of evil. From this it follows that just as God uses good angels as his ministers—who are thereafter called angels of light—so conversely the Devil has many troops of demons under his command. These are divided into legions, to whom it is given to invade and harm the aerial spirit of both the <term>Macrocosm</term> <note>The "Great World," referring to the universe as a whole.</note> and the <term>Microcosm</term> <note>The "Little World," referring to man as a reflection of the universe.</note> in a malignant manner. Therefore, relying on these matters confirmed by the authority of many trustworthy writers, I shall set about distinguishing the multitude of <term>Cacodæmons</term> <note>From the Greek 'kakodaimon,' meaning an evil spirit or traditionally a "bad genius."</note> in this manner:

From this place, the malignant angels—on account of their ambitious rebellion—were banished into exile, as it were, to the dense and lower region of the universal spirit. To this upper region of the worldly spirit corresponds the **intellectual or rational spirit** in man, which is the angelic seat of the mind.

Next, in the world, there is the middle seat of this universal spirit, which is called the **Aether**. In this region, the Olympic Angels or Demons <note>In this context, "demons" refers to spirits or intelligences that act as intermediaries, not necessarily evil ones.</note> act. It is from these that both the good and evil sublunary demons receive their powers of acting and their commands. From this it is clear that Satan, who is the Prince of the Air, can do nothing without permission and various influxes, according to the varied disposition of each <term>Sephirotic</term> <note>Referring to the Sephirot, the ten attributes or emanations in Jewish Kabbalah through which the Infinite reveals itself.</note> numbering or "luminous gate." To this middle region of the world-spirit corresponds the **vital spirit** in man, which sometimes inclines toward higher things and sometimes toward lower and fleeting things.

Finally, the spirit of the sublunary world is that which (by divine permission) the great Prince of darkness commands. To this corresponds the **natural spirit** in man, which Paul seems to call the "animal soul" <note>Original: *animam animalem*. Castaliensis"</note> reports. From these things, it is evident that to us, the number of demons, both bad and good, in this elementary region where we breathe, is infinite. Some are from the Eastern part, others of a Southern nature, several are Western, and others Northern with respect to the quarters of the world, and also according to the triplicity whose temperament and condition they share.

I also propose that by the nature of the planet whose influences they are chiefly animated and quickened by, some are called Saturnine, others Jovial, Martial, Solar, Venerean, Mercurial, and Lunar. These are subjects of the Angels or Intelligences presiding over the Planets. Thus, when Saturn predominates in the horoscope or celestial scheme, because of his abundant influence at that time, the spirits in the elements that share his nature tend to predominate, and so it is for the others.

Finally, each of these is called by a general name based on the element in which he naturally participates, and in which he commonly and most willingly lives as if in his own native country; many experts in the mysteries of demons agree on this. For first, the Kabbalists and Hebrew Doctors say that the demons are squalid and most foul enemies of the human race; hence, in contrast to the good angels, they are called Angels of opposing strength. They admit that some of these wander through the highest region of the air, and these they call fiery; those who tend to wander closer to us they call aerial; those who terrify the land they name terrestrial; and those who inhabit lakes and rivers and often shake the sea they name aqueous; finally, those they call light-shunning and dark, they place underground. Psellus <note>Michael Psellos, an 11th-century Byzantine philosopher and demonologist.</note> also seems to confirm this from the confession of Marcus, saying that only six kinds of these demons are found in the elementary region.

[The following are grouped as types of demons:]
1. The first is **Fiery**, which is seen to wander around the high region of the air.
2. The second is **Aerial**, which wanders close to us.
3. The third is **Aquatic**, which plunges itself into fluids, namely lakes, ponds, rivers, and the sea.
4. The fourth is **Terrestrial**, which for the most part occupies itself around the earth.
5. The fifth is **Subterranean**, which usually dwells under the earth.
6. The sixth and last is **Light-shunning**, inscrutable, and dark.

These kinds of Evil Spirits <note>original: "Cacodaemonum"</note> are said to hate God, Angels, and even men; we shall soon speak more widely of their properties and conditions.

*Concerning the evil demons that surround the human spirit.*

<note>The following list is grouped in the original by a large bracket, indicating these are the eight specific ranks of 'Cacodæmones' or evil spirits.</note>
Evil spirits <term>Cacodæmones; from the Greek 'kakos' (evil) and 'daimon' (spirit)</term> who surround the human spirit are distinguished into eight ranks, of which:
The first infects with idolatry and vain or false worship, and lures one to adore them.
The second contaminates with lies and deceives with false whispers, leading one into error.
The third inflames with anger and fury, and discovers arts to kindle various passions in people.
The fourth fills one with vengeance, retribution, and cruelty.
The fifth mocks with illusions and false miracles.
The sixth ignites with the discord of wars and the heat of devastation.
The seventh slanders, scouts, and accuses before the sight of God.
The eighth casts one into errors and danger through temptations and snares, and pollutes one with despair.

The first rank of evil spirits harassing the human spirit is the order of those called **false gods** <note>original: "pseudothei"</note>, for it is their habit to falsely attribute the name of GOD to themselves, and to entice the human spirit toward their own worship and adoration through false and deceptive demonstrations. The prince of these is thought to be **Beelzebub**, which means "the ancient god," <note>The author interprets Beelzebub here as 'vetustus Deus' (ancient god), though it is more commonly translated from Hebrew as 'Lord of the Flies.'</note> who is so bold that he did not hesitate to tempt the spirit of the Savior of the world himself, saying: *If you will fall down on the ground and worship me, I will give you all these things* (Matthew 4). To this rank also belonged the gods of the Midianites, who—through the daughters of Moab (with whom the people of Israel committed fornication)—seduced that people away from the worship of the true God, and persuaded them to adore them and offer sacrifices or burnt offerings (Numbers 25). Such also was the spirit of the Oracles, namely the Delphic Apollo, and others.

The second rank includes those who usually bring and whisper falsehoods into the spirits of men; to this order belonged that lying spirit which, by divine command, entered into the mouths of the prophets of Ahab (1 Kings 22). Similarly, it includes that spirit which strikes terror and dread into the spirits of men, of whom it is written: *Behold, I will put a spirit in him, so that when he hears a rumor, he shall return to his own land* (2 Kings 19). The leader of this order is called **Python** <note>Associated with the spirit of divination or the serpent at Delphi.</note>—that is, "the serpent"—by those skilled in magic.

The third rank consists of those who, through a love of iniquity and with the flames of anger and fury, set the human spirit on fire. To perform this duty more easily, they invent games, such as cards, dice, and other such things by which men are moved to passion and anger. Such was that demon named **Theutus**, whom Plato says was the teacher of games, specifically of dice. The Hebrews appoint **Belial** as the prince of these; his name is interpreted as "without a yoke," "disobedient," or "transgressor."

The fourth rank or order is that which not only drives the human spirit toward vengeance and retribution, but has also itself become the author of Divine vengeance. The royal Psalmist <note>Referring to King David, the traditional author of the Psalms.</note> seems to show a precaution against the invasions of such a demon into the human spirit with this speech: *Refrain from anger, and forsake burning wrath, lest you be incited to do evil; for evildoers shall be cut off* (Psalm 37:8). And the wise man says: *Do not be hasty in your spirit to be angry, for anger rests in the bosom of fools* (Ecclesiastes 7). And elsewhere: *Make no friendship with an angry man, and do not go with a furious man* (Proverbs 22:24). Furthermore, that he is the avenger and the minister of God's vengeance is indicated by this passage cited from Holy Scripture, where such a demon is called: *A spirit of the power of God, winnowing and pursuing the unjust with justice* (Wisdom 11:21). And of him elsewhere: *A spirit of power and a spirit of virtue shall stand against them* (Wisdom 5:24). The Cabalists and Magicians make **Asmodeus** the prince of these, which means "one who executes justice."

The fifth rank is of those who delude with illusions and false miracles. The magicians of the Egyptians required their assistance when, acting against Moses, they produced so many deceptive miracles in the presence of Pharaoh. Dark magicians <term>Cacomagi; literally 'evil magicians'</term> and sorcerers implore such aid in their business. Finally, the magicians themselves affirm that the Prince of these is **Satan**, of whom it is said in the Apocalypse <note>The Book of Revelation.</note> that he deceives the whole world, performing great signs and making fire come down from heaven to earth in the sight of men, so that he may seduce those living upon it.

230 [centered] **Section I, Portion IV, Part II. Book IV. Member II.**

The lowest region of the **Macrocosm** <note>The "Great World" or the universe as a whole, contrasted with the Microcosm or man.</note>, however, is subject to various passions and changes. In this way, its **airy spirit** is observed to be distinguished into various degrees of corporeality. In every such degree, both the external body and its internal spirit are afflicted and driven by the angelic spirits or ministers of God—namely, those of the wind and those of burning flame. For David confessed that *God makes his angels winds, and his ministers a burning fire* <note>original: "Deus faciat angelos suos ventos, & ministros suos ignem vrentem"; Psalm 104:4</note>. And in the preceding psalm: *That the angels of God, most strong in might, perform the word of God, listen to the voice of his word, and that they are the armies and ministers of God doing his pleasure, etc.* <note>original: "Quod angeli Dei validissimi robore efficiant verbum Dei, auscultent voci eius, & quod sint exercitus & ministri Dei facientes placitum eius"; Psalm 103:20</note>. In this speech of the royal Psalmist, we are taught that there are three primary orders of angels: the first and superior order, receiving the outpouring of God directly, is accustomed to "perform"—that is, to receive and emit the word of God; the second listens to and observes that word as if issued by the Supreme Emperor, and then commits that mandate to the legion assigned to its dominion for execution; and the third's duty is to immediately act upon and execute the pleasure of the Creator.

The more recent Theologians also seem to confess this same thing: namely, that the superior orders of Angels receive light or emanation directly from God, which they afterwards impart and communicate to the lower orders by flowing into them.

Furthermore, God uses some of these Angels to execute the effects of his wrath and vengeance; these we therefore call **evil spirits** and **demons** <term>cacodæmones; from the Greek 'kakos' (evil) and 'daemon' (spirit)</term> in respect to ourselves, though they are nonetheless necessary ministers of God. Thus God used Satan as his minister to tempt Job. So also was that destroying Angel of Jehovah, whom David saw with eyes uplifted, standing between heaven and earth with his sword drawn in his hand and stretched out against Jerusalem (1 Chronicles 21). And also that one whom Jehovah sent to cut down every man of valor in the camp of the King of Assyria (2 Chronicles 32). Such also was that evil spirit from Jehovah which possessed Saul, and so on.

On the other hand, He uses some in his kindness, who are called **good and benevolent spirits**. Such was the Angel who appeared to Elijah in the desert and offered him food; and the one whom God sent before Moses and the Israelites to keep them in the way through the desert (Exodus 33). And that Angel who redeemed Jacob from all evil (Genesis 48). And the angels who met him on his journey (Genesis 32). Finally, all those angels whom God sends before the righteous (Genesis 24:7). Similarly, by the ministry of the good angels, the spirit of the Macrocosm is governed kindly and peacefully, just as it is disturbed by the predominance of the tumultuous ones, at which time even sublunary bodies <note>Bodies existing below the moon, i.e., on Earth.</note> are seen to fall ill.

The first **incorporation** <note>The process of spirit taking on a physical or "bodied" form.</note> that occurs between simple air and a perfectly mixed body is **exhalable or cloudy air**, in which various preternatural impressions are produced by evil spirits: namely, inflammation from lightning-storms and flashes, disturbance from winds and whirlwinds, gloom from fogs and thick vapors, the red evening sky, and so on. Regarding the intemperance of the air from lightning-storms, Holy Scripture speaks thus: *Behold, a whirlwind came out of the North, and a great cloud, and a fire infolding itself, and a brightness was about it, and out of the midst of the fire as it were the appearance of amber, and out of the midst thereof the likeness of four living creatures... and the spirit was in the four wheels, etc.* <note>original: "Ecce ventus turbinis veniebat ab Aquilone... Ezek. 1"; Ezekiel 1:4-21</note>. By these things, the Prophet wishes to imply that the soul of both that cloud and that lightning-storm was that very spirit—or rather the charioteer of that chariot—and that the Lord who was carried in it was Jehovah himself, as we can gather from that entire chapter. And *Isaiah says, "By the Lord of hosts shall it be visited with thunder, and with earthquake, and great noise, with whirlwind and tempest, and the flame of devouring fire"* <note>Isaiah 29:6</note>. And Jeremiah says: *Behold, the whirlwind of the Lord, a fury going forth, a rushing tempest; it shall rest upon the head of the wicked* <note>Jeremiah 30:23</note>. And the royal Psalmist: *He shall rain upon the wicked snares, fire and sulfur, and a stormy blast* <note>Psalm 11:6</note>. And elsewhere: *As the fire burns a wood, and as the flame sets the mountains on fire; so persecute them with thy tempest, and make them afraid with thy storm* <note>Psalm 83:15; cited here as Psalm 84</note>. And regarding the whirlwind, Isaiah says *it comes from the South* <note>Isaiah 21:1</note>. And Zechariah: *The Lord God shall blow the trumpet, and shall go with whirlwinds of the south* <note>Zechariah 9:14</note>. And Job says: *Out of the south comes the whirlwind: and cold out of the north* <note>Job 37:9</note>—that is, from the spirits or demons who, by their blasts, do the will of God from the North. We conclude, therefore, that the internal part of a storm is the spirit of God, performing the word and will of God, as the Prophet David recognizes. Whence the wise man also says: *the spirit of the power of God shall stand against the ungodly, and like a whirlwind shall scatter them* <note>Wisdom of Solomon 5:23</note>.

Furthermore, **clouds** are the vehicles of God which are carried and animated, and by violent motion are seen to be borne through the air and disturbed unnaturally by the angels of God and His presence. Angelic ministers always stand by and assist in His presence; hence the Prophet says: *He ascended upon the Cherubim, and flew upon the wings of the winds; and he made darkness his secret place; his pavilion round about him were dark waters and thick clouds of the skies. At the brightness that was before him his thick clouds passed, hailstones and coals of fire. The Lord also thundered in the heavens, and the Highest gave his voice; hailstones and coals of fire. Yea, he sent out his arrows, and scattered them; and he shot out lightnings, and discomfited them, etc.* <note>original: "ascendit super Cherubin... Pfal. 17. 9"; Psalm 18:10-14 in modern Bibles, 17:11 in the Vulgate</note>. In this discourse, the Prophet clearly teaches that the ministers of the Lord are the Cherubim and the winds, as if he had said: the angels listening to his voice, and the winds or angelic spirits, the fiery ministers, performing his pleasure, as he confesses elsewhere. And elsewhere he says: *The waters saw thee and were afraid: the depths also were troubled. The multitude of the noise of the waters gave their voice...*

...your ministers a burning fire, the Abyss like a garment is his covering, the waters shall stand above the mountains, at your rebuke they shall flee, at the voice of your thunder they shall be afraid. <note>original: "ministros tuos ignem vrentem, Abyssus sicut vestimentum amictus eius, super montes stabunt aquae, ab increpatione tua fugient, à voce tonitrui tui formidabunt"</note> Psalm 104:2. By these words, it seems to be argued that Jehovah is the prince and supreme commander, who has his tabernacle in the clouds, whom angels—both fiery and windy—serve, and that the clouds seem to be thrown into confusion, fear, and roar at the sight of his splendor, and finally, that they behave in a supernatural manner. The third degree of progression from the invisible nature of the air to a perfectly mixed body is water, whose primary element is the sea. The sea, along with rivers and lakes, is either made peaceful by the good spirit of Jehovah or is disturbed by an evil spirit of Jehovah, and is stirred up to the harm of sailors. Hence the royal Psalmist <note>A common title for King David.</note> says: *You break the ships of the Ocean with an East wind*, Psalm 48:8. That is, by a violent blast sent forth from Samael <note>In Kabbalistic tradition, Samael is often an accusing angel or figure of severity; here he is linked to the destructive east wind.</note> or the east by divine will. And elsewhere: *You who trouble the deep of the sea*, Psalm 65. And elsewhere he acknowledges that the sea is stirred up by the rebuke of Jehovah, and that *the sea, seeing Jehovah, fled*, Psalm 114:3. And Job says: *By his power the sea grows still, and by his understanding he has struck down pride*, Job 26:12. By this, one may see that it belongs to God both to disturb the sea—the element of water—and to make it quiet.

But the royal prophet also expresses this most excellently and in very clear words elsewhere, saying: *Those who go down to the sea in ships, they see the works of Jehovah and his wonders in the deep; and he speaks, and makes the spirit of the whirlwind blow, and it lifts up its waves; they mount up to heaven, they go down to the depths, so that their soul melts in evils; they are tossed and stagger like drunken men, so that all their wisdom is swallowed up. Then they cry to Jehovah in their distress, and he leads them out of their troubles; he makes the whirlwind fall into silence and their waves are still; they celebrate the mercy of Jehovah, and preach his wonders to the children of men*, Psalm 107:23-31 <note>The text cites verse 33, but the passage begins at 23.</note>. Here, therefore, you see first of all that Jehovah is the commander of all powers, and the first actor and operator of all things; next, that in his severity he deals severely with the elements of the world because of the sins of men; and then afterward, that he acts through his angelic ministers, who are always ready—according to their own office, whether good or evil—to fulfill the commands and pleasure of the Divine. For he says: *And he makes the spirit of the whirlwind blow.* But through the repentance of men and their cries for mercy, he makes the tumultuous whirlwind stand still. This **spirit of the whirlwind** is an angelic wind, executing the severity of God upon the sea. At Jehovah’s command, it acts within the internal spirit of the seas and lakes in a mad, tumultuous, and furious way, no differently than that evil spirit of Jehovah acted upon the internal airy spirit of Saul himself, or the demon called **Legion** in the possessed man, which by the power of Jesus was cast out and entered into the pigs. It is like those vexed by the worst epilepsy, who swell with a great swelling and cast foam from the mouth, or those affected by that rabid disease called **Lycanthropy** <note>A form of madness where a person believes they have turned into a wolf.</note>, who are tossed and carried here and there in a violent manner. So does that violent spirit act with its legions in the sea, lakes, and pools, etc.

Finally, since the earth is a thicker part of water, we have now arrived at it; we say that it too is sometimes tossed and struck by the evil spirits of God. Hence Holy Scripture says: *The earth is shaken and moved, the foundations of the heavens are moved; it is shaken when his anger is kindled against it*, 2 Samuel 22:8. And elsewhere: *God moves the earth out of its place, so that its columns tremble; he transfers mountains*, Job 9:5-6. And elsewhere: *At the sight of God the earth trembled, and at his touch the mountains smoke*, Psalm 104:32. Truly, in such an act of God, he himself uses spiritual ministers destined for that work, who, at the command of the angelic prefect, shake the earth, produce vast gaping holes in it, vomit fires from its bowels, and are accustomed to perpetrate many other terrifying things on the earth. Hence also, when God was angry because of the impiety of the Jews, it was said: *Behold, a great earthquake occurred, for an angel of the Lord descended from heaven, and his appearance was like lightning*, etc. Matthew 28:2. Sometimes also through his avenging angels, Jehovah sends down fire and sulfur upon the earth, by which it is overturned and treated supernaturally. *And Jehovah* (says Genesis) *sent down upon Sodom and Gomorrah a rain of sulfur and fire from the heavens, and he overturned the city and the whole plain, and all the inhabitants, and the fate of the land*, etc. Genesis 19:24. That Jehovah used his angels in such business is explained in that very context. And elsewhere it is said: *The land is burnt with salt and sulfur, so that it can neither be sown nor sprout, nor can any herb come forth in it*, etc. Deuteronomy 29:23. This indeed Jehovah produced through the mediation of ministers for the inhabitants of the earth because of their sins. And elsewhere: *Jehovah will cause your land to be fine dust, or dust shall descend from the heavens upon you until you are destroyed*, Deuteronomy 28:24. Furthermore, in another place the Psalmist says: *He turns fruitful land into saltiness, because of the malice of the men dwelling in it; conversely, he puts the desert into a pool of waters and the deserted land into springs of water*, etc. By these things he seems to argue that in his severity, God makes the land as dry and sterile as it is suffocated by an excessive flood of waters, because of the sins of men; which the Kabbalists <note>Followers of Jewish mysticism (Kabbalah).</note> and those versed in the deeper mysteries of God hand down as being done by him through his ministers.

For just as they have assigned angelic prefects to the elements—namely, **Seraph** to fire, **Cherub** to air, **Tharsis** to fire <note>Likely a clerical error in the original for water (aqua), as Tharsis is traditionally the angel of the water element.</note>, and **Ariel** to Earth, who are good leaders—so indeed under them four malevolent spirits act wickedly: namely, **Samael** on the fiery side, **Azazel** on the airy side, **Azael** on the watery side, and **Mahazael** on the earthy side. Under their command (as was said before) are many orders of inferior demons. Therefore, both fiery and bright tempests with such comets proceed from the fiery angels; likewise, airy impressions <note>A term for atmospheric phenomena like clouds or wind.</note> from the airy angels, and those which disturb the waters from the watery ones. And it is the nature of the earthy spirits—as Psellus <note>Michael Psellus, an 11th-century Byzantine scholar famous for his writings on demons.</note> testifies—to cause chasms in the earth, to shake foundations, and to send upward flame-vomiting winds.

By the **Subtle substance**, diseases of the mind.

By the **Aerial spirit**.

    *   **Turbulent**, such as dizziness or <term>scotomia</term> <note>a condition where the patient suffers from blurred vision and lightheadedness</note>, and windy epilepsy.

    *   **Female discharge**.

    *   **Carbuncle** <note>a severe, painful cluster of boils or a localized skin infection</note>.

...in this way, would he bring the plague upon him? <note>original: "hac via pestem induceret in eum?"</note> 1 Chronicles 21. Once these things are pronounced by God, the evil angel stands ready with his subordinates, as if at a command, to carry out what God has spoken. Thus it is said that the devil struck Job with a most terrible ulcer *from the sole of his foot to the crown of his head, Job 2.* And yet Job, in this adversity of his, said: *the arrows of the Almighty are within me, their poison drinks up my spirit; the terrors of God are arrayed against me to fight me, etc.* And elsewhere: *You have lifted me up to the wind, you make me vanish in substance, Job 30.* By these examples, therefore, one may see that where a destroying angel is permitted to afflict a person with disease, that entire work—though mediated by a servant—is ascribed to God, who afflicts with disease through evil angels, just as He conversely restores health through good ones.

However, the evil angels do not afflict with disease, nor do the good ones bless a person with health, of their own accord; rather, both health and disease come from God through the agency of angels. From this it follows: *If you diligently attend to the voice of the Lord your God, and do what is right in my eyes, I will put none of the diseases upon you which I brought upon the Egyptians, for I am the Lord your Creator, etc.* <note>Exodus 15:26. The author uses "Creator" where modern bibles usually say "Healer."</note>

This means: "I will act and command so that the good angels—such as <term>Raphael</term><note>The name Raphael literally translates from Hebrew as "God heals."</note> and his host—may care for you," or "I will send my word through an angel," etc. Hence the name Raphael is as if we were saying "God healing."

We conclude, therefore, that it is God who strikes and who heals, but He does this through His ministering angels, whose role is to do His pleasure. Thus, there is no evil demon who can strike without the permission of the good angels, nor can they grant permission or desist from their guardianship (for everyone has their own good <term>tutelary angel</term><note>A guardian spirit assigned to protect a specific person.</note>), nor can they be free to act except by God's command. Regarding these types of spirits, which are opposite in their condition, mention was made where it is said: *that the good spirit of the Lord departed from Saul, and an evil spirit from the Lord troubled him. Therefore his servants said: Behold now, an evil spirit of God troubles you, 1 Samuel 16:15.* 

Thus it is also manifest that evil angels, or <term>Cacodemons</term><note>From the Greek 'kakodaimon,' meaning an evil spirit or malevolent entity.</note>, are the instruments of God in His severity, just as the good ones are in His mercy. David also confesses this in plain speech: *he sent upon them the anger of his indignation: indignation, and wrath, and tribulation, a visitation by evil angels; for he struck every firstborn, and did not spare their animals from death, etc. Psalm 78:49.* <note>The text cites Psalm 77, following older numbering systems.</note> From these things it is clear enough that although Moses speaks of "the destroyer" or a single destroying angel, there were nevertheless many angels or Cacodemons assisting in that work. 

Moreover, <term>Arresius</term><note>Likely a reference to an Arabic or Scholastic medical authority.</note> declares the aptitude of demons—by which they have power over humans abandoned by God—in these words: "There are certain infirmities in which the devil joins himself to a humor exiting from its proper temperament and disturbing health itself. This happens most especially in infirmities arising from <term>cholera</term><note>In the context of the four humors, this refers to 'yellow bile,' associated with heat and aggression.</note>. The reason is of this kind: because the devil's internal nature is fire, and his external is air, he can easily be joined, God permitting, with the human air <gloss>breath or vital spirit</gloss>."

So says he. But it is the role of the good angels to bind the elements together in harmonious peace, seeing as they are the "children of concord." Therefore, when these good angels vacate their office by divine will, it happens that the evil demons—who are the "offspring of discord"—suddenly invade and attempt to turn human harmony into dissonance. From this, it is clear that demons, according to their elemental natures, are accustomed to procreate various diseases in the human body.

Hence <term>Albohali</term><note>Abu Ali al-Khayyat, a 9th-century Arab astrologer.</note> says that Melancholy is from a demon. And <term>Alzarabius</term><note>Likely Al-Zahrawi (Albucasis), a famous physician and surgeon.</note> says that sicknesses invade men from the transgressions and curses of demons, who are called the <term>Alhabinables</term>. And <term>Psellus</term><note>Michael Psellus, an 11th-century Byzantine monk and scholar who wrote extensively on demonology.</note>, from the revelation of Marcus, says that aerial spirits or demons bring harm to men by approaching the "phantastic spirit" <note>The 'phantastic spirit' was believed to be the part of the soul responsible for imagination and sensory processing.</note> that is within us, because of the similarity of their two natures. For in this way, words of disturbance and pleasure sound within us—not by emitting a voice through a physical pulse or sound, but by releasing their speech without sound. They speak into the ear in a silent manner, whispering; they present various colors of the imagination according to their will, being aerial in nature (for air is capable of all colors). Thus, the "phantastic essence" transmits figures and colors—and whatever forms they themselves wish—into our animal spirit. From this they cause us much trouble, suggesting desires and plans, representing forms, stirring up memories of pleasures, and frequently inciting images of passions in those who are awake and those who are asleep. Sometimes, by titillating our thighs and groins, they suggest and sharpen insane and wicked loves. These spirits disturb the soul with a certain art and sophisticated fraud. 

But truly, the watery and terrestrial demons devise nothing wisely, nor do they perform anything by craft, except that which is troublesome; they injure in the manner of a <term>Charonean spirit</term><note>Likely referring to deadly vapors or spirits associated with the underworld (Charon).</note>. The property of these is to corrupt whatever comes near, whether it be a four-legged beast, a human, or a bird.

238             Section I. Portion IV. Part II. Book IV. Member II.

      It is also a property of theirs to sometimes assume various appearances and forms subjected to our physical sight, from which it happens that they appear at times in human form, and at other times are seen in the form of fire; occasionally they take on the form of air and wind, and not infrequently they are perceived in the appearance of a river or water. They may also be clothed in the likenesses of birds, or gems, or precious stones; others dwell within the human spirit. Thus also the Prophet Zechariah saw an angel departing from him who spoke to another angel. Sometimes they are discerned in the shapes of letters and characters, sometimes in the sound of a voice, and likewise in many other types of visions which are contained abundantly in the sacred source <note>original: "fonte sacro"; the author refers here to the Bible</note>. The more secret theologians <note>original: "Theologi secretiores"; this likely refers to Kabbalists or those practicing mystical, esoteric theology</note> seem to support this assertion of ours. The reason why they are so fit and suited to take on any appearance is because, insofar as they are endowed with a spiritual and aerial substance of singular purity, they perceive within themselves all <term>intelligible forms</term> <note>In Platonic and Scholastic philosophy, "intelligible forms" are the pure ideas or essences of things that can be understood by the mind, as opposed to "sensible forms" perceived by the eyes</note>, and consequently all intelligible forms are compatible with them. From this, therefore, it follows that they are filled with appearances and images—that is, every kind of intelligence, and consequently every physical likeness which is shaped by intelligence, shines forth in them. This is not unlike how every color exists in the air, or every object in a mirror; however, those objects in the air or mirror come from the surrounding environment, whereas this angelic impression comes from their own center and according to their own will and pleasure, as Psellus <note>Michael Psellus (c. 1017–1078), a Byzantine scholar whose works on demonology and the "spirit-body" of angels were widely cited in the Renaissance</note> seems to suggest.

There are also others to whom the office of consolation is attributed, such as the angel who was the comforter of Hagar <note>Hagar was the servant of Sarah who, according to the Book of Genesis, was comforted by an angel in the wilderness after being cast out.</note> in her great grief. And the angel who redeemed Peter from prison. And that angel seen by the grieving Apostles after the resurrection of Christ.

Others are admonitory: for these are accustomed to set before the eyes of the mind our sins, so that we may correct them; and they are also accustomed to warn us of the Divine will, instructing us in what must be done. Similarly, they often visit men, warning them not to sin, and they rouse and shake them from the sleep of sin and vice.

Others are assistants, who assist men in their ordinary affairs, like the angel who provided food and drink to Elijah and Daniel in their times of necessity.

Others are leaders and conductors on a journey. Concerning these, Jehovah understands when he says: *My angel shall go before thee on the journey. And elsewhere: Behold, I send my angel before thee, to keep thee in this way, and to bring thee into that place which I have prepared. Exodus 23:23-34.* <note>The author cites Exodus 23, referring to God's promise of a guardian angel to lead the Israelites.</note>

Besides these, others have the duty of receiving the souls of the deceased into custody, of whom we read in Luke; the soul of Lazarus was carried into the bosom of Abraham. Finally, the duty of curing diseases and healing wounds is assigned to others; thus it is handed down by holy scripture that Tobit was healed by Raphael; and that pool <note>The Pool of Bethesda, described in the Gospel of John, where an angel was said to "trouble" the water to give it healing powers.</note> was disturbed by an angel, which by the touch of the angel healed those plunging themselves into it; and so it is in many other cases. 

But here, first of all, we think this should be observed: that although these orders seem to vary, inasmuch as they take their names from more particular duties, nevertheless all these orders reported by us here are called, by a more universal office—most aptly following the Apostle Paul in the place previously cited—by the more general term, **Ministering Spirits** or **Angels**, sent for the salvation and preservation of both the bodies and souls of men. Hesiod seems to intend this when he speaks in this sense: *Three times ten thousand are there upon the earth, guardians of mortal men for Jupiter <note>original: "Iouis" (Jove/Jupiter). The author uses the Roman name for the Greek god Zeus while quoting the Greek poet Hesiod.</note>, who indeed observe justice and wretched deeds, clothed in air <note>original: "atrem induti" (likely a typo for 'aerem induti'). Hesiod describes them as 'clothed in mist' or 'invisible'.</note>, going everywhere over the earth;* 

And these guardians mentioned by Hesiod are called **Spirits** by the Latins, each of whom (according to the sense of the Cabalists <note>The Cabalists were Jewish mystics whose traditions were heavily integrated into Renaissance Christian occultism.</note>) is assigned to the care of lower affairs; and these are called **Mamona** or **Mamon**, or by the Greeks **daemones** or **demons** <note>original: "daemones." In the classical sense, a 'daimon' was a guardian spirit or a being between gods and men, not necessarily an evil entity.</note>, not in a bad sense but a good one. 

We conclude, therefore, with a certain wise man in the *Revelation of Divine Majesty*, who thus describes the more open and manifest offices of the angels: that the first among all is that great spirit who holds apart the immense and most widely extended water which is called "the heaven," and preserves it in its essence, and wonderfully grants motion to all growing and living things. In the second place are positioned the **Cherubim**, who guard and observe the Tree of Life; other angels announce future things and teach men; others destroy Sodom and Gomorrah; others kill and repel enemies; others let down snow, rain, lightning, and thunder upon the earth; and so thereafter each one executes his own peculiar gift. 

Yet all together they serve God, while they carry out His will in all things, in the heavens, in the air, and on the earth, and in every place whatsoever, and that in various and wonderful ways. Sacred Scripture testifies to this, namely that spirits and angels have always indicated to those men to whom they were sent that they were dispatched and delegated by God, to announce or command this or that to them, or even to carry out matters among them according to the divine will. Indeed, from this, the status and condition of angelic offices can be gathered and perceived: there is the greatest diligence, devotion, and the highest zeal, omitting nothing, delaying nothing, but performing everything exactly and in the blink of an eye, and bringing back the response of their execution, by which God Himself is praised, honored, and celebrated. In this execution there is no respect of persons, none of reward, of bribes, or of gifts; nothing wicked, nothing perverse, nothing unjust is performed there. There, the words of God, His sanctions and mandates, are not twisted, changed, or corrupted, but all things are carried out without any depravity according to the divine rule.

There is no one there who breaks, perverts, or keeps the word of God in part while rejecting it in part, as the sons of men are accustomed to do.

<meta>This page continues the theological exploration of how God acts in the world, specifically through his Word (the Logos) as it manifests within angelic beings, transitioning from general creation to specific biblical examples like the Star of Bethlehem.</meta>

It has been declared by us that a certain wise man in secret *Theography* <note>Theography: A term referring to the writing or description of divine things.</note>, in a certain treatise of his titled *The Revelation of Majesty* (*Book on the Spirit, Chapter 78*), bursts forth in these words: "All things were created through the word of God <note>original: "verbum Dei"</note>, therefore all things are governed, moved, and led through the word. For this reason, the 'wise men' of the world or philosophers are delirious, for they do not concede that God works all in all, and that his word moves, excites, and preserves all things. Instead, they ascribe these things to created nature, pretending that God works through mediums—namely through secondary and tertiary causes. They are unwilling to understand that God works solely through his word and not through any other means or the aforementioned alleged causes, but only within them. The first body—namely water—God created damp and humid through his word; hence no other cause is seen in water that moistens it or makes it damp. Above and within the water, God created hidden air to float upon the waters, to impel and move them, and to preserve them in their liquid and flowing substance. This same thing happens even today. Together with the air, he also created angels and spirits by his word, who in the air perform their duty and office concerning the direction of storms, rain, snow, hail, frost, clouds, lightning, and the thunderstone <term>thunderstone: A prehistoric stone tool or fossil once believed to have fallen from the sky during a lightning strike.</term>, fire, chasms, floods, heat, cold, warmth, humidity, dryness, and many other things of that kind." Thus he spoke. From these things it is clear that God does not work mediately through angels, but through the Word *within* the angels. This is also what Rabbi Menachem Recanati <note>Menachem Recanati: A prominent 14th-century Italian Kabbalist known for his mystical commentaries on the Torah.</note> says in his commentaries on Exodus 14: "The flying characters <note>original: "Characteres volantes"</note> above in the foundation of spiritual wisdom are the administering spirits, used to perform every thing through them; their operations are known to the Kabbalists."

But lest anyone, led by vain superstition, think that all things are conferred upon human mortality from heaven by the angels themselves, we have therefore asserted with Reuchlin <note>Johann Reuchlin: A 15th-century German humanist who was a pioneer in bringing Kabbalistic study to Christian scholars.</note> in Book 3 of *The Art of the Kabbalah*, that all things are done by the majesty of God even in the angels, as if through organs. This is also witnessed by the Prophet Daniel when speaking to King Nebuchadnezzar: *He does according to his will in the army of heaven and among the inhabitants of the earth.* For the Word of God impressed its character <note>original: "characterem suum"</note> upon every angel. Regarding the Angel whom He placed as a leader for Moses on the journey through the desert, Jehovah says: *He will not bear your transgressions, because my name is in him.* And it is from this that the names of angels end in *El* or *Yah*, such as Michael, Haziel, Hahaiah, Iehuiah, Habriah, and so on. From this it is clear that it is God in the angel who acts and incites the angelic creature to accomplish this or that according to His will, and not the angelic creature itself. However, insofar as the "whole angel" is considered—namely its internal and external nature—it is said by the worldly sense or the men of the world that this or that is done by the angel. Hence, therefore, an angel, whether good or evil, can do nothing against the divine will, but is moved where and when it pleases God (or the Word marked within it) to lead it, so that it may execute its office in this or that place according to the Divine property leading or seizing it.

Concerning the star of Christ, as the Magi intended when they said, *For we have seen his star* (Matthew 2), they spoke as if it were led by his angel. This refers to the pillar of fire in which there was an angel whom Jehovah placed over the Israelites on their journey, of which it is said: *Wisdom was a covering for the Israelites by day, and a starry light by night* (Wisdom of Solomon 10:17).
