<meta>This page continues a discussion on the nature of God, specifically moving from the general difficulty of knowing God's essence to a detailed philosophical and mystical analysis of His "hidden" and "revealed" states.</meta>

150          Section I. Portion IV. Part II. Book IV. Member I.

Although it is permitted for us to distinguish Him by His "garments" <note>original: "vestimentis"; referring to God's outward manifestations in the physical world</note>, nevertheless, to scrutinize His greatness is beyond the capacity of human intellect, for *it cannot be* (as the Prophet witnesses) *grasped, Psalm 145:3.* And much less is His pure essence given to be seen by human eyes and flesh, according to the words of the Prophet and the Evangelist: *No one has ever seen God. Jeremiah 1. John 1:4.* <note>The author combines references; John 1:18 or 1 John 4:12 are the more typical citations for "No one has seen God."</note>

We shall therefore follow, in our description of God, partly the doctrine of the most excellent philosophers, and partly that of the **Cabalists** <term>Cabalists (practitioners of Kabbalah, a Jewish mystical tradition often studied by Christian Hermeticists in the Renaissance)</term>, in matters where they agree with the Holy Bible; and finally, we shall declare in a few words what is to be gathered from the Word of God for a living description of God.

We gather, therefore, from the testimonies of divine writers, that God has a twofold nature relative to us: namely, the **hidden** and the **revealed**. The **hidden** nature is that in which, before the creation of the world, He was seen by human understanding to rest in infinite darkness and to do almost nothing, but rather to reflect His ardor and power back into Himself, and not at all to apply the rays of His light to the creation of the world. And the same must also be said of His rays or essence resting and hidden in the opaque and dark things of the world, in the form described by **Mercurius Trismegistus** <note>The legendary Hellenistic figure associated with the Hermetic corpus</note> in these words: *The Monad (he says) begat the Monad before the creation of the world, and reflected its ardor into itself, that is, it shone back upon itself.* By these words, he seems to suggest that the divine nature—that luminous fountain, the act of all active things, the origin of life, and the **Ocean of form**—reflected the rays of its fiery and purely formal nature back into itself. From this it happened that before there was any will in Him to create the world, an infinite abyss was overwhelmed by shapeless darkness and was empty; which indeed the said Philosopher seems to infer in another place, saying: *There was an infinite shadow in the abyss.* In this discourse, he seems to agree with **Moses**, who says that *darkness was upon the face of the deep.* And this was that "matter in potential" of the **Peripatetics** <term>Peripatetics (followers of Aristotle's philosophy)</term>, which they called "prime matter," whence this kind of hidden nature is called by some "divine power," as will be declared below. Furthermore, as the Philosophers considered that divine nature—hidden in darkness and gloom and not at all expanding itself—mathematically, they called it **Arithmetical Unity**, and sometimes a **Geometric point**. I call it a Unity simple in itself, without any respect to number; and a point with no relation to a circumference. But insofar as they are considered in either art, they are in their nature simple, indivisible, of no quantity, quality, or substance; and yet they are the principle of all these things, since once expanded, it is everything that is, or everything that can be grasped in the **ten categories** <note>original: "decem prædicamentis"; Aristotle's ten classifications of all things that can be known (substance, quantity, quality, relation, etc.)</note>, as will be more broadly declared in the description of the **Revealed God**; in which it will be shown that this most simple Unity is fortified by its peripheral numbers, just as a point is by its circumference.

In the art of the **Cabalists**, the more skilled have called that divine power so hidden the **Dark Aleph** <note>original: "Aleph tenebrosum"; Aleph is the first letter of the Hebrew alphabet</note>, just as they called that which is manifested and shining out of the darkness the **Bright Aleph**. But indeed, by the *Dark Aleph*, they understand a "numeration" <term>numeration (Sephirah; an emanation or attribute of God in Kabbalah)</term> according to the Cabalistic system, namely **Hochma** <term>Chokhmah (the second Sephirah, meaning Wisdom)</term>, or wisdom, or that **Monad** which the Monad begat before any creation, the ardor of which it reflected back into itself. This divine wisdom emanating from the Father, now returning into the bosom of the Father before the act of creation, the wise called the "Beginning," of which it is written in the book **Bahir** <note>An early and influential Kabbalistic text</note>: *Nothing is the Beginning except Wisdom. Reuchlin, Book 3, On the Art of the Cabala.* For, he says, when the most absolute essence of the three highest Cabalistic numerations—which we Christians call the three persons in the Divine—is withdrawn and remaining in the abyss of darkness, as if idle, or as they say, looking toward nothing, it is therefore called **Ein** <term>Ein (Hebrew for "nothing" or "non-existence," referring to God's infinite state before emanation)</term>, that is, nothing, or "non-being," and "without end," because we, due to such a meager poverty of intellect regarding divine things...

### CHAPTER IV.

### What this divine spirit is that creates all things, and how it is sometimes called the **Word**, and sometimes **Wisdom**.

That this spirit of immense power is God himself—being no more to be divided from the divine essence or the "bright fountain" than the rays of the sun from the solar body—we have demonstrated in the preceding pages through the opinions of both sacred letters and philosophers. How, by the same flow from the darkness, the overwhelmed darkness or abyss is illuminated, and how waters both thin and thick are animated and brought forth from nothing into action and being, we shall now explain in what follows. Indeed, we have already stated clearly enough that it is written: *The Spirit of the Lord moved over the waters*, imparting vigor to them. These waters, before this liquid spirit went forth from the bright fountain or the "bosom of the Father," were called the "abyss," upon the face of which was darkness, as is held in the sacred text. Finally, we are taught by many passages of the sacred context that this spirit is the **Alpha and Omega**, the beginning and the end of all things, as it is the source from which, through which, and in which all things exist. *I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the end, says the Lord*, <note>original: "Apoc. 1." — Revelation 1:8.</note> and elsewhere, *I am the first, I am the last; my hand founded the earth, and my right hand measured the heavens; I will call them and they shall stand together.* <note>original: "Isa. 48." — Isaiah 48:12-13.</note> It is certain that *in God himself we live, move, and have our being*, <note>original: "Act. 17." — Acts 17:28.</note> which must also be understood of every created thing, since the incorruptible spirit of God is said to be in all things. <note>original: "Sap. 12. 1." — Wisdom of Solomon 12:1.</note> For this reason, and by account of this spirit, it was said by the Apostle that *God works all things in all*, <note>original: "1. Cor. 12."</note> and thus the same Apostle concludes elsewhere that God is the Father of all, who is *over all, and through all, and in us all.* <note>original: "Ephe. 4. 6."</note> Elsewhere he says that *God gives life to all things.* <note>original: "Tim. 6." — 1 Timothy 6:13.</note> This also seems to be verified by the Evangelist, affirming that *by the Word all things were made, and without him nothing was made that was made,* and that *in him was life.* <note>original: "Ioh. 1." — John 1:3-4.</note> Elsewhere we are taught by the Apostle that *from Christ and through Christ are all things,* <note>original: "Ro. 11." — Romans 11:36.</note> and in another place he says: *Christ fills all things,* <note>original: "Eph. 4. 8."</note> and elsewhere: *from him, in him, and through him are all things, to whom be praise and honor.* In the same epistle, he recognizes that *God created all things through Jesus Christ.* <note>original: "Eph. 3. 9."</note>

And this name **Jesus** is said by the <term>Cabbalists</term><note>Followers of a mystical Jewish tradition that was often adapted by Christian scholars to explain the hidden meanings of the Bible.</note> to comprehend all the names of God within its power; indeed, it contains that most essential name of God, the <term>Tetragrammaton</term><note>The four-letter Hebrew name of God, YHWH, often rendered as Jehovah.</note> or **Jehovah**. That this name is the **Word of God**, and that this is God himself, is declared by the speech brought forth by the Evangelist: *In the beginning,* he says, *was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. Hence it is said: *Even the darkness cannot be so darkened but that you foresee, but the night shines to you as the day, and darkness to God is as light itself.* <note>Psalm 139:11-12.</note> Furthermore, its essence and pure formality are indicated by the fact that it is the light of the world and a light shining in the darkness—nay, the light not only of the world but of man himself. Finally, its office is explained by the fact that all things were made by it, and the reason is that in it is the life of every thing. Hence it is written elsewhere, *In God himself we live and move and have our being,* <note>Acts 17:28.</note> and elsewhere, *God gives life to all things,* <note>1 Timothy 6:13.</note> and elsewhere, *I am God your redeemer, making all things, stretching out the heavens alone, establishing the earth and none with me.* <note>Isaiah 44:24.</note> Hence also the royal Prophet: *By the Word of the Lord the heavens were formed, and by the spirit of his mouth all their power.* Finally, all that we have said is most clearly confirmed by St. Peter: *The heavens were of old, and the earth consisting of water and through water, by the Word of God,* <note>2 Peter 3:5.</note> by which words...

And elsewhere: **GOD**, who makes the earth in his strength, prepares the world in wisdom, and by his prudence extends the heavens (Jeremiah 10). He turns the heaven in a circuit to its place in one day (3 Esdras 4). All of this seems to be hinted at by Hermes Trismegistus <note>A legendary Hellenistic figure regarded as the author of the Hermetic Corpus, a series of sacred texts on philosophy and magic.</note> in *Pimander*, Book 1, where he says: That when **GOD** had revealed himself, all things were turned into a light pleasant to behold; and a little later, a terrifying shadow glided downward with a slanting revolution into a moist nature, etc.

### CHAPTER VII.

### Concerning the first Mover, the first movable sphere, and the Divine will.

We have stated that the **first mover** of all things is **Wisdom** itself <note>Wisdom is personified here as a divine agent of creation, often associated with the Holy Spirit or the Word of God in Renaissance philosophy.</note>, which, being created before all things and by its own nature (as the wise man testifies in the Book of Wisdom, chapter 7), is "more mobile than all mobile things," reaching and touching everywhere because of its purity. For the emanation from **GOD** is the most living act of all, and the origin and fountain of all acts. This Wisdom, having repelled the darkness toward the region of the earth, immediately exercised its primary moving power in that first heaven which is called the <term>Primum Mobile</term> <note>The "First Movable" sphere: in the old geocentric model of the universe, this was the outermost sphere that moved all the inner spheres (the planets and stars).</note>. It is called the "first movable" because all the other spheres of the world derive their motions from it, moving from the east to the west. 

Hence we find it written that the most powerful **GOD**, who is truth, "turns the heaven in a circle to its place in one day" <note>original Latin: "convertat cœlum in gyro in locum ſuum in vno die," citing 3 Esdras 4:34.</note>. And Wisdom herself said that she alone "encompassed the circuit of heaven" <note>original Latin: "circumiuiſxe cœlos ſolam," citing Ecclesiasticus 24:5.</note>, by whose motion—as if by the divine will—the spirit created on the first day is accustomed to move constantly, just as a body moves according to the motion of its soul. From this it is clear that divine Wisdom itself is, as it were, the **will of GOD**, emanating immediately from the Word, being continuous with it and not at all divided from it (Ecclesiasticus 1). 

Therefore, the wise man speaks in these words: "The Word of God on high is the fountain of wisdom, and its entrance is the eternal commandments." <note>original Latin: "ſapientiæ fons verbum DEI in excelſis, ingreſſus illius mandata æterna"</note> Indeed, the Evangelist seems to suggest that the will of **GOD** is the effect of the Word in these words of our Savior: "I came down from heaven, not to do my own will, but the **will of the Father** who sent me" (John 6). Therefore, as the Word is, so is the will of **GOD**, and so is Wisdom. "The Word of our **GOD**," says the Prophet, "stands forever" (Isaiah 40). And the wise man says, "the will of the Lord shall remain forever" (Proverbs 19:22). The will of **GOD** is the word "**LET IT BE**" <note>original Latin: "FIAT." This refers to the creation commands in Genesis, such as "Fiat Lux" (Let there be light).</note>. Elsewhere it is said, "not my will, but yours **be done**." 160

->What can be the meaning of this sentence: **God is a Spirit**?<-

<margin>The Soul is not in a place.</margin> Is it not to say that he is a <term>simple substance</term> <note>A "simple substance" refers to a fundamental entity that cannot be divided into smaller parts, unlike physical matter.</note>, which has no extension, and consequently is not in a place? For, to be in a place, to the extent that it occupies space <note>original: "quatenus est in loco"</note>, can only be said of a being that has parts, and that occupies a certain space by its own extension. Now the Soul is not such a being; it is a simple substance, and therefore it is not in a place. 

It is true that one says of the Soul, that it is in the body; but this is only because it acts there, and because it is there that it receives its impressions. It is in this sense that the <term>Schoolmen</term> <note>The Schoolmen were medieval philosophers and theologians, such as Thomas Aquinas, who developed "Scholasticism."</note> used to say that the Soul is "entirely in the whole, and entirely in every part" <note>original: "tota in toto, & tota in qualibet parte"</note>. It is the same with the Soul as with a **Word**, which is entirely in the mouth of him that speaks, and yet is at the same time in the ears of many that hear it.

<margin>God is not in a place.</margin> What shall we say then of God? Where is he? If we speak of a "where" <note>original: "ubi"</note> in the proper sense, God is nowhere; for he has no extension, and therefore cannot be in a place. But if by the "where" we mean the presence of a being in the place where it acts, then God is everywhere, because he acts everywhere, and nothing can exist or move without him. This is what we call his <term>Ubiquity</term> <note>Ubiquity, or omnipresence, is the state of being everywhere at once.</note>. 

God is not in a place, but he is everywhere; he is present to all his creatures, but he is not confined by them. He is "outside of the world" <note>original: "extra mundum"</note> as well as in the world. We may compare him to the **Sun**, whose light is spread over all the earth, and yet the body of the Sun is not upon the earth. But this comparison is very imperfect; for the light of the Sun is a body, and it is only in the places where it shines; whereas God is a Spirit, and he is present everywhere in a manner that is beyond our understanding.

It explains that while they do not occupy space like matter, they are "present" wherever they act, establishing the concept of divine ubiquity.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the philosophical exploration of the divine nature in man, specifically focusing on how the "Divine Will" relates to the human soul and the origins of human error.</meta>

...or the perverse madness of diabolical error, which clouds the rays of truth and overshadows the vision of reality.

We consider the divine will, therefore, to be the moving act of the divine Word or Wisdom that emanates from the essence of God. It is never to be separated from its ray; it is eternal, co-existing with the Word and its emanation, and no more divisible from it than heat is from fire or light from the sun. We identify this same will as the proper and God-like source of the divine ray within man, which is the primary movement in the human will. For when God said, "Let us make man in our image," the word *Let it be* <note>original Latin: "Fiat"</note>, or the moving power of the Word, was the will of God—the living signature of His will—from which the human will fundamentally arose. For the act not only of life, but of will, followed immediately with the Word itself.

What follows then? Shall we conclude that the will of man is the will of God? Quite the contrary: just as we say that the sublime life and mind of man are by no means separated from the essence of God—since they are breaths from God <note>original Latin: "spiracula," referring to the "breath of life" in Genesis</note> and consequently cannot be divided from His emanation (for the divine essence is indivisible)—so we say that the human will proceeds from the divine. However, that divine will was intended to shape the human species, to sustain it, and to govern and direct it in this life toward good things and away from those foul things that are abominable to God and human nature. This aligns with the words of the Wise Man: *God sends wisdom from the holy heavens to man, so that she may be present and labor with him, and that he may know what is pleasing to Him (Wisdom 9).* And elsewhere: *That He may direct man in his way.* 

Yet this spark of divinity <note>original Latin: "scintilla hæc diuinitatis"</note>, because of Adam's perverse error and sin, has been so obscured and clouded by darkness in our descendants that, although this spark always tends toward the good in its own movement, its impressions are nonetheless poorly received due to the dark disposition of the body. The Wise Man <note>Referring to the author of the Book of Wisdom in the Apocrypha</note> seems to acknowledge this in these words: *Who among men can know the counsel of God? Or who can know what God wills? For the thoughts of mortals are timid and our foresight is uncertain; for the corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that muses on many things. We can hardly guess at the things on earth, and who shall search out the things in heaven? Who has known your mind, unless you have given wisdom and sent your most holy spirit from on high? Thus were the paths of those on earth corrected, and men learned the things that please you (Wisdom 9).*

By this third thread of words, he seems to argue that the weight and darkness of the corruptible body are the cause of the uncertainty of the human path. That God immediately sent the ray of life and intelligence into man, we gather from these sources: *There is a spirit in man, but the inspiration of the Almighty gives him understanding (Job 32:8).* <note>The source text cites Job 9, but the quote is from Job 32.</note> And elsewhere: *The spirit of God has made me, and the breath of the Almighty has given me life.* From these, it is clear that the origin of both human reason and life is the divine spirit or breath. Similarly, we understand that this ray of life and intelligence was the very spirit of wisdom from the discourse of the Wise Man: *God made man by his wisdom so that he might rule over the creatures made by Him (Wisdom 9:2).* And from this, it is said: *God made man in his own image (Genesis 1:27).* <note>The source text cites Genesis 5:1.</note> Thus, it is certain that Wisdom itself (whose act is the effect of the divine will) is the source and origin of the human will no less than the divine.

But the darkness and corruption of the human body, brought upon it by Adam's sin and the cunning and malice of the Devil, are the occasion for error in life and the cause of the wicked effects of the divine will within man. For God, in His first creation, gave man the Holy Spirit to rule him, lead him in His paths, and defend him from corruption; hence it is said: *Man is the temple of the Holy Spirit.* We confirm this through the words of the Wise Man: *God created man to be immortal, and made him in the image of His own likeness; but through the envy of the Devil, death entered into the world (Wisdom 2:23).* And elsewhere: *Do not seek death in the error of your life, nor bring destruction upon yourselves by the works of your hands; for God did not make death, nor does He delight in the destruction of the living. For He created all things that they might exist, and He made the nations of the world wholesome (Wisdom 1:12-16).* 

In these, he indicates that the gift given by God was an act of health, prudence, and happiness, and that it is overshadowed by man’s fault, sired by the malice of the devil. Thus man wanders in his life unless those shadows are illuminated by the influx of divine wisdom sent from the highest heavens—that is, unless ray is increased by rays, all bodily and diabolical darkness is removed, and so nature shall rejoice in nature. For this reason, there is a difference between the human will and the divine: not because they differ in essence, but because the divine is never occupied with vain effects, while the human—though always good in itself—sometimes has its good operations turned into evil and vicious effects by the vile and putrid flesh. 

This is much like how the pleasant rays of the sun are converted into a scorching heat by the violent reflection of a burning mirror <term>burning mirror: a "speculum ustorium," a curved mirror or lens used to concentrate sunlight to start fires</term>. It is not that the mirror or the flesh received evil impressions from that divine act, but that by receiving its good acts poorly, it tends to sin, turning the direct movement of the rays into an oblique path away from truth itself through a rebellious reflection. Thus, this perverse and crooked will, caused by the flesh’s distorted reception, makes man go astray.

Hence it is said that the most just of men errs seven times a day <note>This is a common early modern paraphrase of Proverbs 24:16, used here to emphasize human fallibility despite divine guidance.</note>. I do not say this because the good spirit is the cause of evil, but because an evil object—by perversely receiving the good actions of the spirit's rays—very often produces perverse effects. It is much like a man wandering in a dark place: he intends to follow the path of his own freedom and the vision of light, but being led astray by the darkness, he falls unexpectedly into a pit. 

For the rays of divinity (through which all things subsist, and by whose abundance man is said to rule over all other creatures) do not themselves suffer the assaults of darkness. As it is written: *darkness is not darkness to you, but the night is as clear to you as the day* <note>original: "tenebrae non sunt tenebrae tibi, sed tam clara tibi est nox, quam est dies"; a reference to Psalm 139:12, suggesting that while humans are blinded by darkness, the divine light remains untainted and all-seeing.</note>. However, darkness deludes the animal creature <note>The "animal" part of man refers to the lower, sensory, and biological nature, as opposed to the "rational" or "spiritual" mind.</note> when it is overwhelmed by the false vision of the senses, dragging it toward evil instead of good. At such a time, it is said by Hermes Trismegistus <note>A legendary Hellenistic figure, regarded as the "thrice-great" founder of Hermetic philosophy and alchemy.</note> that the divine mind <term>mens</term> <note>In this context, the "mens" is the highest part of the soul, the spark of divine intellect.</note> within man lies dormant; it no longer governs him in an intellectual manner, but provides him only with the basic functions of biological life.

of our flesh, Ephesians 2. And Christ himself, having overcome the narrow straits of his own flesh by first praying that God might turn away that cup, nevertheless said, "not my will but thine be done," Luke 22, according to that passage in John 5: "I seek not my own will, but the will of him who sent me." But if the human will is united with that divine will, then it is accustomed to perfect that same will; and of this kind of union John speaks: "He who does the will of God remains forever," 1 John 2. That is to say, he has been made one with God. Indeed, so that this might happen in the Royal Prophet <note>The "Royal Prophet" refers to King David, the traditional author of the Psalms.</note>, he himself speaks thus by praying to God: "Teach me to do thy will, for thou art my God," Psalm 143:10. It is as if he had said: let your face shine upon your servant, and in your light I shall see light; or as he has it elsewhere: "Thou, the Sun giving life and glory, and illuminating my lamp, shalt make my darkness shining," so that I may enter upon the right path to execute your will, Psalms 18:29 and 84:12. 

From these things, therefore, one may see that the "lamp" of a human being <note>The author uses the "lamp" as a metaphor for the individual soul or intellect.</note> does not differ in essence from the spiritual Sun—who gives grace, glory, and salvation—except in this: that the lamp resides within a created body as its own particular ray, providing it with being and existence, and holds the place of a creature. This spiritual Sun, however, exists in and through itself, attributing life and being to the worldly spirit, and existing so far beyond all things that he is said to "fill all things." He is the Father of all, who is over all and through all, the God who gives life to all things, the worker of all in all, Ephesians 4:6, 1 Timothy 6. He is the center of every thing whose circumference is nowhere <note>A classic Hermetic definition of God as an infinite sphere.</note>, the unity of unities, the father of fathers, the principle of principles, the fountain of fountains, the root of roots, the "Star of stars" as in Synesius's *Hymns*. He is the Good of goods, the Idea of ideas, immense beauty, the hidden seed of things; the father of ages, the father of the intelligible worlds, the spirit instilling Ambrose <note>Likely a reference to St. Ambrose or a specific theological concept of "breathing into" the soul.</note>, floating upon the mass of the body, who now awakens the world. He is Jupiter or Jehovah, upon whom all the inferior gods depend, as Orpheus and the Pythagoreans would have it. Finally, he is everything that truly exists, in which definition we exclude from him all empty, deceptive, and fantastical things, which are like the children of darkness—things that appear to be, yet are not, as will be made clear in the final examination when all things must be reduced to the one Moon <note>In this mystical context, "the Moon" often represents the final receptive principle or the completion of a cycle of reflection.</note>.

We conclude, therefore, that God acts voluntarily and not out of a necessity driven by impulse, as the Peripatetics <term>Peripatetics: Followers of Aristotle's philosophy, who often argued for a universe governed by logical necessity rather than a personal, voluntary divine will.</term> claim. We conclude that nothing has been made, whether in the heavens or on the earth, which did not receive the motion of its origin from the divine will. If a "spark" within a creature does not produce the desired effects—those that smile upon God and good men—this does not happen because of the incorruptible spirit acting from the center. Rather, it happens because of the deceptive mass of darkness, which is subject to all change and poorly receives the acts of the divine mind. Thus, these dark masses obscure the rays of such great light; the darkness within the creature does not comprehend that light dwelling in the darkness, according to the words of St. John: "In the Word was life, and that was the light of men, and the light shines in the darkness, and the darkness comprehended it not."

We can most aptly compare this light (or spirit of wisdom) to the nature of the Sun. The Sun is simple in itself and always uniform in its action, yet it is manifold in respect to the variety of operations which its rays are accustomed to produce in the world. This does not happen because of any variation in the Sun's action, but because its impressions are received differently according to the variety of bodies—varying according to their existence or the greater or lesser resistance of those receiving the solar acts. For, as the Wise Man <note>A reference to the author of the Wisdom of Solomon in the Apocrypha.</note> witnesses, God composed all things by "number, weight, and measure," making one thing differ from another by proportion, so that he might produce various creatures, both corporeal and spiritual, in this world by his single and simple act. 

Thus we see that various effects are produced in the world by those solar rays, according to the character of the recipients. In one place, the Sun causes grass and herbs to germinate and blossom; at another time, it scorches and dries them up. Sometimes it nurtures and refreshes animals with its beneficial heat, and sometimes it makes the weak and sick suffer by its presence; indeed, it compels healthy men to hasten to shaded places to escape the perfection of its burning rays. Again, the rays contracted into the center of a burning mirror <note>original: "speculi vrentis"; a concave mirror or lens used to focus sunlight to start fires.</note> set fire to and consume cities and royal palaces, reducing them to nothing; yet in water, it is observed not to act in the same way. It inflames stones and rocks with heat, and at other times it warms them only gently. Sometimes, therefore, the effects of generation are hastened, and sometimes they tend toward corruption—and yet the Sun itself, together with its rays, remains the same: permanent and simple in its action. The entire difference lies in the diversity of the object, which receives the solar acts either well or poorly. The matter is no different regarding the rays of the invisible and intellectual Sun, which gives life and being to this worldly sun. 

And so you have my conceptions concerning the divine will and its branches, according to which all things are done in this world. Within it, the will produces various effects based on the variety of those receiving the divine rays—varying by number, weight, and measure in this world. As for the act of the human will, both obscured and illuminated, we have depicted it in this place to the best of my ability for the better understanding of the readers.

->### Chapter IX.<-

->*That, contrary to the opinion of Aristotle and certain other pagan <note>original: "Ethnicorum"</note> philosophers, God works and acts in his creation and in the sustaining of his creatures not out of necessity, but by his own will.*<-

We call that "necessary" which indeed cannot be otherwise; but that which can be otherwise, we call "contingent," which includes both the voluntary and the accidental. Now, a great dispute has arisen among the pagan philosophers as to whether God created the world and the creatures within it in this way—namely, by choice—or in that way—namely, by necessity. The greater part of them have fallen into the opinion that God acts in the world, both in its creation and in the <term>decay <note>original: "corruptionem." In Aristotelian philosophy, "generation and corruption" refers to the natural cycle of things being born and passing away.</note></term> of things produced within it, by necessity rather than by will. They speak as if He were driven to such works apart from His own desire, compelled and prompted by a certain "nature" that was either co-eternal with Him, pre-existing, or at least already created by Him. How profane this is, and how far it wanders from the goal of reason, will be made clear by what follows. For what is more ancient than God, seeing as He is before all things? What is smaller than a "point" in measurement, or lesser than "unity" <note>The number one.</note> in counting? Therefore, it is necessary that God be free and acting by His own will in His deeds, insofar as He exists by Himself without dependence on other things, and was sufficient unto Himself before any creation began.

Furthermore, within **unity** <note>original: "unitate". CHAPTER X.

*On the property of Divine numbers and names among the Cabalists,* <note>Cabalists refers to followers of Cabala (Kabbalah), a school of Jewish mysticism that explores the relationship between the eternal, mysterious Infinite and the finite universe.</note> *and how the various effects of the divine will depend on their natures, tending toward both benevolence and malediction.*

In our "mirror of causes," which is attached to the end of this section, you have it demonstrated how a different name of GOD presides over each Cabalistic <term>numeration</term> <note>original: "numerationi Cabalisticæ." These numerations are the Sephirot, the ten attributes or emanations in Cabala through which the Infinite reveals itself.</note>. This is not because there is any diversity in the essence of GOD, but because His properties in the world are various, according to His good pleasure and His will, wherever it seems good to Him. Some of these properties tend toward mercy and benevolence, while others tend toward severity and ill-will. For a fuller understanding of this matter, it must be known that although many names are attributed to God (according to the opinion of Rabbi Moses the Egyptian <note>This refers to Maimonides (1138–1204), the preeminent medieval Sephardic Jewish philosopher.</note>), all of them—except for one alone, namely the <term>Tetragrammaton</term> <note>The four-letter Hebrew name of God, YHWH.</note> which is called the "separated name"—are assigned to Him in relation to created things. 

The Tetragrammaton is appropriate to Him alone, because it signifies the substance of the Creator in a pure sense, without any shared participation with creatures. Other names assigned to Him denote Him through "participation"—that is, with respect to created things—and consequently, they are derived from His works. It was for this reason that His essential name was not spoken, except in the sanctuary by the holy priests of the Lord, and specifically in the priestly blessing by the High Priest on the Day of Atonement. The rank of this name (says Rabbi Moses) is great, and it was not to be uttered rashly from the mouth, because it signified the substance of the Creator; through this, God is noted to be above all being, and to have existed before any thing was. But other names denote God as He exists *within* all being.

For example, God replied to the questioning Moses: I.H.V.H. <note>original: "I.H.V.H." (Yahweh/Jehovah)</note>, this is my name forever. Therefore, this name alone belongs to eternity—that is, to the Divine essence in its purity. No such name can be composed by a human voice that can equal the nature of divinity. Although there are various surnames of GOD derived from His works, this is the only name appropriated to Him before any created thing existed. Yet, insofar as the divine essence is as much within created things as it is outside of all things, the Tetragrammaton is also common and general, acting in every branch of the <term>Sephirotic tree</term> <note>A symbolic diagram used in Cabala to represent the ten Sephirot and the path of divine emanation.</note>, so that the other various surnames of GOD are merely properties, or offices, or various acts of power of that one and individual essence.

Thus, among the various surnames of God inscribed on the Sephirotic tree, ***Ehieh*** <note>original: "Ehieh," Hebrew for "I Am" or "I Will Be."</note> signifies the source of all creatures, the first of all clemency and all graces, sparing all, the Father of mercies, and the God of all consolation, whom Christ teaches us to pray to thus: *Our Father who art in heaven, etc.* And of Him it is said that the Father judges no one; furthermore, it is appropriated to the Father as one who is always merciful and benevolent toward His children, just as God's mercy toward His children is taught in *Psalm 103.* This name is therefore assigned as the president over the Sephirah—or numeration, or gate of light, or the first branch of the Cabalistic tree—which is called ***Cheter*** <note>Kether</note> or the Crown. For just as *Cheter* is, as it were, the root of the tree, so indeed *Ehieh* is the Father of all creation. From this it is clear that the reason for this surname of God is taken from His property in clemency and mercy which is occupied with creatures—namely, in giving and granting life, and giving the gift of being or existence to the world and the creatures contained within it.

The second surname of GOD in the Sephirotic order is ***Iah*** <note>Yah</note>: which also tends toward the benign property of GOD in the formation of the world, specifically the extraction of the waters from the belly of Chaos. The numeration over which it presides is ***Hochma*** <note>Chokmah</note>, that is, Wisdom, concerning which it is written: *He who made a weight for the winds and weighed the waters by measure, when He set a law for the rains, and a way for the sounding storms, then He saw wisdom, etc. Job 28.* And elsewhere: *When He formed the heavens above, when He strengthened the fountains of the deep, when He set a statute for the sea, when He established the foundations of the earth, I, Wisdom, was with Him as a foster-child, composing all things. Proverbs 8.* From the benign disposition of this Sephirah, He is said to be mild, kind, and loving of good; and elsewhere, it is said to be given by God to men so that He might show them what His will is. Nevertheless, as it is certain that *Hochma* is in the middle between *Cheter* and *Binah*—the latter of which denotes severity, while the former denotes clemency—so the surname of God *Iah*, or Wisdom, sometimes punishes, though very rarely. Hence Jehovah said when speaking of the Angel or Wisdom, *do not provoke him, for he will not bear your rebellion, because my name is in him. Exodus 23.*

The third Sephirah or Cabalistic numeration is ***Binah***, that is, Prudence <note>More commonly translated as "Understanding."</note>, and the surname of the Tetragrammaton attributed to this is ***Elohim***, that is, terror and dread. It is through this name that severe punishments and slaughter come, for in this property GOD exercises His power by punishing the wicked. And in this type of office, He employs angels, who for this reason are called ***Bene Elohim***, that is, sons of *Elohim*. The Doctors of Cabala maintain that the "side of the world" from which such demons are sent...

You see that the effects of these three titles of God, taken from His characteristics toward His creatures, are varied. Specifically, the first leans toward clemency and mercy; the last toward complete severity; and the middle one participates in both natures, yet is mostly inclined toward clemency. To this middle state is assigned the essential name <term>Jehovah</term> <note>The Tetragrammaton, the four-letter name of God.</note>, because it is exercised in this world both in punishment and in beneficence, but it is much more prone to mercy than to punishment. Thus it is written: *The Lord [Jehovah] is longsuffering, and of great mercy, forgiving iniquity and transgression, who by no means clears the guilty, visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children, etc.* (Numbers 14).

But let us proceed to the fourth <term>numeration</term> <note>A reference to the Sephiroth, the ten attributes or "emanations" in Kabbalah through which the Infinite reveals itself.</note> which is <term>Chesed</term> or Clemency, to which grace, goodness, and mercy are attributed. Its presiding title of God is <term>El</term>, whose role is to cherish all things and help all things with the highest piety and clemency; under this characteristic, it is said that bodies received their shapes. From this numeration, grace and mercy flow into the lower worlds through its own channel or "bright gate."

However, we think it necessary to address an objection raised by some: of what use is this Kabbalistic science to us, or how is it to be proven that this or that name of the <term>Tetragrammaton</term> <note>The four-letter Hebrew name of God.</note> possesses this or that characteristic, or an inclination toward clemency or severity? To this we respond: it is proven by the effect seen in the Hebrew text. Hence, the characteristic of the name *El* is openly explained by Moses in the passage where he successfully extracted the gift of health from God for his sister Miriam when she was suffering from leprosy, in this manner: *El na rapha na la*. <note>original: "El na rapha na la." This is Hebrew for "O God, heal her now, I beseech thee."</note> *El* means GOD of grace; *na* means "I beseech"; *rapha* means "heal"; *la* means "her."

The fifth numeration (which is <term>Geburah</term>) is presided over by the divine title <term>Elohim Gibbor</term> <note>God the Mighty.</note>. In this capacity, God is said to have drawn the elements out of murky Chaos. This denotes power, violence, severity, judgment, and the punishment of sinners. This characteristic of God flows into the lower regions—specifically into the world—producing the effects of plague, famine, war, plunder, and desolation. From this it is clear that just as the nature of the name *El* promised every good thing to the creatures of the world, so *Elohim Gibbor* seems to announce every evil and turbulent outcome, such as occurred during the extraction of the elements from chaos.

The sixth numeration is <term>Tiphereth</term>, which denotes grace, ornament, beauty, and delights. The name of GOD assisting this is <term>Eloah</term>. From this, it happens that all those influences poured out from this channel (or this path, or divine property) give form to the sun, returning to it clarity, life, and light, and they adorn the heavens according to the passage in Job: *By his spirit he hath garnished the heavens* (Job 26:13). And also: *By the word of the Lord were the heavens established, and all the host of them by the breath of his mouth* (Psalm 33). From these influences later proceed minerals (of which the leader is gold), vegetables (among which bread and wine are the leaders), and animals (whose head in dignity is man), following the positioning of the sun in the heavens.

The seventh <term>Sephiroth</term> is called <term>Netzach</term>, namely Triumph or Victory. Furthermore, it indicates charity and the love of justice; from here also follow the influences of multiplication and generation. The name presiding over this is <term>Jehovah Sabaoth</term>, the Lord of Hosts.

The eighth is called <term>Hod</term>, namely praise, honor, and beauty. The name derived from this characteristic is <term>Elohim Sabaoth</term>, that is, the GOD of Hosts—not, however, for rigor and war, but for piety, justice, and concord.

The ninth numeration is presided over by the name of GOD <term>El Chai</term> (that is, the Living GOD) or <term>Shaddai</term> (GOD Almighty, or the Self-Sufficient). This numeration is called <term>Yesod</term>, that is, Basis, Foundation, Redemption, and Rest.

The tenth and final Sephiroth is named <term>Malchut</term>, which is the Kingdom, the Church, the Empire, and the Temple of GOD. Hence the Psalmist says, *for the kingdom is the Lord’s* (Psalm 22). The name of GOD presiding over this is <term>Adonai</term> (Lord), and this numeration brings severity and servitude to those upon whom it flows.

From these things, one may see that in all the characteristics or operations of the divine essence upon the world—whether for punishment and the lash, or for beneficence—GOD is more prone to clemency and mercy than to severity. For in the characteristic of His first title, He extends His charity out of the darkness into the world, like a father to a son; hence <term>Hermes Trismegistus</term> <note>A legendary Hellenistic figure associated with a syncretic blend of the Greek god Hermes and the Egyptian god Thoth, credited with writing the Hermetic corpus.</note> calls the world the "Son of God."

In the characteristic of the second title, through His wisdom, He is more inclined toward creating things than toward striking the created human race with a plague for their sins, as is explained by the words of GOD to the Israelites: *Behold, I send my angel before thee, to keep thee in the way, and to bring thee into the place which I have prepared. Beware of him...* (Exodus 23). But I have shown elsewhere that this angel was Wisdom, which was sent to the Israelites for their preservation, yet with that precaution—lest they commit evil—because He said, *he will not pardon your transgressions.* From this it is clear that God is more inclined in this characteristic toward doing good than toward the lash. In the characteristic of the third title, severity and punishment are included, for the name <term>Elohim</term> is by its nature terrible. Thus it happens that as the title of the first Sephiroth, namely <term>Ehieh</term> <note>"I Am," related to the highest crown of the Sephiroth, Keter.</note>, is related to the Father and attributed to the Empyrean heaven, the place of the blessed and of rest...

## CHAPTER XI.

### How the Spirit of Wisdom, expanded everywhere in the world, informing and nourishing its moist nature, forms, creates, and preserves all creatures within it composed of the elements until the very end.

The **Spirit of divine wisdom**, animating, forming <note>The Latin *informans* here means "giving form or essence to," a key concept in Renaissance philosophy where spirit gives shape to raw matter.</note>, and creating the world, binds and arranges all discordant elements in harmonious peace with its breath. By its harmonious spirit, it strengthens and sustains heaven and earth by its will alone, according to that of the Prophet: *He who makes the earth by his strength, prepares the world in wisdom, and by his prudence extends the heavens* <note>original Latin: "Qui facit terram in fortitudine sua, præparat orbem in sapientia, prudentia sua extendit cœlos"</note> (Jeremiah 10). This Spirit, I say, once the universal things were completed, scattered the particulars throughout—namely stars, animals, plants, and even minerals. The Prophet succinctly indicated this to us with these words: *GOD creating the heavens, extending them, strengthening the earth and that which sprouts from it, giving breath to the people, and spirit to those walking upon it* <note>original Latin: "DEVS creans cœlos, extendens eos, firmans terram & quæ germinant ex ea, dans flatum populo, & spiritum calcantibus eam"</note> (Isaiah 42:5). ->...a certain invisible fire, from which they acknowledge all things were born, as if they understood that Spirit of the Lord (which is fiery love) as it was carried over the waters, imparting a certain fiery vigor and, as it were, "Being" to them. From this, therefore, the world was called a living creature <note>Latin: *animal*; in this context, an ensouled being</note> by some, for which they made the sun the heart; similarly, they called the stars living creatures, and they considered the souls of all particular things in the world to be intelligent, as if they were participants in the divine mind. They declared—not without reason—that these souls were rays or sparks emanating from that entire luminous nature. For this reason, they recognized that a soul presides over every single thing, and consequently Democritus and Orpheus, along with many of the Pythagoreans, were of the opinion that all things are full of Gods. They established divine honors for these, dedicating sacrifices and prayers to them, and venerating them with various forms of worship.<-

Furthermore, they reduced all souls of this kind to the one **Soul of the World**, and consequently referred all Gods back to the one Jove <note>Jupiter</note>. From this, therefore, proceeded all the error of the pagans in their adoration; from this, I have no doubt, emanated the fictions of the Poets, demonic sacrifices, and sacrilegious offerings. Hence, the land of Egypt worshiped and adored certain animals and other monsters and portents. But concerning these various species of idolatry—where, namely, the creature is adored instead of the creator—the scriptures speak everywhere, specifically regarding the profane worship of stars, demons, men, and others of that kind.

In this, therefore, those philosophers were deceived: they did not distinguish the simple uncreated light (that is, the creating nature) from the moist created nature. Instead, they considered the created light—that is, the whole illuminated moist nature, namely the **Angel** or "alterity" (as the Kabbalists hold) <note>original: *alteritatem*; a technical term in Kabbalah for the "otherness" of creation compared to the Unity of God</note>—and not that **Unity** which preceded it. Hence, some of them said fire was God, others air; some made the earth the divinity, some water, and so on.

But truly, in their saying that "all things are full of Gods," or rather animated and filled with sparks of divinity (all of which they referred to the one Jove), or that all things are endowed with luminous souls (which they taught have a relationship to the single Soul of the World), in this they do not seem to disagree with the sense of the Hebrew Doctors, or even with Holy Scripture. For **Rabbi Beresith** <note>Likely referring to the *Bereshit Rabbah*, a Jewish commentary on Genesis</note> says that the creator daily creates a host of angels, whom others call **forms**, as they are formal substances with which the entire sphere of things that can be born or perish is filled beyond number. Concerning these Angelic forms, the *Gates of Light* <note>Latin: *Porta lucis*; the title of a famous 13th-century Kabbalistic text by Joseph Gikatilla</note> says: *From the earth even unto the firmament there is no empty place, but everything is full of forms; some of them are pure, some are capable of grace and mercy, and there are many foul, harmful, and tempting images below,* etc. From which he seems to suggest that all forms, both good and bad, are like angels—but of these, we shall speak elsewhere.

However we see it, all these forms in the world are like sparks of divinity and rays of the one spirit, assigned with various properties and images either for the preservation of life or for its destruction—as is sufficiently explained in the divine properties inscribed upon the **Sephirotic Tree**. Yet, all these pure forms or rays of divinity are no less to be divided from their fullness of essence than solar rays are from the Sun. And although, by the divine will, they are enclosed in various dark tabernacles—both foul and pure—to execute His various commands, they themselves (as sparks of truth) will ultimately return to the fountain of unity from which they went forth. Concerning this matter, the Apostle speaks thus: ***GOD will be all in all, when Christ shall have obtained the kingdom of the Father.*** (1 Corinthians 15). Nor do the Holy Scriptures seem to stray far from the aforementioned opinion, in which we find that Christ fills all things. And elsewhere: ***GOD, needing nothing, gives to all life and breath and all things.*** (Acts 17). And elsewhere: ***In GOD himself we live and move and have our being.*** (Acts 17:28). And the wise man gives the reason for this, saying: ***the incorruptible spirit of GOD is in every thing.*** (Wisdom 12:1). In another place, he calls this an emanation or a pure flow of the brightness of Almighty GOD, and the whiteness of eternal light, which gives life to all things. (Wisdom 7).

We conclude, therefore, that it is certain that the life and being of every thing is from GOD, and is like a fiery impression from the "character" or divine seal of the Word (which the Kabbalists call *Emeth* <note>Hebrew for "Truth"</note>), or a ray from the shining Word, which is more abundant and flowing in one creature than in another—for example, in the sun of heaven and in the Man of the earth. Whence the Evangelist says, ***in the word is life, and this life is the light of men.*** And of another it is said, ***by his spirit he adorned the heavens.*** And for this reason also it is said that GOD saw all things created by Him were ***good*** (Genesis 1)—that is, insofar as they participated in the divine essence, which alone is goodness and truth, as the Holy Scriptures testify.

### CHAPTER XII.

### On the Void and the Full.

Here we think it of no small value to explain to you what that **void** <note>This refers to the "vacuum," a central concept in early physics regarding whether empty space can exist.</note> is, which is so avoided by nature, and what is **full**, since the solution to such a doubt seems to pertain especially to our purpose and to be necessary. For indeed, the fathers of the Philosophers, as well as those adhering to the sacred scriptures in Theosophy, have said that this **Void** is **Nothing**.

**Mercurius Trismegistus** <note>Also known as Hermes Trismegistus, a legendary Hellenistic figure associated with hermetic philosophy and alchemy.</note> calls this a **dreadful shadow, destitute of all form** <note>original: "Vmbram horrendam, omni forma destitutam"</note>; the **Cabalists** <note>Followers of Jewish mysticism (Kabbalah).</note> call it a **potential principle looking toward nothingness**. **Plato**, in his *Timaeus*, says it is a thing without sense, perceptible yet scarcely credible through spurious reasoning, and he makes it out to be a fear, like a dream. And **Augustine** says: *When I conceive of something formless, I understand "nothing" sooner than I understood it before; just as by seeing nothing, darkness is seen, and by hearing nothing, silence is heard,* <note>original: "Cum aliquid informe concipio, prius nihil intelligo quàm intelligebam, quemadmodum nihil videndo videntur tenebræ, nihil audiendo auditur silentium"</note> whereby he seems to compare it to **Darkness and silence**. **Job** says: *That GOD extends the North over the empty and the void, and hangs the earth over nothing,* <note>original: "Quod Aquilonem DEVS extendit super inane & vacuum, & suspendit terram super nihilum"</note> Job 26:7. And elsewhere: *He reveals foundations out of the darkness, and brings the shadow of death into the light,* Job 12:22. By these words he seems to argue that the **Empty, the Void, Nothingness, Darkness,** and the **Shadow** are the same thing.

Specifically, it is **Empty** and **Void** because all **fullness** <term>plenitudo: a philosophical state where space is entirely occupied by matter or spirit</term> is from GOD. However, GOD, the parent of light, had not yet shone upon the world; therefore, insofar as the first matter of the world was destitute of all grace and deprived of goodness, it was called **Empty and Void**—indeed, even **darkness and the shadow of death**, insofar as it entirely lacked the rays of life. Thus the earth was said to be **empty and void**, and that darkness was over the face of the deep before the Spirit of the Lord was carried over the waters. But after the appearance of the said spirit, it was said: *And GOD called the dry land earth, and GOD saw that it was good, and it produced tender herbs and seed of every kind, and trees bringing forth fruit, etc.* (Genesis 1). Therefore, the earth, which was once empty and void, has now been made **full of divine grace**, whereby it is rendered not empty but fertile; not void, but completed on all sides by the divine fire and incorruptible rays. 

*The hand of the almighty created the world from formless matter,* (Wisdom 11:12). Whereby "hand," he indicates the word or spirit emanating from his mouth. Hence the **Apostle Peter** says: *The heavens were first, and the earth out of water and through water, by means of the word,* (2 Peter 3); that is, by holy emanation. *Through this light,* says **John**, *the world was made*; indeed, where the rays of that informing divinity are missing, there is the **greatest vacuum**—that is, the absence of completed form.

And this is why the **void** seems so dreadful in the kingdom of nature, for every thing, by a natural appetite for being "informed" <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, "informing" means giving matter a specific shape or essence.</note>, desires it most greatly; therefore, not only a specific nature but even that universal parent of all specific things is accustomed to abhor and avoid deformity above all else. 

From this, therefore, it is clear that all **fullness** in nature is from the divine abundance, which fills everything in the world by its own power so that from nothing and the empty, something actually formal and relatively existing may be made. This gift of existence they received from **Christ** or **Wisdom**, wherefore it is written: *that Christ fills all things,* (Ephesians 4). And elsewhere: *The holy spirit of discipline fills the whole world,* (Wisdom 1). Hence it is that unless GOD had filled all things in the world, there would be a void and nothingness in the world; but truly, since He Himself created all things by His presence, it is therefore necessary that **nothing empty exists in the world.**

He created the earth in its calculated numbers, as we have from the testimony of the royal prophet: *Give thanks to the Lord of lords, who made the heavens in wisdom, for his mercy endures forever; who established the earth above the waters, for his mercy endures forever. Pſal. 135." This is Psalm 136 in modern Bibles.</note>

In its own proper nature, this is assigned to the first "numeration" or Sephirotic emanation, namely *Ehieh* <note>Hebrew: "I Am"</note>, which is the name presiding over *Cheter* <note>Hebrew: "Kether" or "The Crown"</note> or the crown; it is ascribed to the Father and to mercy. From this, we understand the reason why God, being free within himself, wished to create the world and its creatures: namely, out of his pure clemency and mercy toward "deformed" things. That is, out of empty things and those veiled in darkness or lethal shadows, he would procreate good things adorned with divine beauty. He infused into every creature a living soul or a spark from his own lucid fountain, by which it might live and exist in its own being. For this reason, creatures first desire to return great thanks to him, and then they proceed to their assigned duties and to faithfully fulfill the commands of the creator. Regarding this thanksgiving, we read in the royal Psalmist: *Praise God from the heavens, praise him all his angels, and all his powers. Praise him Sun and Moon, praise him all you stars and light, praise him heaven of heavens, and all the waters that are above the heavens, let them praise the name of the Lord, for he spoke and they were made, he commanded and they were created. Praise the Lord from the earth, you dragons and all deeps, fire, hail, snow, ice, the spirit or wind of storms, which fulfill his word, etc. Psalm 148.* <note>Original Latin: "Laudate Deum de cælis... Pſal. 148."</note> Here he runs through all creatures, both of the land and the water. But to declare the office of the stars, we say with the Prophet in the place cited before: that he made the Sun to have dominion over the day, and the moon and other stars—both the fixed and the wandering <note>The "wandering stars" are the planets.</note>—to have power over the night, and this because of his kindness. As for the substance or consistency of the stars (both fixed and wandering), it appears to be exceedingly clean and pure, the better to receive their lucid forms from the creator. This also seems to be confirmed by these words: *The stars are not clean and pure in the sight of God, much less men, Job 25:5.* <note>Original: "Stellæ non ſunt mundæ..."</note> By this speech, it appears that they are indeed very pure, though not *absolutely* pure when compared to God. Yet if they were not very pure and polished in their substance, they would be least capable of receiving such splendid forms; for as Plato rightly says, "form is given by the creator according to the merit of the matter." However, because their substance varies in purity, the Apostle says: *That star differs from star in brightness, 1 Corinthians 15.* <note>Original Latin: "Quod ſtella differat à ſtella claritate."</note>

It remains now to discuss briefly the property and influence of the fixed stars, among which we read: *that when God extended the heavens, he alone made Orion, the Pleiades or Hyades, and the stars of the inner chambers of the South, Job 32:4.* <note>The author cites Job 32:4, but these stars are mentioned in Job 9:9 and 38:31.</note> And elsewhere, mention is made *of the circle of Arcturus or the belt of Orion, Job 38.* The Prophet also speaks thus: *It is God who makes Arcturus and Orion, and turns the shadows into morning, and changes day into night, Jehovah is his name, Amos 5.* Our great God, great in Virtues, whose wisdom is beyond numbering, counts all these stars of the firmament; he counts however many stars there are and has called them by their own names, as David testifies in *Psalm 147.* Doubtless he assigned them names according to their various properties, declaring thereby that many occult <note>In this context, "occult" simply means "hidden" or "not visible to the naked eye."</note> properties exist within them beyond the common and vulgar one (namely, that they rule the night). For it is not likely that he would have assigned them various shapes in splendor and figure if they did not have powers over other creatures—especially since the Prophet adds: *He calls however many there are by name, our great Lord, great in power or virtues, whose wisdom is without number.* From this it is argued that he who is great in virtues and of innumerable wisdom also assigned various virtues to the innumerable stars of the firmament. This can also be understood through these words: *Do you know the laws of Heaven? Do you set its dominion upon the earth? Job 38:31.* By these, the creator seems to indicate that heaven, through its "army" <note>A traditional metaphor for the stars (the "host of heaven").</note>, is accustomed to work in various forms upon the earth. For this reason, some most aptly compare the heaven to a husband <note>The text says "Marti" (Mars), but the context of "feminae" (woman) suggests the masculine principle of the husband/active agent.</note> and the earth to a wife. Consequently, every particular star of the heaven or firmament has a particular virtue of flowing into <note><term>Influence: literally "in-flowing" (influentia). In older science, stars were thought to emit a physical fluid or "virtue" that flowed down to Earth.</term></note> specific things—animals, vegetables, and minerals alike. For example, it is handed down and confirmed by experience itself that the Polar Star (called *Alracuba* by the Egyptians), having the nature of Saturn and Venus, attracts the magnet-stone to itself (as is seen in the nautical needle). And that same magnet attracts iron to itself, provided a diamond is not present; for the diamond, by its presence, hinders the influences of the said star. And Cecco d'Ascoli, writing on the sphere <note>Cichus Esculanus (1257–1327) was an astronomer and poet.</note> in the place where he speaks of the twelve signs of the Zodiac, affirms that each of the 12 signs receives its particular and special name from the nature and property of some animal on earth, the nature of the one seeming to symbolize the nature of the other. And Moses the Arab <note>Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), the Jewish philosopher.</note> says that every living thing claims for itself a peculiar star in heaven, from which it draws and receives influence every moment to protect and sustain its essence; he says this was done by divine command and will. Thus the stars in the constellation of Aries in heaven have a relation to such animals on earth, and the scorpion of the sky to the scorpion of the earth, and so on for the rest. For this reason, Diodorus Siculus <note>A Greek historian of the 1st century BC.</note>, speaking generally, quite sensibly admits that the lower world is ruled by the upper, and the lower world is [subject] to that upper one...

The heavens signify nothing, as stated in the book *On the Heavens and the World* <note>original: "De cælo & Mundo"</note>. Elsewhere he says, "He who asserts that nature does not act for a specific end, removes the providence of God regarding lower things," in *Physics*, Book 2. However, Hippocrates, toward the end of his book *On Fleshes* <note>original: "De carnibus"</note>, describes these matters excellently in the following discourse: "Regarding celestial and sublime things, it seems to me that nothing should be said, except insofar as I shall demonstrate that humans and all other animals living on earth are born and have their origin there; and that the soul is from heaven, and that to grieve, to languish, to die, and finally whatever good or evil is in man, proceeds from heaven." Thus he spoke. Yet Ptolemy, speaking more universally in his ninth aphorism of the *Centiloquium* <note>A collection of 100 astrological aphorisms attributed to Ptolemy</note>, breaks out in these words: "The face of this world is subject to the faces of heaven." And elsewhere he says in the first tract of the *Quadripartitum* <note>Ptolemy’s foundational work on the influence of the stars</note>: "We ought to know that the powers of the celestial bodies are created by divine disposition," as if he had said through both of these statements that the soul and virtue of the celestial bodies come from God, and those of terrestrial things come from heaven, acting as an intermediate place between the seat of God—which is the <term>heaven of heavens</term> <note>The highest, spiritual realm beyond the physical stars</note>—and the earth itself.

We say, therefore, that just as the Angelic world is a <term>type</term> <note>A symbolic model or pattern</note> of that Divine world, so too the celestial world is an image of the Angelic one. Therefore, just as the Angelic world receives influence immediately from the <term>archetypal world</term> <note>The original divine blueprint of the universe</note> and pours it into the celestial, so also the celestial world is a likeness of the terrestrial world. Consequently, its "army" <note>referring to the stars and planets</note> immediately exerts its influence upon the creatures of the earth that are most conformed to it in nature and disposition.

We conclude, therefore, with the sacred Priest in the 4th Book of Esdras, chapter 16: that the stars were founded in the Word or Wisdom of the Lord, who both knows the number of the stars and has given to each of them a name most suited to its property. Through these properties, each star has a relationship with terrestrial creatures, by which it constantly pours its influences into creatures similar to itself. This is done under the direction of the <term>intelligences</term> <note>Angelic beings or spirits believed to guide the planets</note> who preside over them and who, by divine will and command, take care of lower things.

### CHAPTER XIV.

#### The First Part.

#### On the creation of the **planets** in general, and especially on the **Sun**, its creation, dignity, utility, motion, and obedience toward its Creator.

In our discourse on the physical subject of the <term>macrocosm</term> <note>The universe as a whole, viewed as a large-scale reflection of the human being</note>, where we spoke at sufficient length regarding the origin of the fixed stars, I proposed a certain doubt: namely, whether the fixed stars were created on the fourth day of creation along with the planets <note>original: "stellis erraticis," literally "wandering stars"</note>, or at least on the second day. We expressed our reasons then, proving it likely that they were established on the second day of creation. Indeed, if we consider the orders of the <term>Sephirot</term> <note>The ten attributes or emanations in Kabbalah through which the Infinite reveals itself</note> or the "Numberings" of the Kabbalists and the reason for their influences, we will perceive that just as the influence of **Keter** <note>The Crown; the highest Sephira</note>—which is the Crown or first numbering—flows through the Seraphic order of angels into the <term>Primum Mobile</term> <note>The "First Moved" sphere that carries all other celestial spheres</note>, so **Chokmah** <note>Wisdom; the second Sephira</note> flows through the order of Cherubim into the starry heaven. If that heaven were empty and without stars, it would receive those influences from Chokmah in vain. But we shall now briefly approach the production of the planets and their creation in their respective orbits.

It is most certain, and to be conceded without controversy, that all stars are created by God himself, as we have confirmed by many testimonies of Holy Scripture. Moses says: "The Sun, the Moon, the stars, and others, God created for the service of all nations under heaven." (Deuteronomy 4:19). However, how each of these stars has an intelligence presiding over it, receiving influences from the "lucid gates" <note>The Sephirotic channels of divine light</note>, and what the duties of said angels are—both in the ethereal heaven and the elementary region—and who is their Prince, we shall discuss copiously in the second member of this part.

In this place, however, we shall chiefly hold a discourse concerning the noblest creature of the celestial bodies: the King of stars, the corporeal Emperor of the heavens, the heart of the firmament, and the brightest eye of the world—namely, the visible **Sun**. To reach a better understanding of it, we shall first offer a few words concerning the **invisible and uncreated Sun**, which is the life and light of this created sun.

<note>original: "De Causa Meteororum Efficiente." In early modern science, "meteors" referred to any atmospheric phenomenon, including rain, wind, and light.</note>

And with all effort the Israelites were commanded to revere [him]: *My angel (says Jehovah) will not bear your transgressions, for my name is in him, Exodus 23.* <note>Exodus 23:21</note> That is, I wish you to obey his voice, because my Word, who is your creator, is in him; that is, "do this, because I am in him," or "I will be present," whom alone and no one else you ought to adore. It is not, therefore, in honor of the sun that the wise man speaks these words: *It is necessary to precede the sun for your blessing and to adore you at the rising of light, Wisdom 16:28,* <note>The text cites Wisdom 10, but the passage is from Wisdom of Solomon 16:28.</note> or that the Prophet Daniel looked toward the eastern region while praying, or that it is the custom and habit of Christians to pour out our prayers with our faces turned toward the east; rather, it is so that we might worship him with every effort—He who gave form to so excellent a vessel, and who established his tabernacle in this polished vessel, which he chose as his instrument. He did this so that from it, as if from a visible sanctuary of life, he might rain down life, multiplication, and visible light everywhere upon the world and its parts. In this way, the Creator provides solace and joy both to opaque bodies (to which invisible light is least apparent) and to the soul sustained by invisible light. Furthermore, in this manner, he reveals himself and manifests the grace of his essence to both earthly and celestial beings, to both bodies and spirits. Whence he is rightly called the *God of soul and body, God of all spirits, God of all flesh.*

Finally, this sun is called in the highest heaven *Ehieh* <term>Ehieh: Hebrew for "I Am" (Exodus 3:14), representing the self-existent nature of God.</term> the Father, or God giving grace and glory; in the Empyrean <note>The highest part of heaven, thought to be occupied by pure fire or light.</note> he is Wisdom, brighter than the sun, and plunging himself more deeply into the matter of the world, he placed his tabernacle in the sun, and flashes in the thick clouds, and speaks with the voice of thunder. *Revelation 22.* In Christ as man, he is called the bright morning star; "a star (says the Holy Page) shall rise out of Jacob," *Numbers 24.* And elsewhere, the *Sun of Justice, Malachi 4,* who is promised to rise for those fearing his name, with healing in his wings, whence he is also called *Jesus*. Furthermore, Jesus Christ is called "the Sun" in many places of the scriptures, by the sole fullness of his light, life, and all good things; whence he is also the *Word, the light of the world shining in the darkness, John 1.* But I wish for us to arrive at the examination or "Lydian stone" <term>Lydian stone: A touchstone used to test the purity of gold; here used metaphorically as a definitive test of truth.</term> of these matters. The wise philosophers say that in whatever thing a matter has its origin, in that same thing it is usually finished; hence, if we wish to inquire into and prove the beginning of the mundane sun, we shall best perceive it from its end. For in the holy letters we have this: *Thy sun shall no more go down; thy moon shall not wane, because the Lord shall be unto thee, Jerusalem, for a light; Isaiah 60.* And with this place agrees that of *John: And the city has no need of the sun nor of the moon to shine in it; for the brightness of God will illuminate it, and its lamp is the Lamb: and the nations shall walk in its light; and the kings of the earth shall bring their glory and honor into it, Revelation 21:23.* By these things it is indicated that in the last days of the world, this celestial sun shall cast off its thick and dark garments: and it will appear as it truly is, for there is no truth except in the true light of the world, which reveals all fictions and reduces them to nothing by the "Lydian" test. For by an examination of this kind, the moon in the last days will have the brightness of the sun, by laying aside its created garments; and the truly central and divine Sun, by casting off its thick and created clothing, will be in its naked and clear nature, providing light to the blessed servants of God in their purification and, as it were, resurrection—not otherwise (but in a far more exalted degree) than the common sun or the one visible in the heaven. We can clearly gather this from these words of the Prophet: *The light of the moon (he says) shall be as the light of the sun, and the light of the sun shall be sevenfold, as the light of seven days, Isaiah 30:26.* That is, seven times as bright; and the Apostle speaks to this sense, saying, *There shall be one brightness of the Sun, another of the Moon, and another of the stars, 1 Corinthians 15.* From which it is right to conclude that in the end, everything that is a fiction <note>original: "figmentum." Here meaning something fashioned or temporary rather than eternally true.</note> shall perish and be abolished, and be thrust down into the vast abyss of Nothingness; but that which is of the simple truth (with which God filled the entire universe), all that, by being purified through a fiery purification, shall return into its source of unity. And the Holy Bible seems to confirm those things which were said above: for it is said that God fills all things: *That from God and through God are all things, Romans 11.* That *God is the father of all, who is over all, and through all, and in all, Ephesians 4:6.* And that *God works all things in all, 1 Corinthians 12.* Whence, since he himself is the only truth, it is necessary that nothing be true unless it is of his essence. Therefore we say finally, that just as God was the beginning of solar beauty—that is, if his glory be the cause of the excellence of the solar creature—once the "fiction" is laid aside, it will be far more beautiful, and just as it was in the beginning, that is, in its first emanation, when it was called *Hochma* <term>Hochma: Hebrew "Chokhmah," meaning Wisdom; in mystical thought, the first spark of divine creation.</term> or divine Wisdom, which is the brightness of the light of the Almighty. So it was in the beginning, and its beginning shall be justified by its end, as he who is the *Alpha and Omega, Revelation 1,* the beginning and the end; hence the Apostle says, *God shall be all in all when Christ shall have obtained the kingdom of the Father, 1 Corinthians 15.* Whence also he said elsewhere, *When I shall have been exalted, I will draw all things to myself;* that is, everything that is of purity and truth; for nothing is to be reckoned as "nothing" in its mere nature, nor as empty and void.

But let us proceed rapidly to the nature of our created sun, that is, the solar creature.

***
CHAPTER XIV.
Third Part.
On the creation of the celestial and visible sun, and those things which necessarily follow therefrom.
***

We think it will now be worth the effort to treat the created sun. *Let there be (says God) lights in the expanse of heaven to bring light upon the earth, and it was so; and so God made those two great lights, the greater light to rule the day, etc. Genesis 1.* In which speech it is certain that the Lord ordained the fabric of the sun, and put his will into execution by means of the Word, according to that saying of the royal Psalmist: *By the Word of the Lord...*
