By the word of the Lord the heavens were made firm, and all their powers or armies by the breath of his mouth, <note>original: "Ps. 33." This refers to Psalm 33:6.</note> And that eminent High Priest Esdras denotes this with these express words: the stars are established in the word of the Lord. <note>original: "Esdr. 4. 16." This refers to the apocryphal book of 2 Esdras (4 Ezra) 4:16.</note> But truly, to treat of the particular manner of this creature's birth, and to immerse oneself in its mysteries, will seem somewhat difficult for a man, unless we look into the Holy Scriptures with <term>lyncean eyes</term> <note>Eyes as sharp as a lynx; a common Renaissance metaphor for deep, penetrating intellectual or spiritual insight.</note>. Regarding its matter, therefore, it is certain that it possesses the consistency of a most limpid, highly polished, and thoroughly spiritual earth, which emerged out of the darkness (after the bright rays of divine wisdom were reflected back into the center of the world, as was declared in our history concerning the <term>physical history of the Macrocosm</term> <note>A reference to Fludd's own massive work, *Utriusque Cosmi Historia*.</note>), and by the help of divine rays was exalted in the marrow of the heavens like molten metal, and illuminated on all sides by the rays of divine grace and beauty. Thus the body of Adam was formed from choice mud, and was animated and quickened by the breath of life and the bright spirit of the Almighty, and formed in the image of the Almighty; so the earth was said to bring forth the Savior, and our Savior, rising from the tomb and emerging from the gap of death or the lethal shadow of darkness like the morning star, ascended into heaven clothed on all sides with a celestial spirit. Why then should the created sun refuse the earth as the parent of its consistency, seeing that it is the condensed spirit of a celestial nature, in whose marrow the uncreated light of the world placed his <term>tabernacle</term> <note>A "tent" or dwelling place, suggesting the Sun is a physical container for a divine, invisible light.</note>, as the royal Psalmist teaches us? Furthermore, we see that just as our Savior rose from the darkness of death and the abyss of the grave on the third day, so indeed after the third day in creation, and not before—the fixation of the earth in the center of the world or its suspension upon nothing having been accomplished—there was no mention made of the creation of the greater light. Whence it is likely that the sun ascended from the earth, having cast off its dark filth, as if from a tomb, seeing that in it is the tabernacle of the invisible and divine sun, which holds the place of a most bright soul to that most polished body. But however we read it, that ethereal matter is so involved in a spherical mouth, so pure in its consistency, that it is called by the Wise Man a "vessel, the admirable work of the Most High." <note>original: "Eccl. 43." This refers to Sirach (Ecclesiasticus) 43:2.</note> And in that which is announced elsewhere, "The Sun is the work of the Lord, full of his glory," <note>original: "Eccl. 42." Referring to Sirach 42:16.</note> and elsewhere, that "he placed his tabernacle in it," it is clear that it is a vessel in nature very clean and polished, for otherwise it would not be capable of a form so pure and simple, since form is usually given according to the merits of the matter. And yet it is impossible, through the entire created spirit, for matter so exquisitely pure to be given that it could merit a form as pure and simple as that divine essence, which is without any stain or impurity; whence it is written first of the angels and then afterwards of the stars, that in respect to the sincere purity of the divine essence they are not pure; in which sense it is written thus concerning these stars: "The stars are not clean and pure in the sight of God." <note>original: "Iob. 25. 5." Referring to Job 25:5.</note> Indeed, regarding those Angels, we read these words: "Behold, in his angels God found wickedness, etc." <note>original: "Iob. 14. 17." A likely reference to Job 4:18 or 15:15.</note> for it is impossible that the created could be equaled in its Being to the essence of the creator. But truly, among all visible bodies, it is certain that the solar substance is the purest, which is therefore declared because the visible glory of God is indicated to mortals more in it than in any other creature of the world. And hence it is said by Augustine, that as much light as something has in itself, so much more of God does it seem to claim for itself. Hence also the Wise Man says of the sun, "The sun illuminating looked upon all things, and his work is full of the glory of the Lord." <note>original: "Eccl. 42." Sirach 42:16.</note> Whence it is clear that the presence of that divine glory denotes the purity of the subject into which it enters; for in holy writing we read everywhere that the Holy Spirit does not descend except into a pure spirit or a clean heart, that is, into a purified subject. For such ought to be the respect between the bridegroom and the bride, between <term>Cupid and Psyche</term> <note>The classical allegory of Love and the Soul.</note>, between Christ and the Church, between the mind and the spirit, or there will be no firm bond and coupling between them.

Hence, therefore, we ought to gather that insofar as the mundane sun is a creature, and as it were a shadow of the majesty of the <term>archetypal sun</term> <note>The "Original" or "Divine" Sun in the mind of God, of which the physical sun is a mere reflection.</note>; so it is by no means to be worshipped as God by mortals who are consistent in themselves and least seized by diabolical madness. For this would be to adore the house instead of the master, just as those twenty-five men did, who (as Ezekiel witnesses) stood between the porch and the altar with their faces toward the east and worshipped the rising of the sun, having their backs against the temple of the Lord, of whom God speaks thus to the Prophet: "Is it a light thing to them that they should do these abominations which they have done here, for they have filled the land with iniquity, etc." <note>original: "Eze. 8. v. 16." Referring to Ezekiel 8:16-17.</note> But the sacred page also reproves this in express speech: "You shall not look at the sun, the moon, or the stars, or any thing of the host of heaven, that bowing down you should worship them," <note>original: "Deut. 4." Referring to Deuteronomy 4:19.</note> as if he had said, Jehovah is the alone and only God the creator, to him alone you must offer worship, and not to the images created by him—that is, to the Lord creating, and not to the servant or minister created. "The Lord is he who made the Sun," says the Wise Man, "at whose words it hastened its journey." And elsewhere this is expressly explained in this manner: "The sun, moon, stars, and others God created for service to all nations under heaven," therefore he forbade them to be adored and worshipped, as if he had said: I am the creator, therefore those things which I created are not to be adored, but I alone the creator. But how ridiculous would it be to a wise man to revere a servant with honor and not think of the Master, or to affect the smallest things with praise but reject and neglect the greater? What, I pray, is a body or a soul or an informed thing without its form imparting life and glory? Surely nothing—empty, and plainly a deformed and horrendous shadow, as if someone chose the shadow for the true God, but rejected the true subject as nothing. This indeed is the way of the worldly, overwhelmed by darkness and ignorance, who choose things that are seen and are least real, in place of those things which truly are but are least seen, choosing after the manner of the blind. Open therefore, O blind mortals, those eyes which Adam closed because of his sins, and close your carnal eyes, seeing that those who think they see in a deceptive manner see things which are not, but truly they are least able to penetrate to those things which are.

## CHAPTER 15.

->### On the Manyfold Power and Utility of the Sun.<-

The primary power of the Sun consists in its light, motion, and heat, just as its secondary power is accustomed to spring forth from these same effects. Therefore, we shall speak somewhat more extensively about both of these powers as they are blended together; and first, concerning Light.

Since it is certain, and confirmed by what has gone before, that God is the fountain of light, this primary light brought forth its own emanation as the first act or motion. By this motion, the first <term>movable part of the world</term>—that is, the highest circle of the <term>subtle spirit of the world</term> <note>original: "spiritus mundani". This refers to a "spirit of the world," a theoretical substance thought to permeate the universe and transmit celestial influence to the Earth.</note>—was carried around. By its motion, all the enclosed spheres are also rotated along their perimeters. <note>original: "perifericè". The author describes a mechanical universe where the outermost sphere's rotation physically turns the inner spheres like gears.</note>

Moreover, the effect of this mobility or active motion is heat, just as, conversely, the dull and insensible state of rest is the parent of cold. And although it is confirmed by the testimonies of Holy Scripture that God is always abiding in Himself and not at all changeable, yet with respect to His wisdom—emanating from its own bright fountain—He is "more mobile than all mobile things" (<note>original: "Sap. 7". This refers to the Book of Wisdom 7:24, which describes Divine Wisdom as the most active force in existence.</note>). Thus those three in the fiery furnace, glorifying God with one voice, said: *Bless the Lord, O Sun and Moon; praise and exalt him above all forever* <note>original: "Benedicite Sol & Luna domino, Laudate & superexaltate eum in secula" — from the Song of the Three Children in the Book of Daniel.</note>. So it is also said elsewhere, that *the Sun knows its setting, Psalm 104:19.* From these few examples, therefore, it is right to gather how great is the obedience of this solar creature toward its creator. Thus man—a vessel most excellent in his creation, yet most perverse by nature—should long to offer his obedience and duty according to the will of his creator. He should strive with the greatest effort so that, in the manner of the sun, he might shine in such glory as that which the solar creature radiates by its own justice. For according to the Evangelist, *The righteous shall shine like the sun in the kingdom of their father.* We believe that the image of Adam living in Paradise before the Fall was everywhere shining and splendid, radiating with the glory of the divine light dwelling within him, being a vessel formed by the very finger of God, the Light of the Father. Do we not read that the stone tablets, inscribed by the finger of God and entrusted to Moses, flashed with a sapphire-like brightness in the eyes of those who looked upon them? So too we read that the face of Moses (even though he was stained by the mark of mortality) so excelled in light that the Israelites could not look upon his face without a veil or cloth. How much more so Adam, who was not at all contaminated by the stain or mark of mortality before his disobedience!

Finally, we have now come to the **passion** <note>In this context, "passion" refers to suffering or undergoing a profound change, specifically the darkening of the sun.</note> of the sun, which we gather he has been affected by several times in this world’s age, not only from the sacred writings but also by the authority of trustworthy authors. *The sun was darkened at its rising,* says the Prophet, *Isaiah 13.* And elsewhere, *Your sun shall no longer set, for the Lord shall be your light, O Jerusalem: Isaiah 60.* And in Joel we find that *the sun shall be turned into darkness before the great and terrible day of the Lord comes, Joel 2.* And elsewhere, *The sun and moon are darkened, Joel 3,* so that in its place the Sun of Justice may rise for those who fear the Lord, as we have in the Prophet Malachi, *Malachi 4.* And in Ecclesiastes we have that *the sun, the light of the stars, and the moon shall grow dark for man, Eccl. 12.* And in St. Matthew, *The sun shall be darkened immediately after the tribulation of those days, Matthew 24.* Finally, during the passion of the primary sun—or rather, in the death and passion of his very tabernacle <note>The "primary sun" refers to Christ; his "tabernacle" refers to his physical body on Earth.</note>—the secondary and celestial sun lost its light and was obscured. It was as if, when the life of its fleshy tabernacle failed, that celestial body also suffered death (or the deprivation of its luminous form) for a great space of time by an inseparable consensus. Regarding this deprivation of solar life or form, Eusebius writes: *In the 4th year of the 202nd Olympiad, a great and excellent eclipse of the sun occurred, beyond all that had happened before; at the sixth hour, the day was so turned into dark night that stars were seen in the sky, and there were earthquakes in Bithynia.* Thus he writes; and similarly Lucian of Antioch, the Martyr, while in his torments, cried out this to the judges of the infidels and the executioners: *Search your annals and you will find that in the times of Pilate, while Christ was suffering, the day was interrupted by darkness as the sun was obscured.* Furthermore, it is most certain and confirmed by three reasons that this solar passion was 
<margin>*</margin> wondrous and miraculous, and far beyond the ordinary eclipses of the sun (in which the sun does not actually fail, but the body of the moon is placed between its sight and our eyes). The **first reason** is that this passion occurred contrary to the order of natural solar eclipses, which never happen when the moon is full; yet this failure and "syncope" <term>syncope: a medical term for fainting, used here to describe the sun suddenly losing its "vital" light</term> of the sun happened immediately after the opposition of the lights <note>Meaning at the full moon, when the moon is opposite the sun.</note>. **Second**, that the part of the sun facing the east was veiled and shadowed first, and the same part was later restored to light first; from which it is clear that it happened contrary to the common laws of nature. The **third** reason (which would seem monstrous and incredible to everyone) is that in the hour of the eclipse, the moon moved contrary to its own natural course—namely, from east to west—whereas its natural motion is from west to east; and then, immediately after the passion ended, it was observed to travel in its natural motion. From these things we must conclude that this passion and failure was real and according to the nature of the Solar body itself, and not merely in respect to us <note>The author argues this wasn't just a shadow from the moon, but a literal loss of light from the sun itself.</note>, as is usually the case in an eclipse.

And for this reason, this passion or failure was universal, which cannot happen to people simply through the moon’s interposition between the earth and the sun. We conclude, therefore, from these points, that when the life of the tabernacle of the **uncreated sun** <note>Christ</note> failed on earth, that sun in heaven was also affected by a kind of fainting; it seemed to be deprived of its trial and luminous form. It was as if that luminous spirit, establishing a temple and tabernacle in both subjects, hated such an inhuman and cruel act and turned its shining face away from both worlds for a space of time. We also see from this that the solar body is a creature subject to the **will of GOD**, either for life or for the deprivation of its light. Consequently, we see that God does not act in this world by necessity or as if forced into the ordinary course of nature, contrary to that foolish assertion of the **Peripatetics** <term>Peripatetics: followers of Aristotle, who believed the universe functioned by fixed, necessary laws of nature.</term>.

Finally, as to the fact that the sun will be transfigured from its current state on the last day and rendered seven times more splendid in its light—that is, putting off its corruptible garments to put on its incorruptible and immortal nature—this seems first to be confirmed by the words of the Prophet: *The light of the moon itself,* he says, *will be like that of the sun, but the light of the sun will be sevenfold, Isaiah 30.* <note>The text cites Isaiah 62, but the quote is from Isaiah 30:26.</note> And he teaches this more clearly elsewhere when he says: *Your sun shall no longer set, nor your moon wane, for the Lord shall be your light, O Jerusalem, Isaiah 60.* John in the Apocalypse seems to agree with this speech, saying: *The City has no need of the sun or the moon to shine in it, for the brightness of GOD will illuminate it, and its lamp will be the Lamb.* From this it is declared that the spirit of Wisdom will be far more excellent than any brightness of sun or star. By laying aside the solar creature which it wore when it "placed its tabernacle in the sun," it will reveal itself in its own inaccessible splendor and light, which no mortal in this state of mortality can look upon; but when...

<summary>This page argues that the sun is an obedient servant of God, whose light is a physical manifestation of divine spirit. The author highlights the miraculous darkness at Christ's crucifixion as proof that the sun is subject to God's will rather than fixed Aristotelian laws.</summary>

### On the Efficient Cause of Meteors. 187

† When the righteous, like the sun (as Saint Matthew says <note>original: "vt D. Matthæus habet"; referring to Matthew 13:43.</note>), will shine in that kingdom of their Father, then they will see him with garments stripped away <note>A metaphor for the soul being freed from the physical body or the veil of material reality.</note> as he truly is, and so Alpha shall be turned into Omega; the beginning will coincide with its end. Just as things began in unity, so they shall have their end in unity; from God are all things, and into God all things shall return, because in him we live, move, and have our being (Acts 17:28 <note>The text cites Acts 17:9, but this famous phrase is found in 17:28.</note>). From him and in him is the life of all (John 1). He will be "all in all" then, when Christ shall have obtained the kingdom of the Father. He is the Father from whom all things come, and as the beginning is, such is the end. He alone is the one who works all things in all; He is the Father of all, who is over all, and through all, and in all; for he gives life to all things—indeed, he himself, needing nothing, gives life and breath and all things to everyone. Finally, from him and through him and in him are all things, to whom be praise and honor forever (1 Corinthians 15, 1 Corinthians 8, 2 Corinthians 5, Ephesians 4:6, 1 Timothy 6, Acts 17, Romans 11).

And in this, many of the philosophers who were occupied with the more hidden divine mysteries have agreed. Among them, the <term>Zohar</term> <note>A foundational work of Jewish mystical thought (Kabbalah).</note> says: all things are nothing but one in respect to GOD, though in respect to us they are many. Plato and Parmenides say that that which exists—insofar as it is in GOD and proceeds from him—is nothing but one. Hermes, in his <term>Emerald Tablet</term> <note>A legendary foundational text of Hermeticism and alchemy.</note>, says: "Just as all things were through the mediation of the One, so all things were born from this one by adaptation." And <term>Proclus</term> <note>A Greek Neoplatonist philosopher who influenced Christian theology.</note> says in his *Theological Problems*: "As all things proceed from the One alone, so also they hasten continually to return to that One." And these things find a greater peace and concord the more closely they approach it and participate with it.

Plato also speaks thus in his *Letters*: "All things proceed from the Highest, and strive with the greatest effort to return to him again, as it is in him that their final rest and the protection of their essence consists," and so on in other places.

By these things we have it confirmed that all things are, in truth, nothing but one, though they are many in the imagination of common men, whose habit it is to look upon those things which appear in an external manner, which seem to be and are no—

<meta>This page continues a discussion on the creation of the heavens, specifically addressing the origin of the sun and stars. The prefix "bi" suggests a continuation of a word from the previous page, likely "ubi" (where).</meta>

188                                Section I. Portion IV. Part II. Book IV. Member I.

...where, God created the sun, the moon, the stars, and other things for the service of all nations under heaven, <note>Original: Deuteronomy 4. This refers specifically to Deuteronomy 4:19, which warns against worshipping these bodies but acknowledges their creation for all people.</note> It does not say that He created the Sun by His word and then afterwards the other stars from the sun; rather, by His own word, according to His own specific ordering and will, He created the sun along with the others separately. From this, He also made each of them different from one another in shape, property, and position. Thus it came to pass that He calculated the number of the stars, and called as many as there are by their names—our great Lord, possessed of many strengths and <term>virtues</term> <note>In this context, "virtues" refers to the inherent powers or astrological influences the stars were believed to exert on the earthly world.</note>. By these names, the Prophet <note>Likely referring to the author of the Psalms, specifically Psalm 147:4-5, which describes God numbering and naming the stars.</note> seems to suggest that He assigned various names to them based on their various properties and powers; we are persuaded of this because, in the linking of the words, he says, "great is our Lord and of many powers."

In this same way, Adam is said to have given names to the beasts of the earth and the birds of the heaven—names that were, without a doubt, not frivolous or empty, but suited to the specific property of each creature. By these examples, we are reminded that all the stars in the heaven were created distinctly from the sun, and yet on the same day—or rather, it was as if they were created in the same moment...

On the Efficient Cause of <term>Meteors<note>In the 17th century, "meteors" referred to all atmospheric phenomena—including rain, snow, and wind—rather than just space rocks.</note></term>. 189

...[of] divine wisdom dwelling in the sun is sent forth to its own spark, which inhabits and animates the sphere of Saturn. Since this spark is the same in essence as that wisdom, it immediately wills and acts through its instrument according to what the source of its light has commanded. From there, it emits a ray of its will toward its likeness in the northern region, and immediately the North winds blow, producing snow, ice, or hail, and sometimes mixed with thunder and lightning. Hence it is said: *GOD, sending forth his word, sends snow like wool, and scatters frost like ashes; he casts forth ice like morsels; who can stand before his cold?* <note>original: "DEVS emittens sermonem suum niues emittit sicut lanam, & pruinam sicut cineres dispergit, eiicit gelu tanquam frusta, coram frigore eius quis consistat?"</note> Psalm 147:16. And elsewhere: *By his breath, the mighty GOD produces ice; when GOD breathes, the frost thickens,* etc. Job 37. <note>The original text cites Job 27, but the verse actually appears in Job 37:10.</note>
